Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.

Sources indicate that the Samsung S85H is great entry-level OLED TV that can compete with the best TVs of 2026. It offers a near-full feature set, with brilliant performance at a competitive price. While its closest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper at the moment, and arguably the better buy — as I found when I compared it and the S85H side-by-side — this is still a very capable TV.

Sources indicate that the S85H’s picture quality is excellent overall. It delivers punchy, vibrant colors, strong contrast, crisp, realistic textures and good motion handling. It does have a reflective screen, an issue the step-up Samsung S90H doesn’t suffer from, and there are sometimes black-crush issues in darker scenes, but the S85H’s picture is competitive with the best OLED TVs.

In a recent development, sound quality in the S85H is a mixed bag. It has great accuracy, and at times punchy bass, but generally its limited two-channel speaker system can only do so much. Sound feels contained to the back of the screen, and while there is some extension beyond the TV’s frame, it doesn’t offer what one of the best soundbars could. It’s fine for day-to-day viewing, but you’ll want a soundbar if you’re after a more cinematic experience.

For gaming, the S85H is a fantastic budget-OLED option. It has a suite full of features up there with the best gaming TVs — 4K 120Hz, FreeSync and G-Sync, HDR10+ gaming and ALLM — as well as ultra-low input lag and four HDMI 2.1 ports. Its performance is responsive and smooth, and it serves as a superb gaming TV.

Industry observers note that the S85H is good value for money. The 55-inch model I tested costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, putting it in the more affordable OLED bracket. While its nearest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper ($799 / £999 / AU$1,699 for the 55-inch), making it the better-value buy, the S85H still offers brilliant performance and features for the price, and that price is only going to get cheaper.

Recent findings suggest that the Samsung S85H is the entry-level model in Samsung’s 2026 OLED TV lineup, sitting below the mid-range S90H and flagship S95H/S99H. It’s available in sizes 48-83-inch, with the 55-inch model I tested launching for $1,499 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 in May-June 2026 (depending on region).

Since its release, the S85H’s prices have dropped across all sizes and in all regions. The 55-inch is now available (November 2026) for around $999 / £999 / AU$1,899, though you can find it for less at some retailers in some regions. The rival LG B6 55-inch is cheaper at the moment in the US and Australia, costing $799 / £999 / AU$1,699, but it’s likely that the ‘cheaper’ title will change hands a few times during these TV’s life cycles.

Closer to 100% is better. Taken using a colorimeter and test pattern generator.

In a recent development, A lower score is better. Taken using a colorimeter and test pattern generator.

According to recent reports, lower is better. Taken using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Video Signal Lag Tester.

Sources indicate that the S85H uses a WOLED panel, the same one as in the rival LG B6 and the same as the step-up S90H, though some sizes are reported to have QD-OLED. The S90H benefits from the upgraded NQ4 AI Gen 3 Processor, which allows for higher brightness and better color performance, while the S85H has the older NQ4 AI Gen 2 Processor built in. The Gen 2 is no slouch, though, and supports picture features such as 4K AI Upscaling and Real Depth Enhancer Pro.

The S85H supports HDR10+, including the new HDR10+ Advanced, HDR10 and HLG HDR formats, but as usual with Samsung TVs, there’s no support for Dolby Vision.

In a recent development, for audio, the S85H has a 2-channel, 20W speaker system with support for Dolby Atmos. A number of AI sound features are included too, such as AI Sound Pro, as well as Object Tracking Sound (OTS) Lite. Q-Symphony, where the TV’s speakers can be used in conjunction with a supported Samsung soundbar, is also featured.

The S85H supports 4K 120Hz, full VRR including AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming, which works across all of the S85H’s four HDMI 2.1 ports. There’s also a Game Hub, where cloud gaming apps are housed.

In a recent development, tizen serves as the S85H’s smart TV platform, supporting all major streaming apps such as Netflix and Disney Plus. Tizen also features the Vision AI companion, which uses multiple AI agents to make content and even lifestyle recommendations you may ask such as recommended places for dinner.

In a recent development, as the S85H uses a standard WOLED panel, its brightness doesn’t match that of step-up OLEDs like the S90H or LG C6. In my testing it clocked a peak HDR brightness (on a 10% window pattern) of 833 nits and 854 nits in Filmmaker Mode and Standard respectively. Those scores put it in line with the rival LG B6E (which hit 808 nits and 727 nits in the same respective modes), but are much lower than those achieved by the step-up S90H, which measured 1,689 and 1677 in the same two modes.

As for fullscreen brightness, the S85H hit just over 150 nits in both Filmmaker and Standard, which is about right for WOLED, but it’s still a significant drop compared to rival mini-LEDs such as the TCL QM7L/C7L, which hit over 600 nits. This means the S85H can struggle in bright rooms, and without an effective anti-glare coating, dark scenes can be hard to watch in brighter conditions, so this TV is best suited to viewing in ambient or dark conditions. Samsung’s step-up S90H OLED, on the other hand, easily handles bright rooms.

Sources indicate that starting with SDR content, the S85H does a good job of upscaling textures. Watching various programs on Samsung TV Plus, textures did look cleaner and sharpened than you’d get on some standard LED and mini-LED TVs, and with bolder colors. While the step-up S90H did a better job with upscaling, the S85H’s was still impressive nonetheless.

Switching to 4K HDR content, the S85H delivers excellent colors. Watching Elemental on Disney Plus in HDR10+, the bold oranges of the fire people and blues of the water people pop throughout the movie, even in the slightly dimmer Filmmaker Mode. Putting the S85H in Movie mode adds more brightness and a bit more color depth which works well for the animation. As Ember runs across multi-colored minerals, colors have a nice shine to them, showing the S85H’s punchy HDR highlights.

Watching a live-action movie, The Sound of Music, the S85H indicates it can render realistic-looking colors too. The green fields and blue skies of Austria look wonderfully natural whenever they’re on screen, and the S85H shows true-to-life skin tones in the people as well.

Measuring the S85H’s HDR color-gamut coverage, it registered 97.9% of the UHDA-P3 and 73.4% of the BT.2020 color spaces. These numbers are about right for a WOLED TV, but are starting to fall behind those of more premium OLEDs and RGB mini-LED TVs. Still the S85H’s colors were great overall.

The S85H also demonstrates strong contrast. In The Batman, which includes lots of scenes with lights cutting through the dark environments, such as in the Batcave and in aerial shots of Gotham, the S85H shows an excellent balance between these light and dark tones to create an authentic image. The same is true in Project Hail Mary, with both shots of space and scenes inside the ship showing the S85H’s powerful contrast and deep black levels.

It has been revealed that shadow detail is also great, with details and textures legible in challenging dark scenes, such as frames on the wall of Mayor Mitchell’s house in The Batman. I did notice during some particularly dark shots that the S85H was prone to some black crush, even in pitch-black viewing conditions. For the most part however, its contrast was impressive.

The S85H also demonstrated crisp textures in nearly every scene I watched, with people in particular looking true-to-life. This 3D-like level of detail was one of the S85H’s strengths over the LG B6E when I tested the two side-by-side, showcasing the effectiveness of the Real Depth Enhancer feature.

Industry observers note that finally, the S85H demonstrated very good motion for both sports and movies, although some setup is required. I found setting blur reduction to 3 and judder reduction between 3-5 (depending on the content and how fluid you want your picture) was the most effective. There were still some motion artefacts when watching a soccer match on Prime Video, with some blurring of textures in some shots, but the S85H was mostly effective.

The S85H’s two-channel, 20W speaker system isn’t strong enough to allow you to skimp on a soundbar if you want powerful and immersive sound for action-heavy movies and shows, and doesn’t match up to step-up TVs, but is mostly fine for day-to-day viewing and some movies.

It has been revealed that watching the Batmobile scene from The Batman, the S85H’s strength lay in the accuracy of sound, showing how effective the OTS Lite system was. As the Batmobile swerved through traffic, screeching tires and car horns were mapped with real accuracy between the sound and action on the screen.

Impacts also generated some nice punch. As the Batmobile clatters through a barricade, the sound of scraping metal had some weight to it, and as the Batmobile’s engine revved, there was some punchy bass. However, when I pushed the volume, the bass did seem to fizzle out, and high-end sound could be a little harsh.

Sources indicate that while I did hear some extension of sound from the frame of the screen, particularly during the aforementioned swerving manoeuvres, the sound felt contained to the rear of the screen, making it feel like the viewing experience was lacking some depth. Speech was mostly clear throughout, but could get lost at times. Again, you want a cinematic experience, I’d hook up a soundbar.

In a recent development, the most striking thing visually about the S85H is how thin it is compared to rival TVs in this price range. It has a sleek, metal frame and a razor-thin depth that suggest a more premium price. Even its rear panel is fairly trim, with only a small bump to accommodate the connection ports.

Industry observers note that for the 55-inch model I tested, two plastic feet were supplied which, while they felt a little cheap, were very easy to install. You can choose between two positions for the feet, narrow and wide, with the latter being very useful if you have a soundbar. The TV is also very light for a 55-inch model, but still felt sturdy when placed on a TV stand.

It has been revealed that the S85H comes with Samsung’s SolarCell remote, which offers solar and USB-C charging. Its small size means it could get lost quite easily, but it feels light in the hand, and offers all the usual options (streaming app shortcuts, settings, power and volume).

Samsung’s own Tizen serves as the smart TV platform for the S85H, and with it come a host of AI features via the Vision AI companion, which uses AI agents to help with content recommendation, lifestyle advice, and more general questions you might ask of a smart assistant (how long is a day on Jupiter was one of the example prompts). There are also a host of AI Picture and sound features via the AI Mode settings (found under the Advanced Features menu), such as AI Soccer Mode and Adaptive Sound Pro.

Tizen’s main three hubs on the main screen — For You, Live, and Game and Apps — host recommended content, live TV, gaming content and a general apps page respectively. These pages are generally laid out well, but do have banner ads that take up about a third of the page. I also found Samsung TV Plus autoplays on the For You page and can sometimes take over the page if left idle, which can be frustrating.

You can choose from a good number of picture settings, all housed in logical places within the settings menu. Some of these settings, such as Auto HDR Remastering for SDR content, can be effective. Sound settings are a bit more limited, and I’d have liked more than two sound mode options. Tizen is a solid interface overall, but doesn’t quite match up to LG’s webOS or Roku for ease-of-use.

In a recent development, the S85H is an excellent choice for gaming. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, perfect for multiple consoles, and all of these support 4K 120Hz, full VRR including FreeSync and G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming. The featured Game Hub is a useful home for all things gaming, and offers quick access to a connected console and cloud gaming apps.

Industry observers note that the S85H’s input lag registered 9.2ms at 4K 60Hz and 4.5ms at 1080p 120Hz, the latter of which is one of the lowest scores I’ve seen. This translates into actual gaming too. Playing Battlefield V, motion felt incredibly smooth with razor-sharp response times — extremely useful when faced with tons of enemies.

Picture-wise, the S85H’s brilliant quality is great for gaming. The colors of autumnal trees during one mission really popped on screen, while textures were very crisp, and, during night-time missions, black tones were deep and contrast was strong.

The 55-inch S85H I tested currently costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, which is very good for a budget OLED. Considering the features and performance it delivers, it’s great value for money overall.

According to recent reports, right now, its major rival, the LG B6, is cheaper in most places. A 55-inch LG B6 (or in some cases LG B6E, which isn’t markedly different from the standard B6) costs around $799 / £999 / AU$1,699. The B6 offers near-identical features and performance, so right now it’s the better deal.

It has been revealed that the Samsung S90H is a notable step-up over the S85H, offering higher brightness, better picture quality and an anti-reflection screen for bright-room viewing. The 55-inch model costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,999, so if you’re in the UK and US and can stretch your budget, it’s worth the upgrade. Still, the S85H is good value overall, and I expect its prices will drop and fall more in line with those of the B6 as time goes on.

You can stretch your budget to the Samsung S90HIn some sizes, the step-up Samsung S90H is only a little pricier and its big upgrade over the S85H, with an anti-glare screen and higher brightness.

Industry observers note that dolby Vision, HDR10+. HDR10, HLG.

In a recent development, LG B6The LG B6 is the S85H's closest rival and offers similar performance and features, but for slightly cheaper. The B6 has richer colors and Dolby Vision, while the S85H has crisper textures. Both deliver strong contrast as well, and are full kitted out for gaming. This comes down to whichever model is cheaper.

TCL QM7L/C7LThe TCL QM7L (US)/C7L (UK/Aus) is the brand's mid-range SDQ mini-LED. While the S85H delivers better contrast and textures, the QM7L/C7L is much brighter and offers competitive gaming features and performance for a similar price. Pick the QM7L/C7L if you have a brighter room.

Read our TCL QM7L review and TCL C7L review.

I first started my testing of the Samsung S85H with casual viewing to assess which picture mode was best, landing on Filmmaker and Movie modes for movies and TV and Standard for sports and broadcast TV.

I then tested the S85H using reference 4K Blu-ray, analyzing its color, contrast, textures and detail and motion, while also using SDR sports and daytime TV to analyze its upscaling capabilities.

Once these tests were complete, I took measurements using a Murido Six G 8K test pattern generator, a Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer profiled with the a Klein K-10A colorimeter, and recorded the measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.

I tested the S85H's brightness, measuring on a white window pattern in sizes 1-100%, with a focus on 10% peak and 100% fullscreen brightness, in both SDR and HDR.

I then measured its color and grayscale accuracy in SDR using Delta-E averages (the margin for error between the test pattern signal and what's displayed on screen).

Next was HDR color gamut coverage, where I sued the UHDA-P3 (the color space used for 4K Blu-ray and digital cinema releases) and BT.2020 (becoming more commonly used) color spaces.

It has been revealed that I also measured the S85H's HDR EOTF, using 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits targets, which demonstrates the TV's accuracy between light and dark tones. I also measured its Spectral Power Distribution, which measures its color performance.

Finally, I measured its input lag in both 4K 60Hz and 1080p 120Hz using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester.

#463. What Does A 'No Thru Trucks' Road Sign Mean?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (447 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

What Does A 'No Thru Trucks' Road Sign Mean?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most vehicles travel anywhere between 25 and 80 mph, so drivers should ideally be able to understand a road sign's meaning within two seconds.
  • According to recent reports, as the first and final words imply, "No Thru Trucks" signs are meant to restrict road access for trucks.
  • In a recent development, let's construct an example to help you understand how these signs function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most vehicles travel anywhere between 25 and 80 mph, so drivers should ideally be able to understand a road sign's meaning within two seconds. However, some traffic signs are confusing. Usually, these signs provide instructions for the road in the immediate vicinity, but one sign acts as a "do not enter" notification that only applies to specific drivers.

According to recent reports, as the first and final words imply, "No Thru Trucks" signs are meant to restrict road access for trucks. But what is a "Thru Truck" anyway? It isn't some obscure electric truck; it just means that trucks can't use the roads with this sign unless their destination is somewhere along the path. In other words, "No Thru Trucks" signs are just "Local Traffic Only" road signs designed specifically for commercial and construction trucks. You can usually find these signs in residential areas and near (but not necessarily on) highways.

In a recent development, let's construct an example to help you understand how these signs function. Say you are an Amazon delivery driver. You start your route in the warehouse with all your packages and while driving, you come across a street with a "No Thru Trucks" sign. Check what deliveries you need to make that day. If you don't have a package to deliver on that street or a street connected to it, you should find another route, no matter how much more time and gas it will require. If you are supposed to deliver a package there, you are allowed to enter the road.

It has been revealed that depending on where you drive, you could spend your entire life without seeing a "No Thru Trucks" sign. Instead, places might use alternatives, such as "No Trucks Except Local Deliveries" or "Commercial Vehicles Prohibited." Different song, same tune.

As a general rule of thumb, if you drive a commercial truck and ignore a "No Thru Trucks" sign without having a delivery in the area, you might face a fine and court time. The restrictions that dictate truck traffic are from local government, which sets up the signs and catches violators. And that's assuming the sign is installed in the correct location, because while it is rare, sometimes road workers make mistakes.

Even if a "No Thru Trucks" sign is placed seemingly in the middle of nowhere, many drivers follow its instructions anyway. Residents who are sick and tired of hearing trucks speed by their homes might request the sign's installation, so its presence is a regulation meant as a way to give people who live nearby some peace and quiet. Is that really so much to ask?

Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running.
  • This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck. German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024, which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the matter wasn’t caught earlier.

This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still.

Industry observers note that aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few significant tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.

One of the more controversial aspects of Galaxy AI's 2024 launch (besides its uselessness) was that Samsung would only keep Galaxy AI free for a limited time.

Recent findings suggest that however, Samsung quietly postponed the December 2025 deadline, and Galaxy AI remained free for everyone. But recent reports indicate that Samsung is preparing an AI Premium subscription, and if Google's AI subscription is anything to go by, I guarantee I'll be using Galaxy AI less.

A report from Sammy Guru revealed placeholder images and code strings that suggested Samsung is preparing and testing a upcoming AI Premium subscription.

Recent findings suggest that this subscription will give Galaxy AI consumers more access to existing and new features. According to the reports, the free plan will include the following features, labeled as "Standard AI":.

In a recent development, currently, these features offer unlimited access, with a couple of small exceptions. However, when AI Premium launches, they will be subject to usage limits.

On top of extra usage, the premium subscription will grant access to the following features:.

A later report from SamMobile found that Samsung might be testing different subscription tiers.

Overall, it seems like Samsung is trying to recoup its losses by charging users. But when it's not offering much to begin with, why would anyone pay? Certainly not me.

It's been two years since Samsung graced us with Galaxy AI, and since then it has received a host of upgrades. But is it useful?

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Samsung revealed which AI tools in its Galaxy AI suite are the most popular. Ironically, the top feature was Circle to Search, a Google feature that Samsung can't lock behind a paywall.

The next most popular feature was Photo Assist, which appears on Samsung's list of "Standard AI" features it will add usage limits to.

Sources indicate that after you take a photo on a supported Galaxy phone, Photo Assist suggests a selection of edits to improve your photos. These suggestions can range from simple crops to generative AI tweaks.

The problem is that while these suggestions can be useful, Samsung slaps a visible watermark on any images it edits. You can implement the suggestions yourself, but there isn't much to them beyond what a basic photography guide can teach you.

Then there's Now Brief. It's impressive how Samsung has barely managed to improve this feature. Every time I see it, it tells me something like "It's raining. Bring an umbrella.".

Unless you live in a house without windows, its weather reports are completely irrelevant. Then there are the random news articles and health information. None of this information needs an AI to power it.

In short, Galaxy AI is a gimmick, and if I'm forced to pay to use it, I'll just stop using it altogether.

When I bought my Pixel 10 Pro last year, Google generously gave me a one-year trial of Google AI Pro.

Recent findings suggest that through this subscription, I got four times higher access to Gemini, plus access to Gemini 4 Argon and Deep Research. Then there was Gemini in Workspace apps, expanded access to Gemini Notebook, Google Flow, and more.

Nearly a year later, I use none of these features regularly, and I haven't come close to hitting the increased Gemini access.

Gemini has made a mess of summarizing my documents so many times that I'd rather pay Google not to show it while I'm working.

Samsung seems to be modeling its AI Premium subscription after Google's AI Pro prepares. But at the end of the day, all the useful features (like Circle to Search) remain free, and all the gimmicks are locked behind a paywall.

Google hasn't figured out how to add value to its AI prepares for everyday users, so what chance does Samsung have?

Samsung never revealed why it kept postponing the end of free Galaxy AI access, but I suspect it was to lock as many people in to using the features.

Recent findings suggest that the idea of getting people used to a free tier to encourage adoption of a paid feature is nothing upcoming. But when Galaxy AI is still such poor value, I certainly won't be paying Samsung a penny to use its "premium" AI features.

The Pro Tool Innovation Awards bill itself as the "largest and broadest awards program in the power & hand tool, accessory, and fastener industries." The program was launched by Pro Tool Reviews in 2013 to handpick and highlight some of the best tools on the market, based on their features, durability, ergonomics, price, and other essentials that matter to customers. A panel of experts and industry professionals judges the tools each year.

Sources indicate that this year marked the 14th year of the award program, and the winners included products from some of the major tool brands, including several winning titles achieved by Milwaukee Tools. The winners included a circular saw kit, an impact wrench, and other tools that beat the competitors in terms of durability, performance, and other factors to top the list in their respective categories. Nonetheless, there are a few things you should consider before buying Milwaukee tools, such as the product's warranty information, features, and more.

Winning the title in the category of air hammers, the M18 Fuel Striker Hammer Chisel Kit is integrated with a Powerstate motor that can deliver a striking force of up to 7 joules to help separate old and rusty components when performing automotive repairs, such as suspension teardowns, ball joint removals, wheel pin removal, and more. Basically, the tool delivers repeated hammering force using a chisel attachment at one of three speeds, with a maximum of 3,000 BPM.

The RedLink Plus Intelligence technology featured in this hammer gun protects it against overload, overheating, and over-discharge, while there's also an LED light added at the base of the design for workspace illumination. Moreover, it has a .401-inch round-shank twist chuck, which securely connects the attachment to the tool without requiring additional tools.

The Pro Tool Innovation Awards described this Milwaukee power tool as "literally the world's first cordless air hammer specifically designed for automotive applications." For those looking to buy the tool, it is available at Home Depot for $749, with the kit including a hammer chisel bit, a flat chisel bit, and an M18 RedLithium XC5 battery.

The M12 Fuel 1/4″ Extended Die Grinder is the winner in the Cordless Die Grinder category at the awards. It is a multi-purpose tool that can grind, polish, and cut, as well as remove old or unwanted paint, rust, and other material from metal surfaces. Powered by a Powerstate motor, it can generate up to 20,000 RPM, though you can pick one of the four speed ranges. The 4-inch shaft design helps the tool work in confined spaces, while a 1/4-inch collet makes it compatible with a range of accessories.

There's also a push-button spindle lock that keeps the tool locked while performing accessory changes using a simple wrench. The cordless power tool can fit a 2-inch cutting wheel and 3-inch sanding accessories. Also, it comes with a built-in LED light to keep the work area well-lit. "There are a lot of die grinders on the market, but Milwaukee Tool's brings the innovation of an unusually high power-to-weight ratio," the awards page remarked. You can grab it at Home Depot for $249.

The M18 Fuel 3/4″ High Torque Impact Wrench is the winner in the Cordless Impact Wrenches category and is designed for mechanics and professionals who want to perform high-level fastening or loosening jobs. Built with the ability to produce up to 2,000 foot-pounds of nut-busting torque, it can remove old and stubborn lugs and bolts from vehicles and machinery. Meanwhile, the peak fastening torque goes up to 1,800 foot-pounds to tackle large fasteners.

#455. What Are The Disadvantages Of Pontoon Boats?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1090 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

What Are The Disadvantages Of Pontoon Boats?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the pontoon boat has been a staple of recreational boating for decades now.
  • Pontoon boats are particularly popular for parties.
  • These boats can make for a really fun day on the water, but they aren't great for everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the pontoon boat has been a staple of recreational boating for decades now. Though its origins aren't definitive, it's believed the first pontoon boat was invented back in 1952 by a man named Ambrose Weeres. He took a flat piece of wooden deck and tied two hollow aluminum tubes to each side to keep it afloat. Though it's been refined over the years, that's still the basic idea of the pontoon boat. Nowadays, they're no longer made out of wood, and you'll typically have a motor and modern driving controls as well.

Pontoon boats are particularly popular for parties. Because they are generally these wide, flat surfaces, there's a lot of room for many people to be milling about on the deck, and the hollow metal tubes keeping it afloat also offer a good deal of balance as well. Because the design is so simple, there are many different ways you can use the boat's big, open space. Of course, you could also want a pontoon boat for other reasons, be it some relaxing fishing or taking the family out to the middle of a lake for a swim.

These boats can make for a really fun day on the water, but they aren't great for everything. The design of pontoon boats can make it difficult to do certain things other boats can do on the water or actually hinder the more casual experience they're designed for. Here, we're going to look at several of the possible downsides to using a pontoon boat that may make you want to choose a different design when you want to go out on the water.

In a recent development, few people can resist the thrill of driving a boat really fast on the water. When all you have is open water surrounding you, you want to push the capabilities of that boat and feel the wind in your face. Beyond that, many people enjoy water sports like water skiing or wakeboarding. If you're going out to engage in these activities with a large group of people, the natural instinct may be to get a pontoon boat because it will comfortably hold everyone. However, these boats put somewhat of a limit on how fast you're actually able to go.

Sources indicate that pontoon boats typically cruise somewhere between 20 and 30 mph. You certainly can water ski, wakeboard, or tube at these speeds, and for families, kids, or inexperienced people, these speeds are perfectly adequate for a fun time. However, if you're going out on the water looking for some serious thrills, a conventional pontoon boat might not deliver.

For these people, a V-hull speedboat is the preferable option. With a high-quality engine, you can reach speeds up to 50 or 60 mph with these boats. Plus, their design gives them more maneuverability, making it easier to take sharp turns for even more excitement. Speedboats designed for water sports are also better equipped for towing activities, allowing for a better experience when you're being pulled behind the boat. The speed of pontoon boats may be plenty exciting for some, but others may want a lot more from their thrill-seeking.

According to recent reports, one of the major benefits of a pontoon boat is its steadiness. Since its buoyancy is at the opposite sides of the boat rather than at one point in the center, you won't experience as much rocking on the water as you would with a more traditional V-hull design. Some pontoon boats even have a third metal tube along their center, called a tritoon, for even better stability. That's why pontoon boats make for such great boats for parties or entertaining, as deck-focused activities won't be disrupted all that much by the constant back-and-forth swaying of the boat.

Industry observers note that however, a pontoon boat's steadiness is really only achievable in calm or minimally choppy waters. Once the waters really start rocking, whether from inclement weather or even the wake of a larger boat passing by, you could be in a world of trouble. These boats are designed to be flat surfaces that float on top of the water. If water starts flying up onto the boat, you could find yourself with a lot of very wet passengers. If the boat takes on too much water, it could become swamped, potentially causing it to capsize or sink.

A V-hull design is much better equipped to handle rough waters. That centralized buoyancy that is actually beneath the surface allows it to cut through waves far easier. So, if you're planning on going out on the water with a pontoon boat, make sure you double-check the weather conditions and stay away from other boats as best you can. If that's not possible, choose a different kind of boat.

Industry observers note that it's a little tricky to figure out where exactly you should put the motor on a pontoon boat. Most designs opt for an outboard motor. This means that the motor is externally attached to the stern of the boat, fully exposed to the air. Some of the coolest pontoon boats have inboard motors inside the hull, but that's rarer. In terms of driving the boat, there's no issue with an outboard motor in the slightest. Where the issue can come in is with how much noise it produces.

With an inboard motor, you're naturally going to have some muffling of the sound, as the parts of the motor are either underwater or concealed within the hull. An outboard motor being exposed means that there's less of a barrier to block the sound, which can result in a louder experience on the water. Because you likely want to use a pontoon boat for entertaining purposes, a loud outboard motor could make it difficult for people to comfortably talk to one another, drown out music playing onboard, or just be a general irritant to passengers.

Sources indicate that some modern motors have been able to decrease the amount of sound they produce. However, if you're renting a pontoon boat, you have no control over what motor is affixed to the stern, and if you own a boat, that means purchasing an expensive newly introduced motor just for sound control. If your pontoon boat party is okay with dealing with the noise until you get out to a certain part of the water to turn the engine off, great. If not, you could have a lot of people yelling at one another to be heard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's fair to say that the headline-grabbing arrival of the iPhone Duo has made the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feel a little less shiny than they otherwise might have.

Indeed, upon opening my new iPhone 18 Pro Max and restoring my data from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro Max, it was hard not to feel a little disappointed by the lack of bells and whistles on Apple’s latest flagship.

That’s probably to be expected from a single-generation upgrade — and, to be fair, I don’t usually swap phones after just one year — but there is one feature that’s caught my eye during my time with my iPhone 18 Pro Max, and it’s been a game-changer for my everyday life: Apple’s latest C2 modem.

I’ve been using iPhones for around two decades, but since moving to a more remote area in 2021, I have noticed that my mobile signal has been incredibly inconsistent (on some days, it's absolutely awful).

According to recent reports, in truth, this spotty signal has been the bane of my digital life, both as a small business owner and a parent — I could be in the same spot on different days of the week and experience completely different levels of coverage. Worse yet, my recent iPhones have had a tendency to display a weak 5G signal when, in fact, there's been no signal at all.

With the iPhone 18 Pro Max, however, I’m seeing drastic improvements in signal strength just about everywhere I go.

Industry observers note that rather than awkwardly trying to fumble through phone tasks using train or café WiFi, I’ve actually been able to use my paid-for data plan consistently, which has made my iPhone 18 Pro Max feel less like a very expensive iPod and more like a piece of cutting-edge computing. And that’s all thanks to the C2 modem.

Apple debuted its C1 chip in the iPhone 16e, and the C2 makes its debut in the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.

In a recent development, the C2 features in every iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo model sold worldwide, but only in iPhone 18 Pro Max models sold outside of the US. If you’re in the US and have Apple's larger Pro model, you’ve got Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem.

Apple hasn't yet disclosed why this is the case, but we suspect it's a result of contractual obligation (we know it's not a technical limitation, since the C2 modem features in all other iPhone 18 Pro Max models, and indeed even in iPhone 18 Pro models sold within the US).

Sources indicate that as you'd expect from a numbered hardware upgrade, the C2 modem improves on the C1 in several ways. It adds full mmWave support alongside the C1's existing sub-6GHz 5G capabilities, and consumes less energy than its predecessor.

There are other iPhone 18 Pro-specific advantages, too: “If an iPhone encounters congested data networks, the phone’s [A20 Pro] processor can signal to the modem which traffic is the most time-sensitive and put it ahead of other data transfers,” Apple told Reuters of its C2 modem.

According to recent reports, thankfully, I’m not alone in feeling the benefits of Apple’s C2 modem. Plenty of other iPhone 18 Pro people have found that the addition of this small feature is leading to much better 5G connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that of course, as this Reddit post mentions, a new modem will only help if you’re in an area covered by 5G in the first place. Luckily for me, my home isn't so remote as to rely on older-generation networks, but that's worth bearing in mind if you live out in the sticks (Apple's hardware wizardry can only work so much magic).

And don't get me wrong: a new 5G modem is hardly the most exciting upgrade on a phone that costs at least $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099, and perhaps it's the least we should expect from Apple when the year-on-year upgrades are so limited elsewhere.

Still, after years of awkwardly lifting my iPhone into the sky in the hope of securing stronger signal — or just simply not using my iPhone at all — this small improvement, combined with improved battery life and the ever-higher performance ceiling of this year’s chip upgrade, has made me appreciate the iPhone 18 Pro Max more than I originally anticipated.

2026 is still very much an ‘iPhone S-year’, though.

#453. No, A 4-Cylinder Isn't The Same As A 4-Stroke Engine: Here's What's Different

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (810 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

No, A 4-Cylinder Isn't The Same As A 4-Stroke Engine: Here's What's Different

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We drive in cars and trucks every day, but many of us have a limited understanding of how the mechanisms that power them actually work.
  • There are several different types of combustion engines out there, and they all work a little differently.
  • According to recent reports, these are actually completely different specifications, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We drive in cars and trucks every day, but many of us have a limited understanding of how the mechanisms that power them actually work. Some people go their whole lives without considering what controls their car beyond the gas, brake, and steering wheel. Learning about how engines work can often seem intimidating, as the terminology can sometimes be a bit confusing to the mechanically uninitiated. Of course, you don't need to know all the ins and outs of automotive engineering in order to drive a car, but you may wish to have a better understanding of what exactly these motor specifications are saying when it comes time to choose your next vehicle.

There are several different types of combustion engines out there, and they all work a little differently. For instance, you might hear the terms "four-cylinder engine" and "four-stroke engine," and understandably wonder if these two descriptions mean the same thing. They sound similar, and they're closely related in terms of the parts of the engine that they're referring to. A lot of modern car brands have 2.0L 4-cylinder engines, and virtually all modern passenger vehicles use four-stroke engines.

According to recent reports, these are actually completely different specifications, however. One refers to the physical design of the engine itself, while the other refers to the way that the piston and crankshaft move during each individual power cycle. Understanding the difference between these two can help you gain a better understanding of how combustion engines work and what manufacturers are referring to when they use these terms.

Sources indicate that to understand what a four-cylinder engine is, we first need to take a look inside the engine block. At its core, a gas engine is essentially a metal housing containing mechanical components that turn the concussive force of combusting fuel into rotational motion. Every gas engine has a certain number of cylinders. These are cylindrical holes bored into the solid metal block (or blocks). Inside each cylinder, you'll find a piston, intake and exhaust valves, a spark plug, and a fuel injector (or intake port in carbureted engines). A piston is essentially a heavy metal plug that fits snugly inside the cylinder. The combustion cycle taking place in the section of the cylinder that is above the piston is what generates the energy to move the piston downward toward the crankshaft, creating the force required to rotate the crankshaft, which all of the pistons are connected to.

Some engines, such as those found in most push mowers and some motorcycles, might only have a single cylinder while others may have over a dozen. As you might have guessed from the name, a four-cylinder engine is an engine with four cylinders. There are many different kinds of four-cylinder engines, including inline-fours, flat-fours, and V4s. These terms refer to the way the four cylinders are oriented. Different engines will also offer different cylinder sizes. Engines with larger cylinders will offer more fuel displacement, which has a direct correlation to the amount of power and torque that the vehicle is able to produce. There are several pros and cons to four-cylinder engines. They typically don't generate as much power as engines that contain six or eight cylinders, but they're also usually lighter, more fuel-efficient, and cheaper to maintain.

Now that we've established that the number of cylinders refers to the physical hardware inside of the engine, let's take a look at what the term "stroke" means on an engine. There is a physical design aspect to this as well, but the term generally refers less to the layout of the engine and has a lot more to do with the way the pistons and crankshaft move during the combustion cycle.

A combustion cycle consists of four phases: intake, compression, combustion, and exhaust. The intake is when the fuel mixture is sent into the combustion chamber; compression is when the piston pushes up on the fuel in the chamber; combustion is when this fuel is ignited, pushing the piston back down; and exhaust is when the spent fuel is ventilated from the chamber. The components in the engine react differently depending on whether the engine is a two-stroke or four-stroke engine.

Two-stroke engines complete this cycle in just two strokes of the piston: once during intake and compression, and once during the combustion and exhaust phases. In simpler machines, like dirt bikes, boats, and power tools, these require oil to be mixed into the fuel and are typically used. Four-stroke engines are designed to make the piston move on each of the four phases, requiring twice as many strokes of the piston per combustion cycle. They're generally more fuel efficient, cleaner burning, run cooler, and last longer. Four-stroke engines are used in the vast majority of modern passenger vehicles, regardless of the number of cylinders the engine has.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer.
  • The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the important details.
  • The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer. The moniker came from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ), who have confirmed a fight against this crime wave, starting with the seizure of associated cloud infrastructure. According to the DoJ, North Korea is behind these attacks, stealing cryptocurrency to fund its government.

The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the important details. The agency's techs seized "cloud-based infrastructure," containing 900 videos of targeted victims. FaceStealer is an advanced form of spear-phishing, complete with AI deepfakes, usage of the victims' contact networks and personal information, and carefully orchestrated preparation — sometimes months in advance.

The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts. The largest heist attributed to FaceStealer is the recent Binance hack that saw thieves make out the proverbial door with over $5 billion (most of it thankfully frozen and/or recovered), but far from the only one.

Sources indicate that the FBI attributes about $400m in stolen cryptocurrency to the campaign, and importantly, also notes that the hackers have repeatedly tried to sneak into open-source software, chiefly Javascript/NPM modules and Rust crates. Despite not being mentioned by name, one example hack is almost certainly the Axios compromise from March 2026. The Node/Javascript library sees about 100 million downloads a week, and temporarily contained a remote-access tool — thankfully for only a few hours.

Jason Sayayman, the Axios developer in question, got hooked by an attacker posing as a legitimate firm interested in hiring him. The malfeasants replicated the CEO's persona, created a Slack workspace with legitimate-looking channels, then invited him to a Teams meeting with multiple "people.".

This modus operandi is what the FBI warns about. According to the bureau, FaceStealers start by getting access to a person's communication application(s), then lifting all previous conversations, contact lists, and, most importantly, stealthily recording video of them and/or their contacts. The footage and information will then be used to catch the actual targeted victim, who'll often be sent offers for jobs or investment opportunities.

According to recent reports, the victim will eventually be invited to a Zoom or Teams meeting that's actually hosted on an attacker-controlled server, with a typo-squatted domain like "uu01webzoom.us" or "teams.livemeet.us". The meeting will often have deepfaked AI participants and/or previous meeting recordings playing, granting the event an air of legitimacy — particularly because conversations leading up to this point will contain real information and context.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At some point, though, there will be some sort of "technical problem," and the victim will be prompted to install an "update" or software to fix the problem, which is loaded with malware. From there, the attackers have free rein over the victim's computer and data, and will siphon off browser sessions, CI/CD passwords, and all manners of access credentials to eventually get access to cryptocurrency wallets — or just use this information to find a juicier target, like the poor Binance developer through which Binance's hot wallets were broken into.

The FBI notes that the above scenario may play out in multiple cycles until the attackers reach their intended target, collecting loads of precious video and information along the way to make the final strike much more convincing.

I asked Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude to spot Amazon scams

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon took down more than 70,000 phishing websites and 14,000 scam phone numbers in 2025.
  • In a recent development, with Black Friday deals everywhere, scam emails will likely become even more rampant.
  • I gave the free tiers of Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude 20 emails and texts: 15 modeled on scams the FTC and Amazon have warned about, and five written like real Amazon messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon took down more than 70,000 phishing websites and 14,000 scam phone numbers in 2025.

In a recent development, with Black Friday deals everywhere, scam emails will likely become even more rampant. So, I decided to test whether your AI chatbot can catch these scam emails for you.

I gave the free tiers of Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude 20 emails and texts: 15 modeled on scams the FTC and Amazon have warned about, and five written like real Amazon messages.

All three models performed well at the start, but only one could reliably tell real from fake. Let me explain.

I started the test with 15 scam messages mixed with five written like actual Amazon messages.

The scams included fake order confirmations, Prime renewal threats, refund phishing, a WhatsApp "Amazon recruiter" message, a gift card demand, and an Instagram DM asking for my password.

Sources indicate that the three tools got all 20 correct. They flagged the scams and identified the legitimate messages without raising false alarms.

It has been revealed that I also tried a pattern scammers love: a text with the link amazon.com.order-review[.]net. The amazon.com at the beginning makes it look legit.

But the real domain is order-review[.]net. All the tools flagged it and correctly explained why.

Claude gave the most practical next steps. It mentioned reporting scam texts to 7726, the US carrier spam number.

Meanwhile, ChatGPT cited Amazon's help pages, while Gemini leaned on forum posts.

In my first test, I sent all 20 messages together in one prompt.

For this one, I used single messages in latest private chats: an Amazon sign-in alert from account-patch@amazon.com with no links, and a refund email that linked to amazon.com.

Gemini first said it was impossible to tell for certain. In a second run, it said the same email was almost certainly a phishing scam and called the Houston sign-in location a fear tactic.

Recent findings suggest that then I tried the refund email. Gemini gave no verdict and just sent general safety tips.

Like Gemini, Claude initially stated it couldn't verify the sign-in email from the text alone.

It has been revealed that but the second time, it said to treat it as suspicious, whereas Gemini outright called it a scam. It also doubted the refund email, saying the sender's address looked less typical.

Recent findings suggest that in all my runs, ChatGPT correctly called the sign-in email legitimate. It also cleared the refund email.

It still told me to verify by checking the email's headers, Amazon's Message Center, or forwarding the email to verify@amazon.com, which is Amazon's service for confirming messages.

It was the only chatbot to mention that service.

I told all three tools I'd clicked a link in a scam email and entered my password and card details to see which would give me the most helpful tips.

Gemini covered everything you'd want to check in that situation:.

But it also opened with a substantial "WARNING: Immediate Financial Risk" label, which is the last thing you want to see when you're panicking.

Unlike Gemini's panic-inducing opening statement, ChatGPT started with "Act immediately, but don't panic.".

Sources indicate that it was the only one to tell me to secure my email account and check it for forwarding rules a scammer might have added. It also asked follow-up questions to figure out how exposed I was.

It pretty much covered Gemini's advice but skipped the FTC report; still, it's the answer I'd want at that moment.

Claude gave some reasonable tips, like calling the bank first and changing any reused passwords, starting with your email.

Sources indicate that but it skipped signing out of all devices and reporting to the FTC. It also told me to forward the email to reportphishing@amazon.com, an email I couldn't find on Amazon's pages.

Amazon lists reportascam@amazon.com for reporting suspicious messages.

All three AI tools can spot scams, but ChatGPT was the only one that consistently recognized real messages.

Industry observers note that false alarms might not seem like a massive deal, but they can be harmful. You could skip a genuine Amazon warning or ignore a request to secure your account.

If you're still unsure, the safest option is to check with Amazon: check the Message Center in your account or forward the message to verify@amazon.com.

To reduce the number of scam messages you get, check out these Gmail settings for blocking AI scams.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, diesel engines have a number of pros and cons, but they can be a powerful source of extra vehicular oomph, particularly for industrial applications. A diesel engine in a trailer may sound like a bizarre fit, but in Latest Zealand's Kaingaroa State Forest back in the '90s, it was the defining feature of the Pacific P510 logging truck.

It has been revealed that commissioned by the Magee family and driven almost exclusively by Lance Magee, it operated out of Murupara under its Marathon Truck and Trailer banner. Caterpillar, a storied truck engine manufacturer, supplied the diesel in the rig, a 3406B ATAAC engine. Its lead trailer, meanwhile, added another Caterpillar, specifically a 3406A. Together, the two engines produced a massive 900 horsepower, with the trailer's engine packing muscle farther back in the logging train.

Both engines were turbocharged, 14.6-liter inline-sixes, each connected to its own Allison automatic transmission. The additional engine sat between the lead trailer's axles, giving it its own, independent propulsion.

It has been revealed that the combo was built to haul logs from remote skids, the areas in a forest where timber is gathered and staged before transport. Getting a fully laden logging train away from skids was a tall order that required a tremendous amount of horsepower. While 900 HP may sound like a wild, unnecessary flex, the Pacific P510 operated as a double, a triple, and occasionally even a quad, meaning it was sometimes required to haul four lumber trailers simultaneously. A pair of diesel engines, which often provide more torque than their gas counterparts, were the only logical answer to get the sheer hauling power necessary.

It has been revealed that murupara had a history of operating trucks in the rugged Kaingaroa wilderness, a plantation forest planted mainly with radiata pine for commercial logging. Former driver Pat Cox recalled Canadian Pacific trucks assembled locally by Kaingaroa Logging Company, with trailers manufactured in its workshops. According to Cox, the front axles of these trucks were so heavy they couldn't be used on highways. Off-highway roads had to be carved out to give those heavy beasts access to the timber and the skids where it was staged. Specialized trucks pulling multiple trailers were a common feature in Kaingaroa, and this P510 pushed the idea to its logical extreme by slapping a second diesel where another truck would haul cargo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that your car doesn't have to be a "smart car" to know a thing or two about you. These days, modern cars are basically computers on wheels, and they keep track of more than just your gas mileage. Many mechanical components have now been replaced by computerized ones, which allow your car to track more data about how the car operates and, ultimately, learn about your driving habits.

In a recent development, it used to be a substantial deal for cars to have built-in navigation systems, especially in the days of printed turn-by-turn directions. These days, having something like Apple CarPlay or Android Auto is pretty much a given. You might not expect your car to remember everywhere you travel, but this is the case for many newer cars. For example, Ford mentions that its vehicles track location data if your car uses connected services or has factory-installed connectivity technology. Honda also notes it collects trip start and end locations. Many cars have GPS technology that can pinpoint a location via satellite, even if you're not using those same systems to plan a route.

Industry observers note that your car's computer systems build a detailed profile of your daily driving habits, including the time of day you drive the most. This profile comes from a combination of GPS technology, built-in telematics, and other onboard systems that track various parts of your driving. If you're driving your normal morning and evening commute, running errands at lunch, or making an occasional late-night trip, your car will create a timestamp every time you're behind the wheel. Eventually, these records can create recurring driving patterns.

Some cars may track how quickly you accelerate and how hard you brake, often to make sure your vehicle is working properly. Computers and sensors control many parts of your car, and those parts can eventually fail or stop working properly, just like mechanical parts. Tracking this sort of data gives automakers feedback about how your vehicle is working and whether it's doing its job correctly. For example, when you press the brake, you're activating systems like anti-locking brakes and traction control. These systems directly affect how your vehicle handles on the road. This data can help your vehicle to avoid skidding or locking the wheels.

Sources indicate that years ago, when something went wrong with your car, you had to wish and hope it would make the same sound for the mechanic as it did for you. It could take a lot of trial and error (and sometimes hundreds of dollars) to figure out what was wrong. In modern cars, diagnosing issues is a bit easier. Auto techs can look at a car's error codes on its computerized parts and have an informed idea of what to do next. That diagnostic data has to come from somewhere, though.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, your car keeps tabs on data collected from many sensors (including temperature readings, oxygen sensors, emissions, tire pressure monitoring, fuel injection timing). A few other pieces might surprise you, like odometer readings, maintenance history (and whether you skipped recommended services), and crash detection. These data pieces might not mean much right now, but if you were to ever sell or trade your car, they could be telling about how you cared for the vehicle and its history, provided the buyer can access them.

According to recent reports, between things like remote car start and driving cameras and infotainment systems, cars have more features than ever. And your car is probably tracking how you use some of them. For example, Tesla Model 3 has been known to save short video snippets from the car's many cameras. Toyota mentions using data like the vehicle's location and other driving data in relation to its voice commands feature ("Hey Toyota"), which is part of its connected driver services. The automaker cites that this data allows the company to provide its customers with personalized convenience.

Recent findings suggest that tracking battery performance doesn't offer much beyond the battery, but tracking the charging stations you're using also reveals information about where you've been traveling, how much you drive, and how long you go in between charges. Tesla doesn't specify whether this type of data is among the pieces that are not associated with specific VINs or accounts. Each car firm might handle this type of data differently.

In some cases, you can limit the data your car collects about you. Some car-connected services require you to opt in. Take some time to review the privacy policies for these features and see what types of data they collect and who might have access to it. If you're not comfortable with certain features tracking you, you might be able to opt out.

You won't be able to eliminate all types of data collection, because some are baked into how a car functions. For example, braking data affects how the braking system works. In some cases, you might be able to opt out of whether your automaker shares certain data with third parties, however.

Sources indicate that california passed a law in 2020 that allows consumers to opt out of having their data shared or sold. Other states have followed suit. And if opting out entirely isn't an option, you may be able to limit how your automaker uses the data. Since data collection can vary so much between car manufacturers and privacy laws can vary by state, your best option is to explore what's applicable to you based on what you drive and where you live. The worst case scenario is that you're in the same situation as you are now. And the best case: you regain control over some of your privacy while on the road, whether you want to live more privately or just want to make a statement.

The ZGX Fury G1n combines Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra processor with an enormous memory allocation designed for demanding artificial intelligence workloads.

Its starting price of $132,000 makes it considerably more expensive than conventional professional computers, even before customers consider optional upgrades.

The mobile workstation combines two different memory technologies, LPDDR5X and HBM3e, with 496GB allocated to system memory and another 252GB dedicated to graphics processing.

Developers and researchers working with large language models can use the machine to process substantial workloads without depending entirely on remote computing infrastructure.

HP indicates the available memory can accommodate local adjustment of language models containing up to 100 billion parameters.

The system can also perform inference using models reaching one trillion parameters through FP4 quantization, although actual performance depends on workload requirements.

Running powerful computing components inside a relatively compact enclosure introduces thermal management requirements that ordinary desktop cooling systems cannot necessarily accommodate.

HP therefore equips the workstation with liquid cooling alongside a 1,600W Titanium-certified power supply.

The device ships with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, making Linux its supplied operating system rather than Microsoft's Windows environment.

This configuration caters to developers and technical professionals who need software environments suitable for demanding computing and AI development.

Networking is another crucial component, with an Nvidia ConnectX-8 SuperNIC providing two QSFP112 connections rated at 400Gbps.

These connections allow multiple machines to communicate through high-speed networking when organizations need additional computing resources.

The enclosure also supports installation inside a 5U equipment rack, giving organizations another deployment option beyond placing it beneath an office desk.

This flexibility allows organizations to deploy the workstation individually or install multiple units inside equipment racks for larger computing operations.

Getting all these specifications will cost $132,000 for the standard configuration, enough to buy a brand-new 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQL, although not quite a Ferrari.

Customers opting for the RTX PRO 2000 configuration will pay $133,000, while the more powerful RTX PRO 4000 option raises the price to $136,000.

At these prices, the ZGX Fury is unlikely to attract ordinary desktop buyers looking for additional memory or improved everyday computing performance.

Instead, its potential customers are organizations that require substantial local computing resources and can justify spending considerably more than conventional workstation prices.

Sources indicate that over the past couple of decades, Ryobi has positioned itself as one of the biggest players in the cordless power tool market. It's done so by building out an extensive list of budget-friendly, lithium-ion-powered tools and devices that can cover virtually any need a DIYer might face at home, in the yard, and beyond. That tool lineup features devices that run on different levels of lithium-ion power, including 4V, 18V, and 40V, among others.

Recent findings suggest that you may not realize it, but some of those batteries can provide additional functionality apart from just powering your tools. In fact, those USB lithium packs can serve as chargers for your mobile device in a pinch. As for the 40V battery packs, they can provide a similar function; only they might be able to power much larger devices, even some major appliances.

According to recent reports, there is a catch, of course, which is that, unlike the USB lithium batteries, those 40V rechargeables are not equipped with a USB port that allows you to directly connect a device to draw power. Rather, they require the use of an inverter device. Ryobi refers to these as "power sources" or "power stations" on its site, with the devices essentially taking the DC (direct current) power supplied by the batteries and turning it into the sort of AC (alternating current) power required for devices plugged into traditional two- and three-pronged outlets. Yes, if you buy the right one, you may be able to power your refrigerator.

According to recent reports, such a device could prove invaluable in an emergency situation or during a power outage. It could even prove handy in a home garage or workshop setup. If you're curious, Ryobi's power sources and stations are not limited to its 40V lineup either, with the Techtronic Industries-owned brand also featuring a couple of 18V devices in its lineup, and even a USB lithium charger that features multiple ports.

The USB Lithium device is the cheapest available, of course, with Ryobi selling it for $59.97. An 18V Power Source with a single built-in 120V outlet, on the other hand, will set you back $69.97. Sticker prices go up pretty sharply from there, as does the max power output, with Ryobi topping out with 1,800-watt power stations for both its 18V and 40V battery families. Those devices each boast standard USB and USB-C ports, as well as multiple 120V outlets, and are presently selling for $649 each. While they can run on a single battery pack, using multiple batteries can drive the price considerably higher if you don't have them on hand already.

There are things to consider before you make that investment, as power inverters can be finicky and potentially dangerous if not used correctly. And yes, there is a right way and a wrong way to use and care for portable power stations. You should also remove the batteries when storing the station and avoid blocking its vents or overloading it, as overheating and battery damage could result.

  • Texting used to be simple: someone sent a message, I answered, and that was it.
  • Industry observers note that google Messages now does a lot more than handle everyday conversations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A tech writer who enjoys exploring new gadgets, trying out apps, and capturing moments through photography. He likes getting hands-on with technology and sharing what he learns with readers.

Texting used to be simple: someone sent a message, I answered, and that was it. Emojis and stickers were there, but conversations didn't have all the extra effects and suggestions Google Messages offers now.

Industry observers note that google Messages now does a lot more than handle everyday conversations. Some additions help, while others make the app feel busier than I want it to.

I wanted to know whether I was better off without a few of them, so I turned off a handful of features and kept using the app the way I normally do.

For each one, I asked myself something simple: does it help me understand or answer a message, or is it just one more thing on the screen?

Recent findings suggest that there's a Gemini icon on the main screen of Google Messages. One tap opens a dedicated Gemini conversation, where you can ask questions, brainstorm ideas, or get help with other everyday tasks.

I use the standalone Gemini app, so a second way in didn't do much for me. I rarely tapped it.

I turned off the option under Messages settings > Gemini in Messages. This removed the icon and archived my existing Gemini conversation, both of which returned when I switched the setting back on.

Google Messages suggests things in a few different ways. Smart Reply offers possible responses when someone messages you, and even a plain greeting brings up suggested replies and emojis. Suggested stickers watch what you type: write congratulations or thanks, and related GIFs show up.

Nudges does something else. It brings birthdays and unanswered conversations back to your attention. Once it reminded me about a contact's birthday, and another time, it prompted me to follow up on a message that never got an answer.

Those reminders were useful, so I kept Nudges enabled. You can manage these reminders through Nudges settings.

I see why people use Smart Reply and sticker suggestions. A suggested reply saves a few seconds when you're in a hurry, and a sticker suggestion helps when nothing comes to mind.

I don't use them, though. I'd rather type my own replies and pick a GIF or emoji myself. So I turned both off, and sending messages worked exactly as before.

Link previews were harder to give up. I noticed the difference as soon as I turned them off. A shared link appeared without the preview card, so I had to open it to find out where it led. That's not always helpful, particularly when someone sends a link without explaining what it contains.

I tried restricting previews to web links, but that didn't make much difference in my conversations. Turning previews off only affected newly introduced links, since the ones already in my conversations stayed in place. I switched them back on because a preview gives me an idea of where a link leads before I open it.

Industry observers note that I wasn't particularly attached to Expressive animations. When the feature is on, certain emojis, phrases, and reactions move on screen. With it off, I can still send the same emojis and react to messages, but they appear without the animation, and phrases are no longer animated. I didn't miss the extra movement.

Recent findings suggest that voice message transcription was one thing I definitely wanted to keep. I can read an incoming voice message without playing the audio, and the transcripts were clear and accurate when I used the feature. This is useful when playing audio is awkward or when I want to skim a long message.

Bubbles solve a different problem. A bubble lets me reply while I'm in another app, without going back to the full Messages screen. I can keep my place in whatever I was doing. That helps most when I'm busy with something else and want to reply right away.

I kept two other settings enabled. Pinch to zoom lets me enlarge text in conversations, though how much it helps depends on how you use your phone.

Actions come in handy. It picks out dates, phone numbers, and addresses in a message, and when someone texts me a phone number, Messages offers to call it, message it, copy it, or share it.

Google Messages feels simpler now, though I use it the same as before. I still send and receive messages as usual. The Gemini shortcut, the automatic reply and sticker suggestions, and extra animations are gone from my conversations.

Link previews, Nudges, voice message transcription, Bubbles, Pinch to zoom, and Actions stayed because each one gives me information or makes a conversation easier to reach.

Recent findings suggest that I didn't go back to a bare-bones texting app. I just stopped leaving every option on because it was there, and now I choose additions that fit how I communicate.

Sources indicate that your list will probably look different from mine. If you open Gemini from Messages often, keep the shortcut. If suggested replies save you time, keep the shortcut. If suggested replies save you time, keep those too.

In a recent development, google Messages will keep adding features, so it's worth asking the same question of each latest one: Does it help me understand or answer a message? That's what made texting feel simpler for me.
