📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents Across Their Lifecycle.

Nov 15, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent article, Uber Engineering highlights the limitations of traditional identity and API controls in securing AI agents that dynamically reason over external content and take real-world actions. To address this challenge, Uber developed a framework to determine whether an agent's action is appropriate given the user's request, the agent's intended purpose, its permissions, and the context of the interaction.

Identity and authorization systems can determine whether a user or service has permission to access a resource, but they can't determine whether an agent's proposed action is appropriate in context.

This creates multiple risks, including prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions, which Uber's framework addresses through three layers spanning the entire agent lifecycle, from pre-deployment to runtime enforcement to post-deployment continuous assurance.

At provisioning time, agents must be registered in the Uber AI Registry, establishing identity, ownership, persona, permitted intents, constraints, dependencies, and risk classification. This process is automated using Argus, which analyzes the agent's source code, prompts, configurations, dependencies, exposed endpoints, and tool-invocation paths to identify security weaknesses. The same approach is enforced for MCP servers and tools used by the agents.

At runtime, the framework extends the traditional security model based on policy administration, policy decision, and policy enforcement to incorporate behavioral authorization, which evaluates whether an agent's actions are appropriate in a given context.

Behavioral authorization is implemented through three components: the AI Registry, AI guards, and Agent Guard runtime hooks. The AI Registry defines and manages agent policies, personas, intents, and constraints, while AI Guards evaluate interactions and proposed actions against established policies. Agent Guard runtime hooks invoke AI Guard "at critical checkpoints and applying its verdict before an interaction or action is allowed to proceed".

Recent findings suggest that after deployment, the focus shifts to Continuous Assurance, which relies on end-to-end observability, auditing, explainability, and replay. This layer comprises two main main components: a unified execution trace that connects agent actions, tool calls, and security decisions; and recorded interactions that can be replayed whenever policies and guardrails are updated to assess their effectiveness in the new context.

Uber also identified several challenges in implementing security controls in production, including balancing policy restrictiveness to avoid both excessive false positives and insufficient protection, minimizing runtime latency, reducing developer friction during framework setup, and moving beyond generic controls towards agent-specific policies, which "made enforcement more contextual and precise".

Commenting on Uber's approach on LinkedIn, UN senior information technology officer Tristan G. raised several concerns, noting that while "per-agent personas, intents, constraints and calibration" is what adds the most value, they also come at a significant cost, as "the effort scales with the number of workflows". Additionally,.

According to recent reports, by its own account, the strongest control was restricting agents to explicit constraints, which is least privilege rather than a new idea. For me, the open question is how this works for agents you don't build, such as vendor or SaaS agents where you can't insert your own enforcement hooks.

On similar lines, AI architect Pratik Dhanave also observes that:.

It has been revealed that the lesson they call least glamorous is the one they rate most effective: explicit intents and constraints per agent. Not generic thresholds, which failed because every agent has a different purpose and risk profile. The cost is flexibility, and they say it is worth paying.

In a recent development, uber's Secure AI framework is still in evolving, with looks to expand its capabilities across all the areas outlined above. There is much more to the framework than can be covered here, so readers are encouraged to consult the ⁠original article for a more comprehensive overview.

Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits.

According to recent reports, cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the firm was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment.

Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality.

The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot.

According to recent reports, the CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys.

Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell.

#441. Industry News: How Long It Took To Cross The Atlantic By Ocean Liner In The 1950s Vs. Today

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (815 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Industry News: How Long It Took To Cross The Atlantic By Ocean Liner In The 1950s Vs. Today

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's almost baffling that the fastest Atlantic crossing by an ocean liner was achieved nearly 75 years ago and hasn't been beaten since.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, ocean liners are largely a thing of the past.
  • The Queen Mary 2 is the only liner still running a scheduled liner crossing like the express liners of the 1950s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's almost baffling that the fastest Atlantic crossing by an ocean liner was achieved nearly 75 years ago and hasn't been beaten since. The SS United States, set to be sunk off the coast of Florida soon, set the record by crossing from New York to England in just 3 days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes. It did so in July 1952, as part of its maiden voyage. During that era, the typical express liner voyage took around five days.

Recent findings suggest that today, ocean liners are largely a thing of the past. In fact, there's only one that still runs through roughly the same route — the Queen Mary 2, operated by Cunard Line. However, it usually takes seven days to complete it. Cunard's itinerary for a December 2027 westbound sailing says the ship starts in Southampton, takes six days at sea, and concludes in Newly introduced York on Day 8.

It's a fair comparison, too. The Queen Mary 2 is the only liner still running a scheduled liner crossing like the express liners of the 1950s. Even so, it takes two days longer than the average trip of decades ago and nearly twice as long as the super-speedy SS United States.

And it's not just ocean liners that are taking longer, since regular cruise ships are slower, too. Royal Caribbean, a cruise organization, claims that its ships average 18 to 20 knots. At that speed, covering the same 2,949-nautical-mile route non-stop would take roughly six to seven days. However, the actual voyages are slower since these ships tend to spend time at port stops such as the Azores and Bermuda. As an example, Celebrity Cruises says its ships take 11 to 16 nights to cross the Atlantic.

In a recent development, the main reason is that people don't book ocean liners or even cruise ships for the speed anymore. In fact, not long after that record was set, liners were already starting to lose travelers to jets. In 1957, more people crossed the Atlantic by air than by sea for the first time, enabled by propeller planes like the Lockheed Constellation. Then came the Boeing 707, a wholly different beast: It could cruise at nearly 600 mph and complete a transatlantic trip in just over six hours. So obviously, anyone who traveled by ship to cross the ocean in the shortest possible time simply gave up on them.

Recent findings suggest that by 1968, Cunard, a major passenger line at the time, lost more than $40 million on its passenger ships over six years. It then repositioned itself to avoid competing with jets and decided it would focus on the leisure business instead. Naturally, speed stopped being a priority: People on vacation don't normally wish their trips to end in the shortest possible time.

Sources indicate that today, Queen Mary 2 crosses at about 21.5 knots, according to a 2012 Business Travel News report. This is slower than the original Queen Mary, which sailed from 1936 to 1967, at 28.5 knots. Besides the lack of need for speed, some of it has to do with cost. The thing with the Queen Mary 2 is that it runs on two kinds of engines: a pair of gas turbines and four diesel engines, and diesel engines are cheaper to run.

Recent findings suggest that the thing with ships like the Queen Mary 2 is that they rarely go all out. The ship's own chief designer, according to an Ingenia report, notes that it was contracted for a top speed of 29.35 knots, though it could go even faster in sea trials, hitting 29.65 knots. This specific speed, the report adds, was picked after studying the logs of Cunard's previous liner, then tested against five years of real Atlantic weather. It lets the ship make up any lost time if it ever gets delayed by weather.

It has been revealed that beyond operating costs, building faster ships is also pretty expensive. Speed and rough seas are a formula that doesn't mix together — you need a deeper hull and extra strength, especially to push through stormy weather, and that swiftly raises costs. In fact, according to the Ingenia report, building a true ocean liner with its specific strength requirements incurs a 40% increase in the cost of construction versus a cruise ship of the same size.

Supersized ships also need much more power to move fast, which we observe with the Queen Mary 2. The Mary 2 measures about 150,000 gross tons and is the largest liner ever. It's nearly three times bigger than the SS United States, which measured 53,329 tons, and nearly twice as big as the largest liners from the 1950s. It also helps that the SS United States had roughly twice Queen Mary 2's propulsion power. In other words, more power for a significantly smaller overall package.

The 2021 Discovery Sport is five years old as of 2026, and if you're interested in selling yours, you're probably interested in knowing how much your model can fetch in the secondhand market, considering luxury cars typically lose value faster.

Similarly, if you're planning to buy a used 2021 Discovery Sport, you'll want to know what to expect to pay in today's used-car market. According to estimates from CarEdge, a Land Rover Discovery Sport depreciates by 59.1% after five years, which translates to a resale value of 40.9%. The site notes the average resale value for a five-year-old Discovery Sport is $21,611, having lost around $31,189 of its original value. The site's estimates assume the car is in average condition and has clocked about 67,500 miles. iSeeCars' Land Rover Discovery Sport depreciation values differ slightly from CarEdge's.

The site estimates the model loses 54.9% of its value over the same period, with an estimated average resale value of $22,515. Kelley Blue Book's (KBB) data also show that the 2021 Discovery Sport has lost a considerable chunk of its original value, depreciating by 58.27%. The site reveals the model has retained just 41.73% of its original value, based on the combined original MSRP of $182,000 and the total current Fair Purchase Price of $75,950.

Recent findings suggest that overall, based on data from the three reference sites, the Land Rover Discovery Sport doesn't have the best resale value. It loses more than 50% of its original value after five years, which is more than the average car. According to iSeeCars, the average car will depreciate by 41.7% over the same period, which is roughly 13 percentage points less than the Land Rover Discovery Sport. KBB notes that the average car retains 44.7% of its value, which is higher than the Discovery Sport.

iSeeCars also has data on the depreciation rate of different car segments as a whole, and the Disco Sport doesn't fare any better. The average SUV only loses about 44.8% of its value, 10.1 percentage points less than Land Rover's model. Even worse, the overall luxury compact SUV segment, which the Disco Sport belongs to, fares a bit better with 49.6% depreciation after five years, per iSeeCars. If that wasn't enough, CarEdge ranks the Discovery Sport among luxury cars with the worst resale value after five years.

So if you're considering buying a Land Rover Discovery, be warned that it isn't the best option available if you care about resale value. If resale value is important, then you'd better look elsewhere. However, the lower price doesn't necessarily mean you should get the vehicle.

Another key factor you should consider is the model's reliability. Even if you're given a Disco Sport for free, it'll cost you much more if it has recurring problems. Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close. #436. Breaking: The World's Fastest Torpedo Is Basically An Underwater Rocket

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (532 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Breaking: The World's Fastest Torpedo Is Basically An Underwater Rocket

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, torpedoes have existed in various forms since the 19th century, and in 1864, the CSS Hunley became the first successful submarine to destroy an enemy ship.
  • According to recent reports, the United States' Mk.
  • Dodging an incoming torpedo moving more than four times as fast as the fastest sub is difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, torpedoes have existed in various forms since the 19th century, and in 1864, the CSS Hunley became the first successful submarine to destroy an enemy ship. The Hunley was destroyed in the process while using a spar torpedo, but thankfully, the technology has improved since that time. Modern torpedoes are incredibly complex vehicles that combine speed, maneuverability, targeting, and warhead lethality into a single package that often costs millions of dollars to produce.

According to recent reports, the United States' Mk. 48 Heavyweight torpedo is the deadliest in the world, but compared to the fastest torpedo ever made, it's incredibly slow. Speed is one of the most important factors in torpedo operation, and the Soviet Union managed to perfect that particular aspect of torpedo design in the 1970s. The VA-111 Shkval entered into service with the Russian Navy in 1978, and it can travel at speeds in excess of 200 knots, which amounts to around 230 mph. Making something move that quickly underwater is an engineering challenge, to say the least.

Dodging an incoming torpedo moving more than four times as fast as the fastest sub is difficult. The Shkval is particularly effective at promptly reaching its target. To reach 200+ knots, the torpedo employs a process known as supercavitation, which is accomplished by continuously vaporizing water as it travels. This creates a thin bubble of gas surrounding the torpedo, significantly reducing friction from hydrodynamic drag. Of course, it doesn't hurt that the Shkval isn't powered by a propeller, and instead employs a rocket engine for thrust.

It has been revealed that torpedoes typically have domed or somewhat pointed forward sections, but the Shkval's nose doesn't follow this trend. Instead, its design was purposefully made as a means of diverting rocket exhaust out via several openings in front of the torpedo as it travels. This is what creates the gas bubble surrounding the weapon system as it moves, achieving its incredible speed.

According to recent reports, with great speed comes a significant tradeoff in maneuverability, and the Shkval is neither highly maneuverable nor guided like most torpedoes. Instead, it relies on speed to close the distance between the launcher and the target, so it has an advantage there, since it's difficult for a submarine to outrun a normal torpedo, much less a supercavitating one. If the torpedo changes course or direction even slightly, it disrupts the gas bubble, canceling out supercavitation until it reforms around the torpedo's body. Because of this, once it reaches a target area, it slows down and switches on its targeting system to locate its target.

Interestingly, the earliest versions of the Shkval had no guidance system due to the incredible noise the rocket engine made, disrupting its ability to locate a target. When the Soviets designed the Shkval, it was likely meant to carry a nuclear warhead, so maneuverability wouldn't have been paramount in their design process. In terms of its size and specs, the Shkval has a maximum range of a little over 4.26 miles. It carries a 460-lb warhead, and the Shkval torpedo is used by the Russian and Iranian navies; the latter likely reverse-engineered the technology.

In a recent development, the holidays are upon us, and aside from overeating to an obscene degree and finding every excuse to waterboard people with Mariah Carey, it's time to figure out what gifts you're going to give to the people in your life. Especially the picky ones, like the tech geeks. These are the sorts of people you couldn't, for example, just gift any random pair of headphones; oh no, you'd want to give them a pair audiophiles approve of. That could get expensive fast, so here's a list of (relatively) cheap stocking stuffers that are guaranteed to please the sorts of people who care about hardware specs.

Every item on this list uses USB-C in some capacity. They're small, small enough at least to fit into a stocking, though that'll depend on how substantial Santa's feet are. Rather than trawl Amazon for examples, we carefully scoured the internet for items the professionals recommend so your recipient geek is pleasantly surprised that you got their gift right. We recommend these 13.

According to recent reports, we'll never forgive Apple for killing the headphone jack (among other things) and giving the rest of the industry the green light to do the same. But there's no reason to trash those perfectly good, perfectly capable wired earbuds. Let your geek fight back (they will probably have strong opinions about this) with a USB-C to 3.5-millimeter audio adapter. There are quite a few good options to choose from.

The best all-rounder is this USB-C to audio jack adapter that includes a DAC, a little chip that may improve audio quality. UGREEN makes a right-angle adapter that may be preferable over a dongle. They both support 24-bit/96 kHz audio, or in English, some of the highest quality audio available. If your geek is an Apple user, then they can't go wrong with the Apple USB-C to 3.5mm jack adapter — Apple's tacit admission that people still like and want to use wired headphones.

It has been revealed that the most annoying part of using one of these adapters (aside from the burning rage at having your headphone jack stolen) is that you can't charge your phone at the same time. In that case, consider this USB-C to 3.5-millimeter headphone and charger adapter. The extra USB-C dongle supports PD 3.0 and up to 60-watt fast charging. It also supports hi-fi 24 bits/96 kHz audio. All of these adapters cost $20 or less.

A USB-C to 3.5 mm dongle can emit great wired audio, but the next level up is a dedicated DAC and amp combo that can drive a pair of high-impedance headphones. The FiiO/Snowsky Tiny is a perfect example. It claims to support PCM 384 kHz/32 bit and DSD256 on Android phones and PC — no iPhones supported, unfortunately. Headphones that have their own mic and controls will still work. For geeks that want to go deeper, the adapter supports PEQ EQ tuning. It's a lot of technobabble, we admit, but the point is this is a high-performance adapter for discerning listeners.

According to recent reports, note there are two versions of this product, the Tiny A and the Tiny B. The former includes a USB-C port for simultaneous charging; the latter has a second headphone jack for less-common 4.4-millimeter headphones and allows two people to listen at the same time. Both variants cost the same, though, and come in identical CNC aluminum cases that should be durable and stylish in equal measure. We'd recommend the Tiny A, however, unless you know for a fact your recipient has headphones with a 4.4-millimeter plug. People who know headphones recommend the FiiO. Most importantly, this "professional-grade" hardware only sets you back $20.

It has been revealed that have you ever plugged a device into one of those free charging stations at airports? That may have been one of the riskiest things you've ever done, digitally speaking. Hackers use these as honeypots to get a direct, physical connection to your device so they can hit you with a malware payload. It's not something the average person usually knows, but it's certainly something the geek in your life does. They'll appreciate a PortaPow Data Blocker.

According to recent reports, portaPow makes two varieties of data blocker. One, a USB-A to USB-C adapter for a charging cable; helpful if the only available plug at a charging station is USB-A. Or if USB-C is available, a USB-C-only data blocker adapter. Both types have gotten strong reviews over the years and confirm it is impossible to transmit data when using one of these. They work through a very simple principle: they do not have data-transmission hardware whatsoever, entirely eliminating the possibility that a bad actor could gain access. Each set of two costs $9.99.

Sources indicate that geeks are not like the common man. The common man is satisfied with the same charging brick they've been using for the past decade, while a geek can comfortably own two or ten. So you can't go wrong by gifting them something like the Anker Nano Smart Display Charger, which you can buy here on Amazon. This tiny, compact charger has foldable plugs and supports up to 45-watt GaN charging. It includes a little screen to tell you how fast it's charging and how long it will take (supported devices, like the iPhone 15 up) to juice up; the screen can be woken with a tap, too.

What we like about this charger is that it is the perfect middle road between size, feature set, and power. Normally, you'd have to buy a bigger, more expensive charger to get a screen and such high charging rates. Reviewers who have had their hands on this thing can all agree it's an excellent choice for a small, single-port charger. It fits right into a stocking, too.

It is a bit on the pricey side at $39.99, but at the time of writing, it's on sale for $25.99 for Prime Members and it has dipped down to $25.99 for everyone else on multiple occasions already.

Believe it or not, geeks like to go outside. No, really. It's not necessarily social anxiety stopping them (though that could be a factor), but rather that their devices might run out of battery. If that's the case, grab them this 10,000 mAh Anker Nano Power Bank that supports 30-watt charging. This is possibly the best power bank on the market right now at this mAh size for a number of reasons. One, it supports 30W charging, a high charging rate among smaller power banks; two, it has a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a carrying strap, so the recipient doesn't have to bring one more thing when they go out; and three, it has a helpful screen that tells you the battery level and charging time.

According to recent reports, similar to the Anker Nano Smart Display Charger, the Anker Nano Power Bank is squeezing features that would normally be found in bigger, more expensive battery packs into a pocketable — and stocking-able — size. Reviewers love it. Anker is a beloved brand that constantly innovates, making it a safe gift choice. Just make sure it's a geek you love more than the others, because it's priced at $54.99.

In a recent development, the USB-C standard is in a weird place right now. It's more common than ever, having become the default port on phones, some laptops, and even now starting to creep into 2.4Ghz dongles that were once exclusively USB-A. Yet, we still have a ton of USB-A devices that are not going away anytime soon. This can get really annoying for geeks, who want a USB thumb drive that they can use on their modern laptop and that old one they probably put Linux on. A great USB thumb drive for this frustrating transitional period is the SanDisk 128 GB Ultra Dual Drive.

Spec-wise, this is just a typical USB 3.1 Gen 1 flash drive, but with a twist: it has a USB-A and USB-C plug on each side, so you can add files to it from an older USB-A-only device and transfer them seamlessly to a USB-C device, without any intermediaries. Then hopefully one day when devices are using USB-C, it'll still be usable. The 128-gigabyte storage should be plenty for everyday files, and the 150Mbps read speeds ensure it won't take forever to transfer the big ones, like photo libraries. We'd also say it's pretty fairly priced in the midst of this memory crisis at $29.99, and reviews for it are strong.

Sources indicate that A major concern with USB-C is that cables may look identical on the outside, but they can support wildly different charging and transfer speeds and protocols. Unless you know where you bought it, it's effectively a mystery cable that you'll have to hope does what you want it to. Enter: the Treedix USB cable tester.

Recent findings suggest that like other cable testers, you insert both ends of a cable into the provided slots, and the readout will tell you everything about it. It tells you which USB generation it is (USB 2.0, 3.2, 4.0, etc.), its power transmission capabilities (like Power Delivery), what sort of transfer speeds it supports (including if it's a Thunderbolt cable, and what generation), and a lot of other geeky stuff only people who test cables in the first place would know.

It has been revealed that it's an indispensable tool for finding the right cable for the job, including testing cables that you've just purchased against advertised specs, and going through older cables to see if they're worth keeping. Reviewers love it, and geeks will too.

As devices become less and less repairable and things you used to own (like music) shift to subscription models, collecting vintage devices from an era when none of this nonsense existed has become increasingly popular. To get ahead of the curve, some companies remake a vintage product for a new era with basically everything it used to have, but upgraded to work on modern devices. That's where the Sony MBR-3R USB-C Wired Retro headphones fit in.

Industry observers note that the original came out in 1979 with, obviously, a 3.5-millimeter jack. This version uses USB-C with the assumption that you'll probably be listening to music on a post-jack phone. They're not exactly the same as their predecessors; Sony has altered the sound. However, reviewers quite like the newly introduced profile, and the inclusion of modern conveniences (aside from the USB-C connector) like a microphone for calls. With headphone jacks firmly in the rearview mirror and almost nonexistent on modern phones, and retro devices growing in popularity, this is a pretty good mix of old and new—though it may be a tight fit in a stocking.

One of the downsides to buying a PS5 is that you're heavily limited in what Bluetooth accessories you can connect to it. In particular, Bluetooth audio. A PS5 will just flat-out refuse to connect to headphones and speakers not strictly endorsed by Sony — so not even Sony's noise-canceling headphones will connect. Trust me, I've tried. Unless, of course, you use a USB adapter. If the person you're gifting to has a PS5, they might like this Ugreen USB-C Bluetooth adapter that supports Bluetooth audio for the PS5 as well as computers that might not have functioning Bluetooth — though not TVs.

It has been revealed that it actually works, too, with modern hi-fi codecs like aptX (read: really high-quality wireless audio). It claims to have sub-100ms latency, which is pretty good when it comes to Bluetooth audio. Any Bluetooth audio device should work, whether it's headphones, earbuds, or a speaker. Just make sure to double-check that the gift recipient isn't using a PS4 or PS Portal, as it doesn't work on that hardware. In my experience, the USB-C port matters because it lets you connect to the front of the PS5, rather than the back, where the signal might be interrupted.

Sources indicate that we've already discussed the USB cable tester, but another useful tool in a geek's arsenal is a USB-C power meter. Plug it into a device — like a phone, laptop, or gaming handheld — then plug in your charging cable to the back end, and the meter tells you exactly how much current is flowing through. This can be helpful for identifying charging issues, when the device isn't taking as much as it can support, or the brick it's connected to isn't putting out as much as it supports, and so on.

In addition to this, it can identify protocols like Power Delivery. Everything is displayed in real time on an ISP display. Experts who have tested it find it to be reliable and useful. Also, it earns the vaunted "customers usually keep this item" status, the highest praise Amazon can bestow — and it's only $13.97.

Most people these days just use the flashlight on their phone when they need one. Not geeks, though. They buy rechargeable flashlights such as this one that produce a disproportionately large and powerful beam. It's a 1200-lumen LED flashlight, which in practical terms means it can reach 155 meters and runs for 500 hours on its lower settings. Digging into the specs, it boasts a whole bunch of geeky features like an eye-strain-free non-PWM beam and 4000K and 5000K color temperatures. The flashlight sells for a pretty reasonable $35.99, too.

It has been revealed that it's durable, waterproof (IPX8, which means 30 meters underwater for 30 minutes), pocketable, and has a magnetic bottom to attach to things. And importantly for our purposes, it supports USB-C charging, not replaceable batteries. People who review flashlights love it. I don't know about you, but when a geek in a highly niche category gives something the thumbs up, that's all I need.

One too many USB-A devices still exist for the transition to USB-C to be complete, but luckily some of them can be "retrofitted," particularly USB storage devices like sticks and external drives. Take this Anker USB-C adapter. Unlike a lot of USB-C adapters I've used that only support glacial USB 2.0 transfer speeds, this one has USB 3.0, which means 5 Gbps (or 5,120 Mbps), so drives with USB-A plugs are able to move files at not-snail speeds.

It has been revealed that plus, these plugs are high quality, so I've been able to leave them on the devices that they retrofit basically permanently, only taking them off if I needed them somewhere else. Anker says that aside from USB storage, it can support other things like peripherals, printers, cameras, and data transfer from mobile devices. It's only $12.99 for a two-pack, and it's one of those things you can buy blindly for basically any geek in your life, knowing they will, in all likelihood, have a use for it.

Some people use ointments to treat bug bites, but geeks? They want technical solutions. So if they're prone to bug bites, grab them the heat it USB-C Bug Bite Healer. Heat it found a highly unconventional solution to alleviating bug-bite itch that's backed by science: heating the site rapidly to 124 degrees Fahrenheit without burning you. No, really. It's a USB-C dongle you connect to your phone and activate with an app before applying to the site. Done. No more itching, no more pain.

It sounds like one of those sketchy products you'd see in a Walgreens aisle on a shelf labeled "as seen on TV," a shelf you probably avoid. Except this time, the product actually works. People who have used heat it on real bug bites can attest to relief lasting hours, with only really bad bites needing repeat treatments. Since it plugs into your phone, you can bring it with you anywhere, and it uses only an infinitesimally small fraction of your battery per bite. Geeks who go out into Mother Nature — yes, they do exist, raising my hand here — will love it. And for $29.95, it's the cheapest lifelong treatment option money can buy.

As geeks ourselves who know what geeks want, we carefully selected items on this list so they aren't stocking stuffers that will eventually end up in an e-waste bin. Most importantly, we focused on small, relatively cheap gadgets that fit into a stocking and a tight-ish budget; after all, stocking stuffers usually aren't expensive presents. With one exception, we kept the items on this list under a $50 price point. Most fell well below that.

Industry observers note that second, these needed to be items people have actually used and vouched for, so we sought at least one professional review, or recommended items that we have actually used and owned. Voile, a rock-solid list of recommendations we're confident includes at least one perfect gift for any tech geek this holiday season.

5 Google Messages tricks that cut down my daily texting friction

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apps like Google Messages have evolved into rich messengers.
  • The abundance of features has made Google Messages too heavy on my eyes.
  • Sources indicate that I have five tricks that have made my Google Messages experience a lot more seamless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apps like Google Messages have evolved into rich messengers. There are so many features and options to tweak now, from Gemini integration to chat themes.

The abundance of features has made Google Messages too heavy on my eyes. Conversations are loaded with too many functions, and certain settings are buried in menus.

Sources indicate that I have five tricks that have made my Google Messages experience a lot more seamless. See if any of these tips help you, too.

It has been revealed that first, pin your most notable conversations to the top of the list. These make them instantly accessible the moment you fire up Google Messages.

In a recent development, aside from the usual family and friends, I also pin threads from banks and online services. This helps me separate legitimate texts from scam messages.

Recent findings suggest that to do this, press and hold a conversation, then tap the pin icon at the top. However, you can't manually sort pinned chats. Everything is sorted in descending order based on the last received message.

Industry observers note that you can also add a star to individual messages by long-pressing a message and selecting Star in the submenu. This doesn't pin messages to the inbox; instead, they enter their own category in Search.

To remove a starred message, tap the star icon beside the message.

Industry observers note that since we're on the topic of Search, you can find message categories hidden inside the search icon. Tapping the icon reveals the search bar and at least eight categories.

You can go straight to the specific contact or message you're looking for by typing in the search bar, or you can explore any of the categories.

The categories include unread messages, texts from known or unknown contacts, and media files, among others. The most vital one is Starred, which contains the messages you've starred earlier.

Sources indicate that if you have two SIM cards like I do, you'll find your network operators listed here. These categories display the specific chats each mobile operator is involved in.

Here's something that is often overlooked, but makes inbox decluttering easier: You can choose two different swipe actions for chats.

To customize these gestures, open your profile icon in the upper-right corner of the main page, head to the Messages settings, then select Swipe actions.

You can pick between Archive, Trash, and Mark as read or unread. You can choose one gesture for the right swipe and another for the left swipe.

I set Trash for the right swipe and Mark as read/unread for the left swipe. In the rare instance I need to archive a conversation, I long-press the chat and tap the archive icon at the top.

Archived conversations are found inside Profile > Archived.

I often go through my unread messages late at night before going to bed. When I have to reply to someone but don't want to disturb their sleep, I schedule my text for the next morning.

According to recent reports, I start by drafting the message, then long-pressing the Send button. This gives me four scheduling options.

Industry observers note that the first three are pre-made. Examples include: Tomorrow, 8:00; Tomorrow, 13:00; and Tomorrow, 18:00. If none of these suit your needs, select Pick date and time.

From here, you can schedule a message days or weeks in advance. Just make sure you're connected to a mobile network or Wi-Fi during that scheduled sending time.

When group chats become overbearing, it's natural to ignore incoming messages. To stop Google Messages from pushing notifications for a period of time, you can snooze entire chats.

All you do is tap and hold a conversation, then select the snooze icon at the top. You can choose 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or Always.

Sources indicate that to ensure you receive notifications for the messages you're mentioned in, check the appropriate option at the bottom of the submenu. This sends push notifications only when you're tagged.

If you're the type who sets newly introduced messages aside, only to forget to reply later, you can ask Google Messages to remind you automatically. Turn this setting on via Settings > Suggestions & Actions > Nudges > Suggest message reminders.

If you notice key messages going to spam, lower the spam protection. Go to Settings > Protection & Safety and pick Standard protection instead of Enhanced protection.

Much of the texting friction comes from a buildup of annoyances, not a single interface-breaking enhancement. These tricks aim to reduce hassle and boost productivity in Google's primary messaging app.

Google Messages is no longer a basic SMS app. It's now loaded with features that could make or break the flow. By investing a few minutes into configuring pins, swipes, and reminders, you can regain control over your daily messaging.

In a recent development, while many tools advertise their uses on the box, sometimes companies pick odd names. Just look at the catalog of Leatherman camping multitools. By that same token, some people might shop for Leatherman tools wondering what an "EOD" is. It's just a not-so-fancy way of saying army personnel use them to make battlefields safer.

The term "EOD" is little more than an acronym that stands for "Explosives Ordinance Disposal," sort of like how "IED" stands for "Improvised Explosive Device." However, an "EOD" label only means that the multitool was designed with bomb squads in mind. Even though you can easily purchase one through the Leatherman website — such as the MUT EOD, which costs $229.95 — owning one doesn't immediately make you a bomb disposal expert.

So what sets a Leatherman EOD multitool apart from the rest of the company's catalog? Well, they aren't more expensive, and while EOD tools are certainly heavy and seemingly built to withstand a ton of abuse, they aren't heavier than similar Leatherman products. Instead, it comes down to loadouts.

It has been revealed that the MUT EOD, for instance, shares many tools with the standard MUT multitool, including needlenose pliers, a saw, a combo knife (a knife with an edge divided into straight and serrated sections), and a hammer. However, the MUT EOD includes unique attachments such as fuse wire cutters (which cut wires without producing sparks) and a C4 Punch (which punches holes into plastic explosives). This specialization comes at a cost, however: the MUT EOD only includes 15 tools, whereas the vanilla MUT boasts 16 attachments.

Industry observers note that while Leatherman's MUT EOD is a variant of the standard MUT (which is currently sold out), the MUT EOD isn't Leatherman's only EOD offering. Aside from the MUT EOD, the Super Tool 300 EOD is Leatherman's only other dedicated EOD multitool.

As its name suggests, this product is a variant of the Super Tool 300 — one of the best Leatherman multitools for gardening, we might add. Like the MUT EOD, the Super Tool 300 EOD trades out certain attachments for instruments you might find in a bomb disposal unit's toolbox, such as a specialized t-shank metal saw. Don't worry, the Super Tool 300 EOD still has the awl tool you can find on the regular Leatherman Super Tool 300.

Industry observers note that even though Leatherman's catalog of EOD multitools only consists of two products, the firm also offers EOD attachments, such as a wire cutter kit and that C4 punch. These aren't standalone tools, however; they are primarily designed to replace the specialized instruments that come with EOD multitools, as they wear out with regular use.

Recent findings suggest that then there's the MUT EOD Accessory Kit, which can either serve as an inventory of replacement tools or retrofit a standard MUT into a MUT EOD. And yes, Leatherman sells a MUT Accessory Kit that can replace broken MUT tools or turn a MUT EOD into a regular MUT.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good. But fresh hardware and some new features can’t fix the core problem. Google’s Find Hub network has been restricted from the very start, and it’s not something Google can easily fix.

The good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the latest “gold standard.”.

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

It has been revealed that google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

Sources indicate that google had a privacy focus when launching what was originally called the “Find My Device” network, defaulting the network to only be active on Android phones in “high-traffic areas” only. Customers could switch this to “all areas,” but the initial rollout defaulted to effectively cutting off anywhere that wasn’t a major metro, airport/travel hub, etc. It left the network useless to many. Google defended this as a “first-of-its-kind safety protection,” but I’d argue it hindered the network into a state of inefficacy.

Again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing owners to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a upcoming device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone.

According to recent reports, all of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but newly introduced hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

#426. Why Your Air Conditioner Might Sound Like Running Water

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Why Your Air Conditioner Might Sound Like Running Water

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after installing any type of newly introduced air conditioner, you might hear a variety of sounds.
  • Recent findings suggest that the sound of water flowing is usually caused by the refrigerant flowing around the system.
  • You might also hear a similar flowing sound when the system is first switched on, as the refrigerant flows more quickly in order to promptly start cooling your home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after installing any type of newly introduced air conditioner, you might hear a variety of sounds. Some of them are nothing to worry about, and others are a potential cause for concern. One sound that's common to hear is the sound of water flowing or running. In most cases, this sound is simply a result of the system's normal operation, so you don't have to concern yourself with trying to fix it.

Recent findings suggest that the sound of water flowing is usually caused by the refrigerant flowing around the system. If your system has both an indoor coil and an outdoor coil, you're likely to notice it more during the winter months, when the system is going through a defrost cycle. This is because colder temperatures can eventually lead to condensation collecting and freezing on the outdoor coil, even if the ambient temperature outside isn't below freezing. The defrost cycle switches the direction of the refrigerant to temporarily heat up the outdoor coil, melting any condensation and therefore ensuring that the system can keep working efficiently.

You might also hear a similar flowing sound when the system is first switched on, as the refrigerant flows more quickly in order to promptly start cooling your home. In any case, a running water sound on its own isn't a reason to worry. Other similar watery noises can also be part of a system's normal operation, like dripping or occasional sloshing sounds. However, there are some other air conditioner sounds and smells that could be an indication that something is amiss.

According to recent reports, if you've already had your air conditioner installed for some time and it suddenly starts making louder sounds than it did before, it's worth investigating further. An unusually loud sound when the system starts or stops can indicate that there's an concern with the system's compressor or capacitor. Unusually loud humming or clicking sounds while the system is running can also indicate a fault, with various components potentially being the cause.

A sudden hissing sound might be the result of a leak in the system, and this isn't definitely something that should be ignored. It's best to shut off the system and call in a professional to diagnose the issue. Aside from that, an unexpected sound on its own isn't an immediate sign that you'll need to replace your HVAC system. But if it's paired with other red flags — like a sudden loss of heating and cooling performance or a strange, unpleasant smell — the system may need repairs. Make sure you're on top of routine maintenance to keep an air conditioner system in good working order and minimize the chance of encountering the most common problems. That includes cleaning out the air filters and servicing the air conditioner itself regularly to prevent issues.

The sole reason I have stuck with Google Keep for so long is its simplicity. I don't need a complicated note-taking system with nested folders or elaborate formatting options.

While those features are nice to have, they aren't what I want when I need to jot something down promptly. That's where Keep excels, and that's why, despite its flaws and shortcomings, it has remained an integral part of my workflow.

But most of the time, the information I capture ends up sitting in Keep until I remember to search for it.

According to recent reports, sometimes I forget I saved something useful. Even when I remember, I need to manually find that note and copy its content into whichever app I am using.

This workflow made sense until last year. However, the more I integrate Claude and ChatGPT into my workflow, the more I realize how significant a bottleneck Keep is becoming.

Sources indicate that I use both ChatGPT and Claude to brainstorm ideas, research topics, organize information, and work through tasks. For that, these assistants need access to the relevant information I stored in Keep. But they can't see those notes, and that's a problem.

Sources indicate that until a few months ago, my biggest complaint with Google Keep was its limited formatting options and basic organization features. Now, it's the lack of an official Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration.

MCP allows AI assistants to talk to external apps and services. Instead of making you copy information between apps and an AI assistant, it lets the assistant access that data and take relevant actions.

It is an open standard, so nothing stops Google from bringing it to Google Keep.

For example, if Google Keep supported MCP, I could ask Claude or ChatGPT to search my notes about useful Android apps I have come across this year, summarize the information, and turn it into something useful.

Or I could ask ChatGPT to go through my saved ideas, tell me their pros and cons, and suggest how I could implement them.

It has been revealed that since Keep doesn't integrate with ChatGPT or Claude through MCP, I have to do all this manually: search for the notes, copy their content, and paste it into the AI assistant I'm using. All of this slows down my workflow.

The frustrating part is that Google has started embracing MCP across its Workspace products. It offers developer preview MCP integrations for Google Drive, Docs, Gmail, and Calendar. But for some reason, Keep is missing. And while there are some unofficial Google Keep MCP servers, I am not comfortable using them.

There's also a Keep API; however, it's primarily meant for enterprise and security use cases.

According to recent reports, keep only talks to Gemini, Google's own AI assistant. However, it's not my preferred assistant for several reasons.

I would love to end this article by saying that I have found a perfect Google Keep replacement with MCP integration. However, that's not the case.

Many note-taking apps offer MCP integration, so finding one isn't difficult when you look outside Google's ecosystem. The problem is that they are not as simple or quick to use as Google Keep. Plus, some excellent note-taking apps are still only available on iPhones and Macs.

Sources indicate that for me, a replacement needs to get the basics right first. I should be able to swiftly open the app and capture a thought in a few seconds. I don't want to select a folder, pick from a template, or deal with an overly complicated interface.

In a recent development, google Keep gets a lot right, which makes moving away from it harder than expected. But my workflow has changed, and I need my note-taking app to change with it.

Recent findings suggest that quickly capturing an idea or note is now only one part of the equation. I also want my AI agent to take action on it automatically, even when I am away from my PC.

Until Google opens up Keep to those assistants, I'll have to look for an alternative that fits how I work.

#423. Should You Sharpen Your Chainsaw At A Higher Or Lower Angle In Cold Weather?

Should You Sharpen Your Chainsaw At A Higher Or Lower Angle In Cold Weather?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So long as you maintain it properly, a chainsaw chain can last a reasonably long time.
  • The reasoning behind this comes down to how wood reacts to colder temperatures.
  • Additionally, this angle lowering will put less strain on your guide bar, since you won't find yourself pushing it through the wood with prematurely dulled blades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So long as you maintain it properly, a chainsaw chain can last a reasonably long time. This entails not pushing it beyond its physical limits, remembering to clean it, and, naturally, sharpening it once the blade edges begin to dull. Adding further nuance to that third task, you should be mindful of the angle you're sharpening the chain blades. As it turns out, when temperatures drop and winter is in full swing, you want to slightly lower the blade angle more than you normally would. This is done to make wood-cutting easier, and put less stress on your tool in the process.

The reasoning behind this comes down to how wood reacts to colder temperatures. Temperatures drop and lead to freezing, which makes trees and branches notable harder than they would be during warmer weather. Thus, you don't want an especially sharp, high-angled series of blades on your chain, as their cutting edge will struggle and break faster on the hardened wood. Instead, you should bring your sharpening angle down by about five degrees, finding a nice balance between your chain's ability to bite through the wood and remain durable enough to avoid breaking down swiftly.

Additionally, this angle lowering will put less strain on your guide bar, since you won't find yourself pushing it through the wood with prematurely dulled blades. That said, as vital as lowering your chainsaw blade's angle is, it's just one part of winter chainsaw use to keep in mind. There are other precautions and chainsaw additions to consider before trimming branches or felling trees in the cold.

It has been revealed that by keeping your blade angle low during the freezing winter months, you've taken care of just one key element of chainsaw use and maintenance during this time of year. There are a few other elements worth highlighting to further ready your chainsaw for winter, such as changing out the chain and bar oil for a winter-specific blend. For the latter, this oil type not only prevents rust and keeps essential parts moving smoothly, but its lower viscosity nature prevents gelling when temperatures get especially low. Therefore, you don't have to worry about performance struggles in this regard during wintertime.

Another great way to prepare for winter chainsaw use is to invest in winter-specific parts for your chainsaw, like starter housing and a winter air filter. This housing piece is excellent for keeping snow from entering the engine area and inhibiting performance, while a winter filter prevents ice formation that could bring similar negative impacts.

Industry observers note that additionally, like in any season, you want to keep your chainsaw clean during winter. That means wiping away debris, and not leaving it covered in snow and water, which could soon become ice. Snow can enter the fuel tank and impair performance, sawdust can trap moisture, and ice can expand and crack sensitive plastic and rubber components. When the work is done, don't forget to store your chainsaw properly, too.

Recent findings suggest that chainsaws, especially great ones, can accomplish a lot, even in the worst of conditions. Still, there's no need to make winter especially hard for your tool, hence why something as simple as adjusting your blade sharpening angle and other minor winter preparation tasks are paramount for making the season's labor just a bit easier.

  • Sources indicate that undaunted, Claude figured out how to retrieve live vehicle information, and as Zulali drove around, temperatures, voltages, and fuel consumption could be analyzed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What do you do when your 32-year-old Jeep Cherokee keeps failing the California emissions test because it's producing too much nitrogen? In the age of AI, you connect Claude up to the vehicle and get it to diagnose and fix the problem for you.

Sources indicate that that's what developer Muhammad Zulali did, using a $3 Arduino microcontroller to sit between Claude and the Jeep's computer system. As you can imagine, the 1994 on-board system was rather outdated, and there wasn't even an OBD2 port to make use of.

Sources indicate that undaunted, Claude figured out how to retrieve live vehicle information, and as Zulali drove around, temperatures, voltages, and fuel consumption could be analyzed. However, the real breakthrough came when the AI copied the Jeep's entire computer system.

That revealed what was potentially the crux of the problem: there was a California-only quirk in the programming that reduced fuel delivery under certain scenarios, which would in turn increase the amount of nitrogen produced.

Not only did the combo of Claude-plus-Arduino figure out what was going wrong, they were able to put a fix in place, writing and applying custom code that changed the fuel delivery settings on the Jeep.

Ultimately, it was enough to get the vehicle passed, around a week after Claude had begun to get to work — another example of how advanced these AI bots are now, and their ability to reverse engineer everything from webcams to Adobe software suites.

"Claude did most of the diagnostic work and Codex did pretty much all of the memory work," says Zulali. "I didn't need a mechanic or a Chrysler dealer tool for any of this... and so the question is, what else can you plug your agent into?".

That said, we wouldn't necessarily advise trying this at home: AI is still very much prone to mistakes, and there's a less than zero chance that meddling with your car with Claude will cause problems rather than fix them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, scoring a game about a young James Bond was "harder than it looks" because they had to avoid using iconic melodies before the player earned his 007 status.

"One of the most important pillars of the game is James Bond earning his 007 status," Henson said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming.

The composer explained that with this in mind, he and Smith "wanted to hold off on the memorable themes for as long as possible, until the player had completed missions worthy of the number!".

"It sounds simple, but it is much harder than it looks," Smith added.

Industry observers note that unlike other Bond stories, whether the long-running film franchise or the video game adaptations, 007 First Light finds James in his late 20s during the early stages of his career in the elite Double-0 training program. The narrative builds across a series of high-octane missions, leading Bond to officially "earn" his agent number, which Smith remarked was an important aspect they needed to demonstrate in the soundtrack.

"The player has bought a James Bond game; they want to feel like the spy they already know," Smith noted. "We had lots of back and forth with the developer, and in the end, I feel the result is successful, teasing the themes until we feel the player really deserves them.".

First Light's James Bond is played by Patrick Gibson, and when asked how the music connects to the younger version of the iconic character, Henson explained that the actor has qualities that not only brought Bond to life, but informed the music.

"Patrick is a young man who is very witty and charming, but with a palpable confidence and inner strength," Henson noted. "These qualities naturally lend themselves to be able to portray a great James Bond at the beginning of his career.".

In a recent development, he added. "We’ve tried to give the music similar qualities, youthful but confident, hopefully reflecting on his unique 007 and the world he navigates through on his first adventure.".

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

#414. Why do camera makers partner on phones? I toured ARRI to find out

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1562 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidcentral

Why do camera makers partner on phones? I toured ARRI to find out

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smartphone makers have long turned to the world’s best camera makers to perfect and refine their smartphone cameras.
  • Recent findings suggest that the birth of the iPhone a couple of years later changed the trajectory of the mobile phone industry, with companies forced to focus on building a smartphone.
  • According to recent reports, since that partnership began in 2016, the same year as Motorola and Hasselblad, we’ve seen many of the world’s biggest phone makers follow suit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smartphone makers have long turned to the world’s best camera makers to perfect and refine their smartphone cameras. The trend has grown considerably over the past 10 years, but it dates back more than 20 years to Nokia’s partnership with Zeiss, which began with the legendary Nokia N95 in 2005.

Recent findings suggest that the birth of the iPhone a couple of years later changed the trajectory of the mobile phone industry, with companies forced to focus on building a smartphone. It would take another ten years before the next big partnership began, but Huawei’s partnership with Leica bears fruit to this day.

According to recent reports, since that partnership began in 2016, the same year as Motorola and Hasselblad, we’ve seen many of the world’s biggest phone makers follow suit. From Vivo to Oppo, Xiaomi to Sony, and this year, even Honor, it’s become commonplace to see companies like Hasselblad, ZEISS, Leica, and more all adorn the back of smartphones.

In a recent development, however, is this just a marketing exercise? How much impact can camera makers have on a smartphone camera? Or is this the inevitable direction for smartphone cameras? To learn more about these partnerships – and how they manifest in the fresh Honor Magic 9 Pro Max – I flew to LA for a tour of ARRI’s labs to understand more.

Here’s the fascinating history of these partnerships, and why camera makers actually partner with smartphone makers.

The Nokia N95 was the first global partnership between a smartphone maker and a camera tech giant, and its partnership with ZEISS produced some of the most iconic smartphone cameras in history, ultimately leading to the legendary Nokia Lumia 1020.

Sources indicate that nokia’s ultimate demise in the face of the iPhone then led to a decade-long hiatus, until 2016, when two companies partnered with two camera makers. The irony? Both camera companies still have phone partnerships today, but neither is with the original partner from that year.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Motorola’s partnership with Hasselblad lasted one year and focused on the Hasselblad True Zoom Moto Mod for devices like the Moto Z Play. The other? Huawei and Leica, a partnership that produced some of the best smartphone cameras of that decade and helped birth the modern zoom-toting flagship smartphone camera.

According to recent reports, huawei’s problems with US sanctions cut the partnership short, but Leica didn’t take long to bounce back: the partnership ended on March 31, 2022, and less than two months later, Leica and Xiaomi declared a new partnership on May 23, 2022. Four years later, Xiaomi and Leica continue to release excellent, distinctive smartphones, including the special-edition Leica-branded Xiaomi 17 Ultra earlier this year.

Industry observers note that not to be outdone, both Oppo and Vivo have turned to camera makers. Oppo’s partnership with Hasselblad started with OnePlus in 2021 and has yielded some of the best smartphone cameras over the past two years, including the new Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, the world’s first phone with three 200MP cameras.

Meanwhile, Vivo’s partnership with Zeiss began a year earlier, in 2020, but it comes with a key difference: the two companies debuted the partnership with a joint Imaging Lab that has produced some of the most powerful smartphone cameras to date.

In a recent development, this leads to Honor and the tech giant announced a partnership with the 109-year-old ARRI earlier this year. The first two phones have both proven unique for different reasons, but why did Honor choose ARRI, and is this just a marketing exercise? My tour of ARRI yielded answers that may surprise you in their refreshing candor.

You probably haven't heard of ARRI, but you've felt the effects of their extremely expensive, extremely precise cameras. Founded in Munich in September 1917, the company has numerous cameras that have made incredible breakthroughs, without which we likely wouldn’t have the smartphone video recording capabilities that we do today.

The biggest impact has been on filmmaking: ARRI is the filmmaker’s camera of choice for many reasons, not least because each camera is individually tested and precisely made. Every tech giant notes this, but after seeing ARRI’s labs in LA, I can attest to their precision. Don’t take my word for it; just look at the awards the company has received:.

The latter point is key, but it's even more pronounced over the past 20 years. Of the last 20 Best Picture winners, 17 were shot on ARRI cameras, and you’ve likely heard of many of them, including Oppenheimer, Everything Everywhere All at Once, CODA, Parasite, Argo, and Slumdog Millionaire.

With such pedigree, what prompted the move to smartphone cameras, and how does Honor fit into this?

According to recent reports, A lot has changed in ARRI’s 109-year history, but the biggest threat the manufacturer likely faces is the generational divide that has coincided with the smartphone. As traditional cameras have fallen by the wayside, the latest generation of consumers likely has no brand affinity for ARRI or other traditional camera makers.

The partnership between Honor and ARRI has the makings of something special. Before this partnership kicked off, Honor had already proven its imaging chops with the Honor Magic 8 Pro last year, but the two devices released with ARRI could yield the biggest jump yet, this time in video.

Sources indicate that the partnership with ARRI focuses purely on video, and the latest Magic 9 Pro Max has an ARRI-branded camera mode reminiscent of the organization’s actual cameras. The partnership focuses on color science, accuracy, and quality in video recording, but crucially, ARRI does not make any of the hardware, at least not right now.

There’s a simple reason: although ARRI cameras have gotten considerably smaller over time, they are still much larger than you can conceivably fit into a smartphone. Further, the firm insists on devices meeting the ARRI quality barometer that its customers have come to expect from its cameras. Instead, it turned to the devices customers use most and, in Honor, found what may be the perfect partner.

Flying to LA to meet ARRI, I had one key question: why Honor… and why ARRI?

To find out, I spoke with Stephan Ukas-Bradley, VP of Product Innovation, who has worked at ARRI for over 20 years, and he gave a surprisingly honest, transparent answer: ARRI’s goal is to introduce customers to its moviemaking magic, no matter what device they’re using.

This highlights up especially well in the first two phones in the partnership. As I discovered, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max takes excellent photos and videos, but the first device in the partnership is the most unique: the Honor Robot Phone.

The world’s first smartphone equipped with a gimbal stabilizer, the Honor Robot Phone is a videographer’s dream… and a moviemaker’s dream, too. Both phones are videographers’ and moviemakers’ dreams, but the most interesting part is how ARRI’s color science is being used.

Both phones can shoot in LogC3, but what makes them unique is the ability to preview the effect of different LUT profiles directly in-camera, rather than waiting for post-production. Taking it further, ARRI has almost 90 different LUT profiles that can be downloaded from its website and installed on the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, and these are the same LUT profiles used in its actual cameras.

This also offers a unique ARRI benefit: the Magic 9 Pro Max and Robot Phone can dramatically change how you scout movie locations.

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, a filmmaker needs to hire a cameraman, several production assistants, and camera gear just to scout locations. ARRI’s best cameras can cost almost $100,000, but a smartphone can dramatically reduce these costs and complexities.

The ability to preview LUTs is the biggest unlock for moviemakers; walking around a shoot and filming on the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max with one of the LUTs – or a custom LUT – installed means you have a strong understanding of the final result while you're on site.

Beyond the current partnership, both companies see an opportunity to expand. For Honor, ARRI provides critical insight into color science, processing, and features, starting with video and possibly extending to photography. For ARRI, it lets it introduce the organization to the next generation of moviemakers, especially those focused on social media content creation.

Whichever direction this partnership heads – and as history has taught us, not all partnerships last forever – one thing is clear: ARRI and Honor are a powerful partnership that has already yielded some of the most impressive video recording on a smartphone to date. I can’t wait to see what this leads to in the future. There's a strong chance that Honor and ARRI will make every best smartphone roundup if this partnership continues to bear fruit.

According to recent reports, nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive, reports The Wall Street Journal. Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future. Whoever succeeds Huang will be the company's second CEO in 33 years. Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into the matter on November 8.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the Fresh York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March. The allegations follow an earlier report that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

A similar controversy cost Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich his position in June 2018, when an internal investigation confirmed that he had maintained a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated the organization's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. It is noteworthy that Nvidia's code of conduct explicitly identifies personal relationships as potential conflicts of interest and instructs employees to consult the company's legal department when such conflicts arise. Whether Huang violated Nvidia's internal policies remains unclear, as the code of conduct does not explicitly prohibit all relationships between managers and subordinates.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team. Although chief financial officer Colette Kress could potentially serve as interim chief executive if Huang is ousted while the BoD searches for a permanent replacement, it remains to be seen how Wall Street would react to this assignment.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who used to be the firm's senior vice president of engineering and operations and remains a member of the company's board and an Nvidia Fellow, could also play a role in the succession process, given his extensive knowledge of Nvidia's technology, corporate culture, and history. However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.
