  • That's because Google is bringing several features that were previously exclusive to the Pixel 11 series to last year's flagships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has announced the November Pixel Drop for Pixel phones, bringing a massive list of newly introduced features to both newer and older Pixel smartphones.

Recent findings suggest that google releases Pixel Drops every few months, bringing fresh features and improvements to its Pixel devices beyond the usual security patches and bug fixes. While some of these updates are relatively minor, the latest November Pixel Drop is a pretty substantial one, especially if you're using a Pixel 10 series smartphone.

That's because Google is bringing several features that were previously exclusive to the Pixel 11 series to last year's flagships.

According to Google's official announcement, the November Pixel Drop brings Gemini Intelligence to the Pixel 10 series, including features like Rambler, Gemini's ability to handle multi-step tasks, and personalized suggestions.

For example, if someone sends you a text asking about your ETA while you're already using Google Maps, your Pixel can provide timely suggestions and actions based on what you're doing.

Another interesting addition is Create My Widget, which lets customers create home screen widgets with natural language prompts. Instead of relying on existing widgets, you can simply describe what you want, and Google will generate one for you.

The feature is available on the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series, although the Pixel 10a is notably missing from the list.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

In a recent development, google has also introduced new custom icon styles with the November Pixel Drop. The company has added 10 different styles to choose from, which use its Nano Banana AI model to generate matching app icons and give your home screen a more consistent look.

Recent findings suggest that beyond customization, Google is bringing its Pixel Search experience to older devices, allowing users to search across apps, messages, photos, emails, and device settings directly from their phones. The feature is now available on the Pixel 6 series and newer devices.

According to recent reports, google hasn't forgotten about its latest phones either, and there are a couple of features exclusive to the Pixel 11 series. Google is upgrading Call Screen with Gemini, allowing the AI assistant to have more natural conversations with unknown callers while showing a live transcript on your phone.

There are upgrades to the HiLight feature on the Pixel 11 Pro phones as well, which can now light up when you receive a Google Messages notification. Unfortunately, there's still no support for third-party messaging apps like WhatsApp or Telegram.

In addition to the Pixel Drop, Google has also announced the availability of the Pixel Tag, which it first unveiled alongside the Pixel 11 series in August. The tracker is now available individually for $29.99 or as a four-pack for $99.99. It uses Google's upgraded Find Hub network and supports ultra-wideband (UWB) for precision tracking.

Sources indicate that as for availability, Google states the November Pixel Drop started rolling out on November 10 and will continue reaching supported devices over the next several weeks. We haven't received the OTA patch on our Pixel 11 Pro just yet, but considering Google's usual rollout schedule, you should hopefully see it arrive on your device within the next few days.

Quietly rolled out over the past few days, Walmart has raised the price of its Google TV streaming devices by $10 a piece. The lineup now starts at about $40, up from just $15 prior to this year. Walmart’s streamers started getting higher prices back in March.

#369. Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal power supply review: 1000W Platinum efficiency with an eye-catching transparent aesthetic

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3012 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal power supply review: 1000W Platinum efficiency with an eye-catching transparent aesthetic

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that built by CWT, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a showpiece that backs its looks with real substance.
  • It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • In a recent development, corsair needs very little introduction to anyone who has built a PC over the past two decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that built by CWT, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a showpiece that backs its looks with real substance. Efficiency is excellent, regulation and ripple are tight, and the fanless window covers half of its rated output at room temperature. Taiwanese capacitors, a noisy hot run and a 200 mm long chassis are the compromises, while the ten-year warranty and iCUE LINK integration add genuine value.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In a recent development, corsair needs very little introduction to anyone who has built a PC over the past two decades. Founded in California in 1994 as a manufacturer of memory modules, the company has since grown into one of the largest brands in the PC component and peripheral market, with a catalog that covers cases, cooling, keyboards, mice, streaming gear, and of course, power supplies. Corsair entered the PSU market in the second half of the 2000s and built its reputation there by choosing its OEM partners carefully rather than manufacturing in-house. Channel Well Technology (CWT) has been one of the most important of these partners, producing a large portion of the RMx and HXi units over the years. The HXi series in particular has long been Corsair's high-end, digitally monitored family, positioned just below the flagship AX models.

Industry observers note that we take a closer look at the HX1000i Shift Crystal to see if it deserves a spot in our best power supplies list. The HX1000i Shift Crystal is a bit of an odd bird, and Corsair is clearly fine with that. First shown at Computex 2026 and launching on November 12th, it combines the side-mounted connector layout of the SHIFT models with the digital HXi platform, and then wraps everything in a chassis with clear polycarbonate panels on three sides, turning the internals of the PSU into a part of the build's aesthetics. Beneath the show, the platform is built by CWT. It holds a Cybenetics Platinum certification at both 115 VAC and 230 VAC, and it is fully compliant with the ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 design guides. It also integrates an iCUE LINK System Hub and Corsair's PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring for the native 12V-2x6 connector. The 1000W model that we are reviewing today is rated to deliver its full power output continuously at ambient temperatures up to 50°C and comes with a ten-year warranty.

Sources indicate that the HX1000i Shift Crystal ships in a very large and sturdy black cardboard box, with a large render of the unit on the front that does a good job of showing off the transparent panels and the lit fan. The model name is printed in substantial yellow and white letters across the bottom half, while the badges in the top right corner - ATX 3.1 with PCIe 5.1 and 12V-2x6 support, the Cybenetics certifications, and the iCUE LINK logo- tell you most of what you need to know before even opening the package.

Industry observers note that the bundle is rather spartan for a product of this class. Inside the box, we found the AC power cord, four mounting screws, a handful of black cable ties, and a leaflet with safety and compliance information. There are no Velcro straps, no cable combs beyond those already on the cables, and no other accessories of any kind. It is not a deal breaker by any means, but a premium unit like this that is focused on aesthetics could have been a little more generous in this department.

According to recent reports, all of the cables are fully modular and black, with individually sleeved wires and low-profile cable combs. There is a 24-pin ATX cable, two 4+4-pin EPS cables, three PCIe cables carrying four 6+2-pin connectors in total, and a native 12V-2x6 cable rated for 600W, alongside two SATA and two Molex cables with four connectors each. Eight Molex connectors on a modern 1000W unit is extremely generous, frankly more than any reasonable build will ever need. Corsair also supplies two iCUE LINK cables of different lengths and a USB cable that connects the PSU's monitoring interface to the motherboard.

Recent findings suggest that with dimensions of 150 x 86 x 200 mm, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a long ATX unit, which is a non-issue if you are getting the matching Corsair 4500X case anyway. In any other case, you will need to check your case's specifications before buying one. The side-mounted SHIFT connectors also require some free space next to the PSU, as the cables plug into the side of the unit instead of its face, which is great for cases with a hidden PSU compartment but not suitable for every chassis. The design is unlike anything else on the market. The steel frame is black, with Y-shaped cutouts forming the fan grille and a debossed pattern of the same shape on the opposite panel, while three of the sides are clear polycarbonate panels that reveal the white fan frame, the bulk capacitors, the coils, and the white PCBs. With the RGB fan lit, the unit very much looks like a piece of display hardware rather than a power supply.

In a recent development, the rear of the unit is a little more conventional, with the AC receptacle, a rocker on/off switch marked with the "HX1000i SHIFT" logo, and a large perforated area with the same Y-shaped cutouts for the exhaust. The modular connector bay is on the side, behind the clear panel. The face opposite the AC receptacle hosts the white control PCB, also visible through its clear panel, with two iCUE LINK ports, a USB Type-C port, and a small port marked "TACH". The hexagonal specifications sticker is on the solid steel top side of the unit and is an envelope-type that can be closed to hide the text.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The CRYSTAL is fully compatible with Corsair's iCUE software, which can be used to monitor the PSU, adjust its fan speed, and switch the 12V overcurrent protection between single- and multi-rail modes. Corsair also integrated an iCUE LINK System Hub that, according to the company, supports up to 24 iCUE LINK devices without the need for a separate hub. The most interesting addition, however, is PinProtect+, Corsair's per-pin current monitoring for the 12V-2x6 connector. If the current on a pin exceeds a user-customizable threshold, the PSU cuts power to the connector, and the RGB fan lighting turns red to signal the fault. Given the history of melting connectors, this is a genuinely useful feature rather than marketing fluff. We can confirm that it is working as intended, as we tried pulling 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector and the PSU shut down instantly.

Cooling is handled by a 140 mm Corsair NR140HL-RGB fan. Corsair calls it a magnetic dome bearing design, and in practice it is a rifle-bearing fan with a half-domed shaft magnet, rated at 0.55A on 12V. The fan is white with addressable lighting, which also doubles as the visual alarm for PinProtect+. It is a decent fan, and the magnetic shaft should help with longevity, but it is worth mentioning that the regular HX1000i SHIFT uses a fluid dynamic bearing fan, which we would normally consider the better choice for a premium unit.

Industry observers note that the OEM behind the HX1000i Shift Crystal is Channel Well Technology (CWT), Corsair's long-time partner for its HXi units. Almost every part inside the unit has been relabeled as "Corsair", including the capacitors and the magnetic components, so the OEM is not obvious at a glance, but the Cybenetics report confirms it. The layout is extremely clean and obviously optimized for aesthetics, which also explains the excessive length of the chassis. The bridge rectifiers have their own heatsink, the APFC components sit on another large heatsink, and the primary switchers have their own heatsink as well, while the secondary side components are on a vertical PCB right after the main transformer. All heatsinks are of good size and quality.

The transient filtering stage has four Y capacitors, three X capacitors, and two filtering inductors. Two bridge rectifiers sharing a large heatsink feed the APFC stage, which relies on two Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs and two fully encased filtering coils. The APFC stage also includes two bulk capacitors, one Corsair 560 μF / 420 V capacitor and one Corsair 470 μF / 420 V capacitor, for a combined capacity of 1030 μF. According to the Cybenetics report, these capacitors are supplied by Elite, a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, and they are rated for 105°C. They are not capacitors that we frequently encounter in anything above mid-tier, though, and we feel they are not a great match for a premium unit.

Sources indicate that the primary inversion stage uses two more Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs in a half-bridge LLC resonant topology. On the secondary side, ten Infineon 014N04LS MOSFETs handle the synchronous rectification of the 12V rail, and the minor rails are derived from DC-to-DC converters. All of the capacitors on the secondary side are rebranded as Corsair, with black and white sleeves that match the color scheme of the unit, and are also made by Elite. These are mostly good parts, but it is a bit ironic that Corsair advertises 105°C Japanese electrolytic capacitors for the regular HX1000i SHIFT, while the version built to show its capacitors off uses Taiwanese ones.

For the testing of PSUs, we are using high-precision electronic loads with a maximum power draw of 2700 Watts, a Rigol DS5042M 40 MHz oscilloscope, an Extech 380803 power analyzer, two high-precision UNI-T UT-325 digital thermometers, an Extech HD600 SPL meter, a self-designed hotbox, and various other bits and parts.

According to recent reports, at 25°C ambient, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a very efficient power supply. It averaged 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC across the nominal load range, with the efficiency peaking at 93.6% (230 VAC) and 92.2% (115 VAC) at around 40% load. The curve is relatively flat after that, with the unit still achieving 91% at 230 VAC and 88.5% at 115 VAC while delivering its full 1000W. The efficiency at very low loads is good as well, at just over 88% with a 50W load on 230 VAC. These figures are in line with the unit's Cybenetics Platinum certification at both input voltages. There is no 80 PLUS certification for this unit.

The acoustics at room temperature are very good. The fan stays completely off up to 50% load, so a typical gaming system with a powerful graphics card will rarely ever wake it up. Once it starts, the unit registers 31.6 dB(A) at 500W, and the fan ramps up very gently, staying around 33 dB(A) at 700W and below 37 dB(A) at 900W. Only at full load does the noise climb to about 39 dB(A), which is still a low figure for a 1000W unit. Thermal performance gives no reason for concern at all, with the primary and secondary heatsinks reaching just 55°C and 58°C respectively at full load.

Inside our hotbox, at roughly 45°C ambient and still within the unit's 50°C rating, the HX1000i Shift Crystal hardly lost any efficiency at all. It averaged 91.7% at 230 VAC and 90.1% at 115 VAC, a drop of just 0.4 percentage points compared to the cold test. The peak efficiency dropped to 93.3% and 91.9%, respectively, and the full-load efficiency to 90.6% and 88.1%. That is a very strong result that shows how well the platform tolerates high ambient temperatures.

The fan is the part that changes its behavior the most in the heat. It starts spinning a bit earlier, at about 400W, registering 32.2 dB(A), and the noise climbs relatively fast to about 36 dB(A) at 600W and 39.5 dB(A) at 700W. Beyond 800W, the fan profile becomes much more aggressive, with the unit reaching 45.7 dB(A) at 900W and 46.8 dB(A) at its maximum output. That is definitely loud, though it takes very adverse conditions to get there. Internal temperatures rose considerably, with the primary heatsink reaching 84°C and the secondary heatsink 89°C at full load, figures that are high but comfortably within what the platform can handle.

Sources indicate that voltage regulation is very good. Across the 20% to 100% load range, the 12V rail deviated by 1%, from 12.10V down to 11.98V; the 5V rail by 1% as well; and the 3.3V rail by just 0.7%. These are not the sub-0.5% figures of the very best digital platforms on the market, but all of the rails are well controlled, and the 12V rail stays very close to its nominal voltage across the whole load range. The ripple suppression is excellent. The 12V rail peaked at 48 mV under maximum load and 44 mV during the 12V cross-load test, while the 5V and 3.3V rails both topped out at 26 mV. Compared to the ATX design limits of 120 mV and 50 mV, that leaves a margin of 60% on the 12V rail and about 48% on the minor rails, which is very comfortable headroom for a 1000W unit.

During our thorough assessment, we evaluate the essential protection features of every power supply unit we review, including Over Current Protection (OCP), Over Voltage Protection (OVP), Over Power Protection (OPP), and Short Circuit Protection (SCP).

All protection mechanisms were verified and triggered correctly during testing. With the unit hot, OCP tripped at 148% (37A) on the 3.3V rail, 144% (36A) on the 5V rail, and 132% (110A) on the 12V rail, with OPP shutting the unit down at 130% of its rated output, or 1300W. These thresholds are on the high side, especially for the minor rails, but they are not unusual for an ATX 3.1 unit.

In a recent development, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a power supply designed to be looked at, and that is not something we often get to say. Corsair took a CWT-built HXi platform, cleaned up its layout to the point that it can be shown off, and placed it behind three polycarbonate panels with an RGB fan on top. The result is unique, and it is backed by a genuinely modern feature set, with ATX 3.1 compliance, full iCUE support, an integrated iCUE LINK System Hub, and a native 12V-2x6 connector with PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring. The latter is more than a bullet point on the box, as the unit shut down instantly when we pulled 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector.

It has been revealed that most importantly, the looks did not come at the expense of performance. The efficiency is excellent, with averages of 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC, and it barely moved when we raised the ambient temperature to 45°C. Voltage regulation is tight on every rail, and the ripple suppression is excellent, leaving a large margin against the ATX limits. At room temperature, the fan does not even spin up before the load reaches 500W and it stays quiet all the way up to the maximum output.

The compromises are few, but some of them are hard to ignore on a unit like this. The capacitors are all made by Elite and rebranded as Corsair. Elite is a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, but its capacitors are not something we frequently encounter above the mid-tier, and they are not a great match for a premium unit when the regular HX1000i SHIFT advertises Japanese capacitors. The fan uses a rifle bearing with a magnetic shaft instead of a fluid dynamic bearing, and it becomes loud under heavy load in a hot environment. The bundle is also spartan for an aesthetics-focused premium product. Finally, the 200 mm long chassis and the side-mounted connectors mean that not every case will accommodate the unit, although most buyers are likely to pair it with Corsair's matching 4500X case anyway. On the bright side, the ten-year warranty covers the unit for a period that very few users will ever need, and it makes the component choices easier to accept.

At the time of this review, Corsair had not made the price of the HX1000i Shift Crystal public, which makes a definitive value judgment impossible. The regular HX1000i SHIFT is the obvious comparison, as it offers the same side connector layout, iCUE integration, and iCUE LINK hub for $339.99 at Corsair's own store, along with a fluid dynamic bearing fan and Japanese capacitors. Compared to other showy high-end units, such as the Asus ROG Thor 1000W Platinum II or the Lian Li Edge 1000, the CRYSTAL is the only one that actually puts its internals on display, and its Cybenetics Platinum efficiency and tight electrical performance mean that it does not need its looks to justify itself. If it arrives at a reasonable premium over the regular HX1000i SHIFT, it is an easy recommendation for anyone building a showcase system, and a well-performing 1000W unit for everyone else who simply likes how it looks, as long as they can live with its parts selection.

Android 17 QPR2 is here, and it’s more than just a Pixel makeover

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that google just pulled a fast one on the calendar by releasing Android 17 QPR2 a month early.
  • According to recent reports, the enhancement, shared by Google's Mishaal Rahman on Reddit, comes after a lengthy beta period, and while some of the changes are currently exclusive to Pixel devices, others may eventually be coming to phones from other Android manufacturers.
  • One of the more apparent changes is a more robust color customization system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google just pulled a fast one on the calendar by releasing Android 17 QPR2 a month early. Riding shotgun with the November Pixel Drop, the patch is rolling out to supported Pixel devices, from the budget-friendly Pixel 6a to the latest hardware.

According to recent reports, the enhancement, shared by Google's Mishaal Rahman on Reddit, comes after a lengthy beta period, and while some of the changes are currently exclusive to Pixel devices, others may eventually be coming to phones from other Android manufacturers. There’s more than just more bug fixes here, especially if you like to have control over how your phone looks and behaves.

One of the more apparent changes is a more robust color customization system. Customers don't have to stick with Google's preset color schemes anymore but instead can bring up a rainbow hue slider and pick a custom system color. There are also four intensity options: Neutral, Soft, Bright, and Bold.

According to recent reports, google is also introducing adaptive light and dark wallpaper support. Compatible wallpaper collections can automatically switch between light and dark versions of their wallpapers depending on the system theme.

Google is giving users more control of the status bar. There’s a new settings page to select whether to show all notification icons, priority notifications only, or none. You can also hide individual system indicators like battery percentage, mute, and vibration.

Another welcome adjustment is the brightness controls. Previously, some apps could lock screen brightness at maximum, preventing people from reducing screen brightness through Quick Settings. QPR2 removes that restriction so you can change the brightness even if an app overrides the setting.

Bluetooth LE Audio gets a major upgrade with the addition of a fresh Voice Broadcast feature. Users can broadcast their voice using the phone’s microphone or a connected wired headset, with nearby listeners tuning in using compatible Auracast headphones, hearing devices, or Android phones. You can also password protect private broadcasts.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Google is improving Auracast discovery with QR codes, NFC tap-to-join, and a dedicated Quick Settings tile. Compatible devices can also make broadcasts easier to follow with Live Caption and Translation.

Foldable owners also get a new handle at the top of app windows, making it easier to move between full-screen apps, split-screen layouts, and floating bubbles.

Recent findings suggest that security-wise, Android has a cleaner app-install dialog, letting you choose between temporary or permanent permission options for sideloading. It also prevents some risky actions during calls from unknown contacts, such as enabling Developer options, and asks you to confirm before executing call-forwarding codes.

There’s also a new Private Compute Core logging option that lets customers see data shared with on-device AI features.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the Linux Terminal app now supports guest-to-host file sharing. The Android file manager will let users manage the Linux virtual machine files and browse, edit, and move them.

Android 17 QPR2 also brings accessibility improvements, lets you customize the keyboard’s vibration, offers better hearing-device controls, and adds an option for a home time zone.

Make sure to opt out of the Android Beta Program first if you want the stable OTA build without wiping your storage. Pixel owners can pull down the over-the-air update from system settings right now, while non-Pixel owners will need to wait for their respective manufacturers to adapt the codebase.

But hours before this move, when it was just rumored that the Nvidia board was planning to oust him, Elon Musk had already stated his willingness to hire the former Nvidia chief on X. @zerohedge That would be an honorNovember 12, 2026.

Despite the scandals that Jensen is currently facing, he still has the engineering know-how, deep knowledge of the industry and its inner workings, plus multiple connections across the world, which would be extremely valuable for any manufacturer looking to break into the semiconductor industry.

This is exactly what Elon Musk is doing with his Terafab project, which he first mentioned in November 2025. Jensen Huang even warned that this was going to be a challenge, pointing out that “the engineering, the science, and the artistry of doing what TSMC does for a living is extremely hard.” Nevertheless, Musk poured his resources into the project, with construction on the Terafab facility in full swing and with plans to hit volume chip production by the second half of 2028. Musk himself noted that the site targets a production capacity of a million wafers a month by 2032. Tesla has an ambitious AI accelerator roadmap, and SpaceX has even touted making its own GPUs in the future.

We still don’t know what Jensen Huang’s intends are, but even though he’s no longer a part of the Nvidia board and its leadership, Jensen and his wife, Lori, still jointly own approximately 800 million Nvidia shares through various trusts and LLCs, while Huang himself personally owns around 70 million Nvidia shares.

Aside from that, he still has an outstanding invitation from Congress to discuss Nvidia’s security protocols, which could turn into a subpoena if he snubs them, although we don’t know how his resignation would affect the closed-door meeting. There’s also a reported FBI investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive who was allegedly instrumental in the import of $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI GPUs into China and is suspected of working with China’s Ministry of State Security.

According to recent reports, jensen Huang is just the latest in the long list of executives who resigned or were ousted from their leadership position because of a relationship or an affair with a subordinate. This includes former Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher in 2005, HP CEO Mark Hurd in 2010, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich in 2018, and former McDonald’s CEO Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Musk himself is known to have had relationships with subordinates from his various companies, and that he has even fathered four children with Shivon Zilis, a top executive at Neuralink who started working at Tesla in 2017, through IVF.

It’s still not confirmed if Musk’s reply is a serious offer for Jensen Huang. But if the former Nvidia chief ever decides to work for Musk on his Terafab project, then Jensen could put his effort and expertise into turning it into a formidable competitor to Nvidia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in my role as TechRadar's Senior Fitness and Wearables Editor, I test a lot of smartwatches and fitness trackers. I've tested around a dozen wrist-based fitness trackers this year alone, and what I haven't tested, I've asked other writers to put through their paces for me.

My personal testing bank this year includes the following:.

The devices that other writers have tested on my behalf include the Garmin Forerunner 70, Samsung Galaxy Watch 9, Amazfit Active 3 Premium, Coros Nomad, Suunto Race 3s, Huawei Band 11 and many more. Then there are the items from previous years, as well as devices such as heart rate monitors and smart rings. Over the years, I've tested a lot of smartwatches and fitness tech, and I'm well placed to advise on which Black Friday smartwatch deals to consider.

So, some readers might be surprised when I say that my advice to the majority is to give most of the above trackers a wide berth on Black Friday, with the possible exception of the Google Fitbit Air and Garmin Cirqa.

Most smartwatches, like smartphones, work on churn: every one to two years, a company will release a newer model of the same watch, with a few newly introduced features and perhaps a minor tweak to the design. It's keeps their watch lines up to date, delivering the best-in-class health metrics for buyers, while ensuring that the range regularly stays level with the competition, rather than becoming outdated and requiring a total overhaul. Technology moves swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that for example, this year saw Apple deliver new Siri AI features and a more accurate, redesigned LED sensor array to the Watch, which better detects your heart rate overnight. Wear the Watch overnight and it will give you a Readiness Score the next day, which tells you how much energy you're likely to have in the tank for the day ahead. This can aid in planning your training sessions, and help you tailor your habits to ensure maximum Readiness when you need it.

These features aren't available on the older watches — but previous models do include everything else. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 look and operate the same as the Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra 3, bar a few other quality-of-life fixes, making them an excellent buy on Black Friday. And retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy in the US, and Argos in the UK will be offering significant discounts to clear old stock.

Recent findings suggest that the Garmin Forerunner 170 isn't likely to see much movement in price, but its predecessor, the Garmin Forerunner 165 will see larger discounts. The Forerunner 165 includes the same Elevate V4 heart rate sensing technology embedded in its case, so it's the design, features and software support that are slightly different in the models rather than any accuracy gains.

The same is true of last year's edition of the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra and the Google Pixel Watch 4, both of which were released in 2025: their 2026 successors are iterative updates on these watches. If the price cut is significant on those older models (and it's already the case on the Samsung model below), you should probably buy the older model instead of the newer one.

In a recent development, we loved the device in our Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra review, praising its tough exterior, user interface and its awesome range of features. However, we did note that the screen is the exact same size as the less expensive Galaxy Watch 7’s and we'd have preferred a bigger battery. That said, if you’re an athletic person looking for an Android-based smartwatch, the Galaxy Watch Ultra is one of your best options.

The same is also true of the Garmin Fenix range: the all-newly introduced Garmin Fenix 9 might be super expensive, but the Fenix 8 from 2024 has already dropped significantly in price:.

According to recent reports, save 24% on the stellar Garmin Fenix 8 in its 47mm size. I rated this watch five stars, calling it "rugged, expensive perfection" in my Garmin Fenix 8 review.

Next year, I'm sure I'll be offering the same advice, but with devices replaced by this year's models instead — it's the nature of consumer technology.

Industry observers note that if you're interested in getting yourself a newly introduced smartwatch or fitness tracker, look at the previous iteration of a product instead of the latest tech. The cycle of small upgrades rather than giant overhauls means that older tech is still plenty good enough for most people's needs — and it's more wallet-friendly, too.

Of this year's crop of devices, the models I recommend picking up are the Google Fitbit Air and the Garmin Cirqa.

Recent findings suggest that why? Simply because they're first-generation devices, so there aren't any historic discounts on older models to be found. In addition, they're unlikely to see a refresh for a couple of years at least — certainly not annually, on account of their limited feature set, the nature of screenless trackers, and the fact that they're both fairly high-quality pieces of kit worthy of a space on your wrist. In particular, the Garmin Cirqa is my pick for one of the best fitness trackers this year. If you see a discount on either, I'd advise you grab one.

Are you getting a newly introduced wearable in the Black Friday sales this year? Let us know in the comments.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's pretty much nothing that Samsung's Galaxy Watch lineup can't do, but deep body fat tracking is one area the tech giant hasn't quite been able to master — not yet, anyway.
  • This speculation comes from a new Samsung patent filing describing a possible upcoming tool as a ’Method and system for estimation of abdominal fat’.
  • According to the patent description, 'the technical result is reduced complexity and increased accuracy and speed of estimation of the abdominal subcutaneous fat area and the abdominal visceral fat area with portable devices'.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's pretty much nothing that Samsung's Galaxy Watch lineup can't do, but deep body fat tracking is one area the tech giant hasn't quite been able to master — not yet, anyway.

This speculation comes from a new Samsung patent filing describing a possible upcoming tool as a ’Method and system for estimation of abdominal fat’. Additionally, the patent says the system would use an ultra-wideband (UWB) radar and would be combined with existing Galaxy Watch tracking metrics to present you with a result.

According to the patent description, 'the technical result is reduced complexity and increased accuracy and speed of estimation of the abdominal subcutaneous fat area and the abdominal visceral fat area with portable devices'.

In a recent development, I know what you're thinking: Samsung wearables have been able to measure body fat since the launch of the Galaxy Watch 4 back in 2021, so what makes this rumored feature any different? Turns out, quite a lot!

When it comes to the upcoming patent, the tracking feature is designed to target and analyze visceral fat, which isn't like standard (or subcutaneous) body fat, which sits just beneath the skin. Visceral fat is found much deeper, mainly around your internal organs, and can only be read with the help of clinical tech such as MRI and CT scans.

In a recent development, not only does visceral fat require advanced tools to be measured, but it's also much more difficult to burn than regular body fat. If the tech in the patent is used, it means that Samsung could be one of the first consumer tech companies to embed a feature into a wearable that's historically been in the control of medical professionals. Smart scales can give you an estimated visceral fat reading, but can come with some inaccuracies.

As mentioned, Samsung's visceral fat tracker would be used against existing features for analysis. As per the finding, the system's UWB radar emits radiation into the abdominal region and measures reflected signals, combining this information with Bioelectrical Impedance (BIA) data and basic metrics including your weight, height, age, and gender.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

The only thing that isn't mentioned in the patent is through which device Samsung intends to introduce visceral fat tracking, but the Galaxy Watch is the safest bet since it already packs BIA sensors that measure patterns and changes in body fat percentage, skeletal mass, BMI, and much more.

The next step for Samsung would be to integrate a UWB sensor — could this be the biggest upgrade for the Galaxy Watch 10?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last week, I was sitting on a plane, thousands of feet above the ground, making changes to a project running on my MacBook Pro at home. I wasn't carrying my MacBook, and I wasn't even using an iPad. Instead, I did everything from the iPhone Duo, and it made me realize how much Apple's first foldable has transformed my workflow.

Recent findings suggest that I've spent much of this year figuring out how to make remote development work for me. I wanted to leave my MacBook Pro running at home, access it from anywhere, and continue working on projects without carrying another computer. The solution was Astropad Workbench, a remote desktop app that lets me interact with my Mac wherever I am.

The only problem? It's iOS-only, so I've been using it on the iPhone 18 Pro instead of on one of the best Android foldables. Whenever I've needed more screen real estate, my iPad Pro has been the natural companion, offering a more comfortable on-the-go desktop experience. That is, until the iPhone Duo arrived.

Apple's first foldable finally brings together the two things I've wanted: an iPhone's portability and the larger iOS screen I've relied on my iPad for. The result is the best balance of portability and screen size I've found for coding on the go. The Duo hasn't fundamentally changed the type of work I'm doing, but it's made the experience of working so much more convenient that I reach for my iPad far less often.

And thanks to a remarkable upcoming feature in Astropad Workbench, it's arguably become an even better way to interact with my development environment.

Industry observers note that an vital note: I'm not writing code directly on the iPhone Duo. Instead, I use Cursor, an AI-powered code editor, to make changes to my projects through its built-in chat interface. It's a fundamental change I made to my workflow earlier this year, and one that's crucial to maintaining and building three large platforms and four mobile apps simultaneously.

It has been revealed that my MacBook Pro stays at home, running Cursor, the local development servers, and everything else my projects need. With Workbench, I can access that desktop remotely, ask Cursor to make changes, scroll through its summaries with two fingers, review the results, and check the running build in Cursor's built-in browser.

According to recent reports, on a Mac or iPad, Workbench feels like a fairly traditional desktop development experience. Its unified display mode resizes your Mac's desktop to fit your remote device's resolution and form factor, aiming to offer a more natural, single-app experience. However, switching between apps isn't particularly straightforward, and navigating the interface can sometimes feel a little jittery.

It has been revealed that on the Duo, I generally keep unified display mode disabled, which lets me pinch and zoom into different areas of the remote desktop. It's a surprisingly effective way to navigate a full macOS interface on a smaller screen, particularly when I want to focus on Cursor's chat or inspect a specific part of a project.

Sources indicate that I can also open Chrome to check a locally running website, although I generally find it easier to do everything within Cursor when using the Duo. The workflow is essentially identical to what I was already doing on my iPad; the difference is that I now have access to it on a device that folds into my pocket.

That sounds like a small distinction, but in practice, it's enormous.

The massive unlock is being able to leave my Mac at home and check progress on any build, including previewing it, without needing to configure every device with my login credentials, SSH keys, or local codebase. Instead of waiting until I'm settled on a plane or pulling out my iPad Pro and Magic Keyboard, I simply unfold my iPhone Duo and keep coding.

It has been revealed that the only problem? It's so convenient that it's taken up even more of my life.

In a recent development, if you've ever tried to use a conventional desktop terminal through a remote desktop app or on a touchscreen, you'll know how frustrating it can be. Tiny text, awkward cursor placement, keyboard shortcuts, and interfaces designed for a mouse and keyboard can make even simple tasks unnecessarily difficult. Add in a Delete key that doesn't always work — a common problem I've encountered across several apps — and text that fails to render properly due to input lag, and even the simplest tasks can rapidly become incredibly frustrating.

That's why a new feature recently introduced in Workbench's Duo-optimized app has promptly become one of my favorite parts of this setup.

Workbench now offers a native terminal interface that lets me interact with the terminal on my Mac remotely, without navigating a traditional macOS Terminal window through the screen viewer. Better still, I can display the terminal alongside the remote desktop in a split-screen layout. It's brilliant.

I can interact with the terminal using an interface optimized for foldables, but with a familiar Terminal design, and then glance across at Cursor or the running build without constantly switching views or changing apps on the remote Mac.

It's a much more natural experience than trying to control a desktop terminal on a folding phone, and it addresses one of the biggest frustrations I've encountered with remote development.

What makes this particularly interesting is how Workbench has embraced the iPhone Duo itself. The team developed a series of experiences optimized for Apple's new form factor, even without a retail sample of the phone to work with.

This is precisely the potential I highlighted in my iPhone Duo review on TechRadar's sister site, Android Central. The hardware is compelling, but Apple's developer ecosystem is the hidden superstar. Give talented developers a upcoming canvas, and they'll find ways to create experiences that simply weren't possible before.

Astropad Workbench is already one of the best examples I've encountered. At $79.99 per year, it might be the best money I've ever spent on a software subscription.

The biggest change isn't necessarily what I can do, but how often I can do it.

Sources indicate that I originally set up Workbench earlier this year because I wanted to keep my development environment running at home while traveling, particularly when flying. Airplane Wi-Fi can be unpredictable, and trying to run development processes directly on a machine with an unreliable connection usually ends badly, especially when you're dealing with code changes or migrations.

With my Mac running everything at home, I can use the connection to interact with my development environment instead of relying on it to keep the underlying processes running. Even if the connection drops, the Mac keeps working. Instead of needing a stable connection for minutes or hours, I only need to stay connected long enough to issue instructions or check progress. The actual work continues on my Mac, whether I'm connected or not.

Over the past week, I've used the Duo to move coding sprints forward, review changes, work through migrations, and have some fairly intense planning discussions with Cursor, including during that flight. I can make meaningful progress without having my actual development machine in front of me.

But the real revelation has been the moments when I'm not traveling.

Sources indicate that I've used the Duo to check on projects while waiting for an Uber, make progress while standing outside, and interact with my Mac during the few minutes before walking into a shop. These aren't situations where I'd ordinarily pull out an iPad, let alone a MacBook.

It has been revealed that that's what makes the Duo so much more useful than my iPad for this particular workflow. The iPad offers a larger screen and a more desktop-like experience, but I have to consciously decide to carry it. The Duo is already in my pocket.

Industry observers note that its folding design gives me useful screen real estate when I need it, and the versatile hinge makes it easy to prop up at different angles. The nano-texture folding display is also a pleasure to use, especially when reading through longer summaries or spending extended periods interacting with the remote desktop.

Recent findings suggest that none of these things fundamentally changes how Cursor works or what my Mac can do. They simply remove the friction between having a few spare minutes and actually getting something done.

And that has completely changed how I approach my projects.

Industry observers note that there are compromises, of course. The iPhone Duo doesn't offer the same expansive workspace as an iPad or MacBook, and Apple's multitasking features still aren't as flexible as those on Android foldables like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. Sometimes, too, a larger screen and a proper keyboard are simply better tools for the job.

Sources indicate that but I'm not trying to replace my MacBook Pro. I'm trying to make the most of the powerful machine I already own, without needing to sit in front of it every time I want to accomplish something.

My iPad made coding remotely possible. The iPhone Duo has made it effortless.

Sources indicate that that's why the combination of the iPhone Duo, Cursor, and Workbench has been so transformative. The Mac provides the processing power and persistent development environment, Cursor handles the code changes, and Workbench gives me a practical way to control everything from a device I always carry.

It's also a compelling demonstration of why software optimization matters so much on foldables. The Duo's hardware makes this workflow convenient, but Workbench's thoughtful approach to the form factor, particularly its latest native terminal, is what makes the experience genuinely powerful.

In a recent development, I've spent years using foldable phones, and I've always believed their potential extends far beyond simply offering a bigger screen. This is one of the clearest examples I've encountered of that potential becoming something genuinely useful in my everyday life.

In a recent development, my Mac hasn't moved from my desk, and my coding workflow hasn't fundamentally changed. But the iPhone Duo has made that workflow available in moments when I would've done nothing at all.

My iPad made coding remotely possible. The iPhone Duo has made it effortless.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all have some old phones lying around, and one Italian Android developer has come up with a nifty way to repurpose them as retro music players.

NostalgicPod is an app that transforms your Android phone into an iPod-inspired music machine, complete with that classic, simple menu interface and simulated click wheel navigation. There are no ads and no distractions — unless you count the small handful of throwback games that are built in, including the likes of Snake and, of course, Brick Breaker.

I've been testing the app throughout the morning, and it's a pretty impressive package that offers a cool way to play local music files. Despite the retro appearance, there are plenty of modern features here too, such as the ability to connect your Apple Music account to access your virtual libraries and a separate menu that lets you browse a selection of internet radio stations and podcasts.

If you host your own music collection, you can even hook the player up to your personal Plex, Jellyfin, or Navidrome servers — something I've been meaning to set up for a while in order to digitally preserve some of the rarer items in my CD collection and might finally now get around to.

According to recent reports, "There are millions of old phones sitting in drawers that still work perfectly fine, but we simply don't use them anymore. With NostalgicPod, you can turn one of those phones into a dedicated music player," NostalgicPod developer Jesús Manuel Curreri tells Android Central.

Industry observers note that "I've always loved that era when devices had their own personality. The iPod Classic, for example, was something special: a wheel, a screen, and all your music," he adds. "You didn't need much more than that. My brother and I actually had one that we shared, and I remember thinking it was the perfect device for listening to music.".

He argues that most modern music apps are too focused on recommendations and algorithms, losing some of the "magic" of truly curating your own library.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Sources indicate that the app, first released a few months ago, was an immediate success and has since been introduced on iOS. "I honestly never imagined the project would go this far," notes Curreri. "When I first launched NostalgicPod on Android, the response was incredible. Several tech publications covered the app, and some of my Reddit posts received an amazing response.".

In a recent development, "I eventually decided to bring the project to iPhone, although getting Apple's approval turned into quite an adventure. It took months of rejections, appeals, and conversations with Apple, but I finally got there!".

Sources indicate that the iOS version of the app shot up to the number three spot in the paid Music category in the US and became number one in Germany. Curreri estimates that across all platforms, NostalgicPod has reached "around eight thousand users over these past few months" thanks to pure word of mouth.

He also says that he intends to continue updating the app with new features, customization options, and performance improvements based on user feedback: "My goal is to keep NostalgicPod a complete, fast, customizable music player that people can enjoy for years, without losing the simplicity of the original experience.".

If you're interested in giving it a go for yourself, you can pick up NostalgicPod for $4.39 / £3.99 on the Google Play Store.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.
  • Industry observers note that effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls.
  • Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Industry observers note that effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an upgrade as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Recent findings suggest that depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware upgrade or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that yandex, sometimes called Russia’s Google, has updated its customers in the wake of extensive damage to its data centers in drone strikes. In a blog post this week, the firm’s cloud business boasted that it had “restored access to more than 97% of customer data” [machine translation]. That might sound like a great success, but in the small print, as highlighted by The Register, there’s the admission “the remaining 2.84% cannot be restored due to critical damage to equipment.”.

Industry observers note that data centers operated by Yandex have been under attack from Ukrainian drones for several weeks now. We covered reports about withering online troll activity and online payment system disruption last month. We know of at least three Yandex locations that have been damaged by Ukrainian drone assaults to date.

In a recent development, the recent Yandex blog post also appears to blame the small proportion of people who suffered unrecoverable data loss for not making backups. When talking about the 2.84% of data that cannot be restored, it says that was partly due to “the lack of customer backups on the platform.” In contrast, those who made use of the Yandex Cloud backup tools “did not lose any data,” says the firm.

Industry observers note that yandex has now changed the backup policy, so that “at the moment, all virtual machines created in Yandex Cloud work with the backup function enabled by default.” Even if Putin decides to end his war on Ukraine, it might be beneficial to stick with a backup-by-default policy. People are advised to have their own data backup systems in addition to the cloud. Following the 3-2-1 backup strategy, for example.

Yandex is also opening a fresh ru-central1-f availability zone at a new location. This is designed to improve the cloud’s fault tolerance and disaster resilience. Servers at ru-central1-f will be more limited in the range of services they can offer, for now. Yandex didn’t share any geographic details of the newly opened datacenter site.

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the tech giant’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

Industry observers note that “BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

Industry observers note that I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

Sources indicate that the other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”.

Recent findings suggest that technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Booklight is also on the Play Store.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

The anticipation for the next installment of The Hunger Games saga has never been this fierce (I should know; I've had my IMAX screening tickets booked for weeks), and it seems Google is holding its own celebrations ahead of the Second Quarter Quell.

If there's one thing Google is great at, it's the fun Easter eggs in its web and mobile search engines, especially when it comes to huge movie launches. The organization did one for Wicked (2024), making your search results 'defy gravity', but its latest one is all about the upcoming The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping movie, which arrives in cinemas on November 20.

Recent findings suggest that when you search 'The Hunger Games', 'Sunrise on the Reaping', or 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' on Google, you'll find a symbol depicting a snake entwined with a mockingjay bird (or the 'flint striker' as hardcore fans know it). Click on it, and you'll be transported down an interactive rabbit hole that tests your knowledge of all things from the world of Panem.

Basically, the feature is a 12-step quest that leads you through a series of questions intertwined with interactive games you have to play to unlock the answers. Split into six sections, once you complete each one, it unveils one digit of a six-digit code that you can crack to unlock files and 'access The Capitol vault'. It's simple, but once you get sucked in, you'll find it's quite addictive.

According to recent reports, starting off simple and easy, Google tests your Hunger Games literacy with questions such as 'Who stated "I volunteer as tribute"?', which you have to unlock by completing a memory game. It seems like a breeze at first; you're also asked questions about other characters, but then it really tests your Panem knowledge — I can't lie, I started to sweat a little.

Sources indicate that as you complete each quest, the tasks and questions get progressively more challenging to the point where you're quizzed on each District's specialty trade, which, if you've read the books back-to-front, should be a piece of cake. For someone who hasn't read the books (me), this part takes some time to complete.

In a recent development, luckily, these rounds are quite lenient, eliminating the options you get wrong until you find the correct answer. Although that does mean you have to keep track of which District matches which trade. I played them multiple times, and I still can't remember if District 3 is technology or fishing.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

It has been revealed that once you've completed every quest, you unlock access to a video that stars one of the actors from the upcoming movie, along with one final clue to complete the final puzzle. However, each outcome is different for each player, but when you combine the final clues, it forms the phrase 'the snow may fall, but the sun also rises'.

Type this into the Google search bar, and you'll be taken through to an exclusive, unlisted YouTube video with additional trailer footage from the movie, marking the end of Google's Hunger Games scavenger hunt.

Google's Hunger Games search engine quest is still live, but it's likely to disappear when the movie is released on November 20.

#345. macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (650 w)
Gadgets 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomshardware

macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the eternal spiral of computing gets yet another loop.
  • Stela is a minty-fresh fresh project from Tyler Smith, and it's just gotten started, with three releases since the first 0.1 version in barely half a day.
  • The developer answered a couple of questions in the project's Discord server, and he remarked that the macOS image to be used is not modified at all: "Stela provides the translation and hardware behavior underneath that lets macOS go through the exact same restore process you might do on a real Mac.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the eternal spiral of computing gets yet another loop. Apple introduced its own Arm-based chips in 2020, surprising the world with a series of SoCs with a particularly high power-to-watt ratio, a perfect fit for the organization's quality portables. As the designs improved on raw performance, Apple shifted away from Intel-based Macs. That meant that enterprising hackers who ran macOS on their PCs could no longer do so — until today, thanks to the Stela Apple Silicon translation layer.

Stela is a minty-fresh fresh project from Tyler Smith, and it's just gotten started, with three releases since the first 0.1 version in barely half a day. The author warns that "it is slow and not very stable," but those warnings are somehow invisible to techies trying out a new toy. For practical purposes, Stela is a Linux-based UEFI application for loading macOS 27, presenting a virtual M2 Mac Mini to the operating system.

The developer answered a couple of questions in the project's Discord server, and he remarked that the macOS image to be used is not modified at all: "Stela provides the translation and hardware behavior underneath that lets macOS go through the exact same restore process you might do on a real Mac.".

The server has seen a substantial influx of users, many of them posting photos of their PCs near-booting macOS. Predictably, most of the questions were about supporting their own particular hardware, but the excitement is palpable.

It has been revealed that to get started, all you need is to download Stela from the release pages, provide a USB stick to then boot your PC with, and, naturally, your own copy of macOS. Stela will take care of translating AArch instructions into x86-64. The translation layer uses a combination of ahead-of-time and just-in-time (JIT) compilation for the CPU, and translates Apple's Metal graphics layer calls to Mesa's NIR instructions.

The hardware requirements are basically potato-level, requiring only an x86-64-v2 — a 2008 Intel Core chip, or a 2011-vintage AMD FX processor. The author mentions that AVX2 and AVX-512 "are used when present," but woe betide you if your processor is that old to begin with. You'll need 8 GB of RAM, UEFI support, a GPT partition or entire drive, and an Nvidia card from the 16xx series to present-day 5000 models.

There's no Wi-Fi support yet, and Bluetooth is limited, but the list of working Ethernet controllers is extensive, covering models from Intel, Realtek, Broadcom, Aquantia, Atheros, and even USB Ethernet sticks. The author says that he intends for Stela to eventually support all the hardware the Linux kernel does.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Purely hypothetically, with AI automation, it's not completely insane to think that much of macOS could be pre-translated to x86-64. Yet such an endeavor has many caveats, namely the fact that a lot of code, like a browser's JIT JavaScript compilation, doesn't exist on the disk image to begin with.

There's also the fact that no matter how efficient a translation layer is, the OS still needs to cryptographically accept it and run it, perhaps requiring further modification still. But we can, in fact, dream of ditching Windows for macOS without being tied to Apple's pricey and barely-repairable hardware.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at latest hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing customers of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but reveals the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.

Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe, but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera prepares we’ve seen to date.

Personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for upcoming ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. Cutting lenses and skimping out on upgrades (again) doesn’t help matters.

Sony’s 1000X The Collexion succeeds in what it sets out to do: create an immersive bubble of sound you can lose yourself in for hours, with supreme comfort and serious audio quality. To celebrate the 10th anniversary of the 1000X, first debuted in 2016, Sony’s 1000X The Collexion is meant to be the pinnacle of its design aesthetic, offering “a spacious, wide-range sound designed for relaxed, immersive listening.” Sony truly delivers on those promises, elevating the 1000XM6 to new heights.

If you already enjoyed the previous 1000X over-ear headphones, you’ll love The Collexion.

Nothing is perfect, though, so let’s dive into Sony’s luxury headphones, and I’ll get into all of the details that you need to know!

Bluetooth 6.0, 3.5 to3.5Multipoint support.

30 mm carbon fiber/unidirectional carbon composite bespoke drivers.

Industry observers note that max. 24 hours(ANC ON), Max. 32 hours(ANC OFF).

USB-C, 3.5 hrs for full charge; 5 min charging for up to 1.5 hrs playtime.

10-band EQ (app), DSEE Ultimate AI upscaling.

In a recent development, I’ve reviewed luxury headphones from Bowers & Wilkins, Noble Audio, FiiO, Dali, and others, and the 1000X The Collexion feels every bit as luxurious. While the 1000XM6 headphones are very comfortable, I have a huge melon, and the earcups can feel a bit too cozy after long periods of wear.

According to recent reports, that’s no longer the case with 1000X The Collexion (1000X going forward). They are beautifully crafted, from the yokes to the accents. Though they no longer fold into a “ball” like the XM6, their case is only slightly larger.

According to recent reports, the cans glide on new metal arms with ease and look every bit the high price you’re going to pay for them. The metal, soft faux leather, and soft-touch materials create a tactile experience unlike what the XM6 offers. The 1000X feels hefty, substantial, but not heavy on my head at all.

The earcups are deeper and softer than the XM6, and though those have plenty of vertical travel to adjust to the right fit for you, the 1000X just feels more premium in its glide and fit. They kept the springs that let them tilt so they sit firmly against your head, but the clamping force never felt fatiguing for me. Not even after hours-long listening sessions.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

It has been revealed that the oversized silver grommets around the ports and silver buttons give the headphones an industrial-art aesthetic that complements the mirror-polished yokes. During my testing period, I found the 1000X more comfortable than the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2, which cost $150 more. That's largely because of the generous earcups and their soft faux leather.

All of the embellishments and comfort should be expected, though, at $650 for this limited-edition pair of active noise-canceling headphones that you can pick up directly from Sony or at various online and brick-and-mortar retailers.

I listened to my test playlists, utilizing Bluetooth 6.0 with both the LDAC and LE Audio codecs, connected to a Google Pixel 11.

In a recent development, I also connected via wire to the FiiO M21 DAP and listened to Hi-Res audio and MP3 audio to test the DSEE Ultimate. During my testing, I compared them to the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2, Sennheiser HDB 630, and the Sony WH-1000XM6 over-ear headphones, with some interesting results.

It has been revealed that the venerable WH-1000XM6 sits atop many people’s lists for its sound quality and its active noise canceling, but Sony has taken sound quality even further. Let’s talk about ANC first, though, because what you get with the 1000X ultimately comes from the decision to upgrade the sound quality.

When it comes to top-tier over-ear wireless headphones, there are generally two camps: those that prioritize ANC potency over audio quality, and those that prioritize audio quality over ANC. For the former, we’re talking about Sony, Bose, and Apple. For the latter, we’re talking about Sennheiser, Bowers & Wilkins, Noble, Dali, and Focal.

So, how does Sony do with its everyday-use XM6 against the luxury 1000X? ANC efficacy across the frequency spectrum is better with the XM6. You’re getting better mid- and high-frequency performance out of the XM6, and that’s because sound quality is prioritized with the 1000X.

It has been revealed that that said, most people who do a 1-to-1 test between the two and their ANC strength probably won’t notice a significant difference. The difference I did notice was an audible improvement in soundstage size with the 1000X with ANC on. While ANC may be slightly weaker with the 1000X, they’re more open.

Industry observers note that they have a noticeably larger soundstage where the airy feeling of Lady Blacksmith Mombaza’s intro on Paul Simon’s “Diamonds on the Souls of Her Shoes” feels like you’re listening to it at the Hollywood Bowl. Jazz arrangements like that on Thelonious Monk’s “Monk’s Dream (Take 8)” sound more like live productions than the somewhat constricted headspace you get with the XM6.

My only complaint with the stock sound of the 1000X is that it’s missing a bit of sparkle, like what you get with the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2. Listening to those, music really comes alive and feels live, like you’re sitting next to the musician. The Px8 S2 also excels with microdetails, though the 1000X has very good detail retrieval.

It has been revealed that the 1000X exceeds the Px8 S2 in bass response, though. The Px8 S2 can’t match the 1000X’s low-frequency rumble and sub-bass reproduction, and if you want to dial that low-end frequency response back a bit, you have more control with Sony’s Sound Connect app’s 10-band EQ. Bowers & Wilkins gives you only five bands.

According to recent reports, the next-best option is the Sennheiser HDB 630, which has a stock EQ and bass response very similar to the 1000X, but you get even greater sound-shaping control with Sennheiser’s parametric EQ. What you don’t get with the large HDB 630 is the same level of ANC as the 1000X or the same portability, since the HDB 630 has a larger case and feels bulkier.

In a recent development, sony’s Sound Connect app is very well done. It’s well laid out, easy to customize, and gives you plenty of options to tailor the headphones' listening, calling, and ANC experiences.

Recent findings suggest that I really like the case, too. It is a bit large, but I like the styling, with the built-in handle. That detail feels like a luxury upgrade over the XM6. As much as I do like the Platinum color that I have for review, if I were buying, I’d go with black. I can see the soft-touch surface on the earcups becoming problematic with smudges.

In a recent development, these don’t have enough clamping force to wear to the gym. Also, for $650, I’d avoid getting them sweaty. If I need tunes to propel me through workouts, I’d worry a lot less about gym-centric headphones like Apple’s Beats 360.

You can listen to them via a wired connection, which I don’t think many will take the time to do. You should, though, because that opens up a whole world of lossless audio options. Given that these are more for static passive and active listening sessions, wired listening could be a “no-brainer.” Just keep in mind that they support wired via a 3.5mm cable, not USB-C.

Like a spa treatment for your ears.

The Sony 1000X The Collexion is one of the most comfortable over-ear ANC headphones I've reviewed to date. Add very strong ANC, solid detail retrieval and clarity, and excellent app-based customization options, and you have a solid contender in the luxury headphone market.
