💡 Key Takeaways
  • An AI enthusiast managed to get his old 1994 Jeep Cherokee to pass the California smog tests, all thanks to the help of AI and a little electronics wiring skill.
  • Industry observers note that the above video documents Muhammad Zulali’s journey from the Jeep failing consecutive smog tests, to managing to hook it up and get readings from the ECU, to tuning and fixing the engine emission issues.
  • In a recent development, this rather old Jeep was failing the California smog tests due to producing too much NOx at certain test speeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An AI enthusiast managed to get his old 1994 Jeep Cherokee to pass the California smog tests, all thanks to the help of AI and a little electronics wiring skill. This 32-year-old car had only a primitive engine computer, but after connecting it to a laptop via an Arduino Nano board, many settings could be read and eventually controlled.

Industry observers note that the above video documents Muhammad Zulali’s journey from the Jeep failing consecutive smog tests, to managing to hook it up and get readings from the ECU, to tuning and fixing the engine emission issues. All the while, Claude provided guidance, and Codex wrote any required code.

In a recent development, this rather old Jeep was failing the California smog tests due to producing too much NOx at certain test speeds. It initially failed at 25mph. Then, after Zulali made some adjustments to the oxygen mix, it failed at both 25mph and 50mph. Yes, it got worse.

Zulali admits he was effectively making adjustments blind, and subsequent regulatory pollution tests cost nearly $100 each time. That’s clearly a big problem, but we have AI to help us in 2026. Actually, it was AI and a $3 microcontroller, contributing to a total bill of materials of no more than $15.

In a recent development, the first hurdle facing the possible AI solution was the question of how to interface an old car and a upcoming laptop. Claude told the Jeep owner that the engine communicated on a Chrysler SCI bus at ~7,800 baud, which was electrically inverted compared to a typical serial port. An Arduino Nano can handle the required inversion and hook up the data to a modern computer. The Nano was breadboarded, with a few necessary wires, three of which connected to the 6-pin diagnostic plug in the Cherokee.

Industry observers note that the first connection attempt was a success, but only coolant temperature and battery voltage were charted by the system to begin with. Zulali wanted more data points plus some controls to fix the smog test problem. After a couple of red herrings regarding the engine “running rich” with 22% extra fuel, based on other car model data, the Jeep owner got Claude to collect data from test drives. The AI logged engine data and fault codes during a drive at 25 mph and at 50 mph to see what was happening. It was also let loose to control things like fuel pressure.

With what looked like a credible diagnosis and solution in hand, Zulali wanted to reflash the car’s main ECU with AI-tweaked code that would mean it could pass all the California smog tests. Unfortunately, this car’s computer was just a few months too old to feature reflashable firmware. Instead, the Jeep owner got Codex to inject and run custom code inside a nearby EEPROM.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

“Claude did most of the diagnostic work and Codex did pretty much all of the memory work,” admits Zulali. “I just did the wiring and the driving.” He added that he didn’t need the services of a mechanic or a Chrysler dealer tool for this feat.

In addition to the video, the Cherokee emissions fixer has created a GitHub repository for this project, dubbed xj-scanner. It is free software distributed under the GPLv3 license.

Logitech has revealed a upcoming worker initiative which gives employees a day off to play video games - just days before the release of GTA VI.

The company claims the thinking behind 'Logi Game Day' is to formally recognize "the cognitive and professional benefits of gaming" - and that the timing is purely coincidental.

Employees will be able to take one day off from this month until the same period in 2027 to play a game of their choice.

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” said Hanneke Faber, Logitech’s chief executive officer. “As a manufacturer designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”.

The idea is backed up by official findings - the company’s recent Logitech Ctrl Tomorrow study found 81% of gamers believe that gaming builds real-world confidence, reduces anxiety, and correlates with stronger day-to-day work performance.

Similarly, another company study found a staggering 98.8% of enterprise ITDM respondents reported gaming skills directly translate to workplace capabilities, including strategic thinking, complex problem-solving, and performing under pressure.

According to recent reports, "Play is not the opposite of work," Elaine Laird, Logitech's chief people officer, added. "When people have dedicated time to log off, decompress and immerse themselves in play, they return with clearer focus, renewed energy and fresh approaches to complex challenges.".

The launch of GTA VI is one of the most hotly-anticipated events in entertainment history, with millions of gamers around the world set to download and get playing on its November 19 release date.

However that is a working day for many, so worldwide productivity may see somewhat of a drop - with one report suggesting the US economy alone could lose as much as $1 billion in productivity as 1.5 million workers potentially skip work.

For its part, Logitech will be hosting a streaming event at its Americas headquarters to celebrate Game Day.

#337. Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI proposal has a giant Gemini problem

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1499 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google

Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI proposal has a giant Gemini problem

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, good morning.
  • Read previous problems here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.
  • The relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, good morning. Today I’m trying desperately not to buy Sony’s newly introduced nostalgia-bait headphones, reeling from how emotionally invested I was in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (yes, I know I’m late), trying to figure out what a “private, agentic notebook” is, and slowly coming around to the idea of the New York Times owning Letterboxd.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous problems here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

The relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence. Samsung is Android’s physical emissary, powering a plurality of all its handsets globally. But Google, and in particular its services, is the glue that holds Samsung’s smartphone experience together.

It has been revealed that the back and forth is over a decade old; back in early 2014, Samsung shipped a refreshed magazine-style skin with its Galaxy tablets that eschewed many of the design tenets Google had been pushing its partners to adhere to. Not only was Samsung willfully defying its most important partner, but it made a point of barely mentioning Android during its press conferences.

Around the same time, it transitioned its smartwatches from Android Wear to Tizen and began shipping duplicative apps on its devices (many of which persist to this day). The goal was to distance itself from Google as much as possible.

It has been revealed that while we don’t know exactly what happened behind closed doors, we saw the outcome quite clearly: Magazine UX lasted one product cycle, and the two companies signed a 10-year cross-license patent deal, which may have helped Samsung prevent any future lawsuits with Apple. Google then sold Motorola to Lenovo, clearing the way for Samsung to continue building its burgeoning hardware business on the back of Google’s mobile ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that since then, the two companies have grown even closer. In 2021, they co-revealed a new Wear OS along with an overarching wearables partnership that has since grown to include Android XR as well. And Google is still the default search engine for Samsung devices, despite reported inroads made by Microsoft in 2023 to convince the Korean giant to switch to a ChatGPT-powered version of Bing Search. (Samsung’s ongoing relationship with Microsoft, which bundles its Office suite on most Galaxy devices, could be seen as a point of leverage for negotiations with Google, too.).

This brings us to today, and to AI. Samsung was among the first companies to adopt Google’s full suite of Gemini Intelligence products, and its phones often get upcoming AI features before anyone else. But like a decade ago, when Samsung shipped Bixby to kind-of-sort-of compete with Google Assistant, it still wants to offer its own services alongside Google’s.

So a rumor that Samsung may launch a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription next year for $5/month piqued my interest for the same reason Magazine UX did 12 years ago. Galaxy AI features today are a blend of first-party and third-party capabilities, but none of them are especially useful, particularly when compared to Google’s own Android equivalents powered by Gemini Intelligence. Now Bar and Now Brief, two heavily promoted features in Samsung’s marketing, are wildly disappointing.

In a recent development, at I/O this past May, Google confirmed Spark, an agent that goes out and performs actions on your behalf. And while it’s since been somewhat eclipsed by more capable mobile options like Meta’s Muse, it’s obvious that Google is working on a follow-up that will perform functions both on the phone and inside apps.

That’s exactly what Samsung is rumored to be working on with Bixby Action, a spiritual successor to its namesake that, when it debuted, prioritized on-device tasks like turning on Wi-Fi over web-based actions Google Assistant did better.

According to leaks from SamMobile, Galaxy AI Premium will offer agentic upgrades for phone customers to “create commands triggers and system routines for daily tasks” or “automate routine daily tasks using Galaxy AI.” Gen Video will reportedly “convert static photos into dynamic video clips,” while a new Daily Briefing likely does what it says on the tin.

Will Samsung users see enough value in this hodgepodge of features paywalled only because they use a surfeit of compute? And what models will power them on the backend?

Right now, Google is in the enviable position of being able to offer its AI at three distinct layers: the model itself, which is invisible to the user; the OS level, which can promulgate Gemini across every Android phone that runs Google services; and the hardware level, where Pixel lets it specialize and optimize.

Samsung, not particularly known for its software prowess, will likely need to step gingerly around Google’s AI shadow while also justifying the cost to shore up its much-needed services revenue. Based on this leaked roadmap, though, I’m not confident it will work out.

Instead, Samsung may want to acquire one of the many up-and-coming AI agent startups whose valuations are rising more quickly than their user bases. While Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have taken up most of the recent conversation, I’ve been using Hark, Town, and Instinct pretty regularly for a month or so and could see them being brought in-house by Samsung and offered either as standalone products or customized for Galaxy devices. As Google is doing with its own AI plans, Samsung could provide Galaxy users a year of free service, after which they would be expected to pay.

Industry observers note that samsung doesn’t have a great history of building software, but many of its acquisitions, from SmartThings to Viv Labs (which became “next-gen” Bixby) to LoopPay (which became Samsung Pay) to Whisk (which became Samsung Food), have proven successful. Given the current urgent state of mobile AI, I’d forgo the hodgepodge and bring in some outside expertise.

Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy is the only thing tech media can talk about right now, likely because it has implications far beyond just Nvidia’s stock price. The Nvidia CEO, who is one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech executives, is believed to have been targeted by Chinese intelligence to potentially influence American trade policy around AI.

Alex Kantrowitz’s Major Technology piece is a useful starting point for why this matters at a global scale:.

In a recent development, beyond the affair, the real issue is that Huang’s love interest, ex-Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, is someone the United States government believes passed information to the Chinese government while building data centers with Nvidia’s help in Asia. There’s simply no getting away from this detail. This isn’t just an affair, it’s a corporate and national security issue.

Whether Huang can survive the impending investigation by Nvidia’s board remains to be seen, but the CEO has been a stalwart in the tech space for 33 years, and there is no clear successor to his position should he be forced to resign.

Damien reviewed DroidDeck, which I wrote about last week as part of a broader look at Android’s gaming renaissance.

Over the last few days, things have become even more preposterous: the Ocarina of Time remake, which was released on Thursday, has already been recompiled to run natively on Android (though it runs better on PC), largely with the help of frontier AI models.

All of these AI-powered shenanigans come after Anthropic remarked it would stop making it possible to recreate copies of games, claiming that “recreating someone else’s specific game using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.” Good thing there are no other models capable of doing the same thing.

I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.

—David Ellison, Skydance CEO, when asked about how AI could impact the movie-making process.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, google faces a fresh EU setback as Advocate General Kokott backs a €1.49 billion antitrust fine over AdSense practices. An EU court overturned the penalty in 2024, and the European Commission is now challenging that ruling.

Google has suffered a setback in its legal battle with the EU after an adviser to the bloc’s top court backed a €1.49 billion ($1.7 billion) antitrust fine against the manufacturer. The penalty was earlier imposed over Google’s online advertising practices. It was overturned by a lower court in 2024. However, the EU is now challenging the decision.

In a recent development, the original case dates back to 2019, when the European Commission accused Google of using unfair practices in the online search advertising market. It was particularly blamed for restricting competition. The watchdog noted the company used clauses in the contract to prevent rival advertisers from placing ads on its websites. Google allegedly used the clause to maintain its dominant position in the market.

Sources indicate that google‘s AdSense platform provides search advertising to publishers. After the EU issued a notice to the company, it removed the disputed clauses from its agreements in 2016. Despite this, the Union continued its case against the company. After all, it imposed a $1.7 billion fine in 2019.

Back in 2024, a General Court overturned the Commission’s decision. It also prompted Google to appeal to the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg.

Sources indicate that in the latest move, Advocate General Kokott has criticised the lower court’s assessment. She said the court did not examine the criteria used to impose a fine on the company. However, her say is not a final decision. The Court of Justice of the European Union will have the final say. While it usually follows the recommendations of its advocates general, the final verdict cannot be predicted. The final decree is expected to be delivered next year, which will decide whether Google will have to pay the fine or not.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yandex has recovered 97.16% of customer data affected by Ukrainian drone strikes against its Russian data centers, although some information remains permanently inaccessible.
  • The Russian technology giant confirmed that the remaining 2.84% could not be restored due to equipment damage and the absence of backup copies.
  • Customers who had activated its backup tools before the incidents retained their information, with no losses reported among those accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yandex has recovered 97.16% of customer data affected by Ukrainian drone strikes against its Russian data centers, although some information remains permanently inaccessible.

The Russian technology giant confirmed that the remaining 2.84% could not be restored due to equipment damage and the absence of backup copies.

Customers who had activated its backup tools before the incidents retained their information, with no losses reported among those accounts.

The attacks began on October 8 2026, when Ukrainian drones struck a Yandex facility in Sasovo, located within Russia’s Ryazan region.

This site, operating since 2014, housed two of the organization's three supercomputers, Chervonenkis and Lyapunov, with respective peak capacities of 29.42 and 20.03 petaflops.

Further strikes the next day hit Yandex installation at Grabtsevo industrial park in Russia's Kaluga region, which it describes as its largest computing facility and among Russia’s biggest installations for commercial data processing and storage.

Another attack followed on October 11, when Ukrainian drones struck a facility in Vladimir housing Galushkin, the tech giant's third supercomputer.

Galushkin has a maximum performance of 20.64 petaflops, adding another significant computing asset to the facilities affected during the three days.

The organization has not disclosed how the lost customer information was distributed across the affected facilities or how many customers were involved.

In total, about five data centers belonging to Yandex, Sberbank, and VK were struck across Russia in October 2026.

Following the incidents, Yandex announced that backup protection would become active automatically whenever customers create latest virtual machines through its cloud platform.

Customers can still switch off the feature through the management console, meaning the new default does not make backup protection compulsory.

The firm also introduced another availability zone, identified as ru-central1-f, operating from a separate physical location to provide additional service continuity.

The latest zone adds another location for hosting workloads, although the announcement does not establish that it can replace information already lost.

The incidents have also prompted some Russian businesses to examine hosting arrangements outside the country, particularly in neighboring Kazakhstan.

Yevgeny Svidersky, vice president of cloud services at ITGlobal.com, told Kommersant that interest in Kazakh facilities had increased.

Two other industry sources claim that certain companies had already started moving operations to facilities beyond Russia's borders.

Those sources linked the decisions to concerns about further damage to domestic computing infrastructure and possible interruptions to business services.

However, there is no mention of the specific companies involved, the volume of data or infrastructure being transferred, or whether the move represents a permanent relocation.

In a recent development, jensen Huang had a stunning fall from grace — from being one of the richest people on Earth and one of the primary drivers of the AI boom to being implicated in two extramarital affair scandals and resigning from Nvidia in under two weeks. While many are focused on the former Nvidia chief’s relationship with Alice Huang, who was allegedly passing on information to Chinese intelligence, the Wall Street Journal dug deeper into the person who introduced her to Jensen — Kang Wei, a star fund manager in Shanghai who also happened to be Ms. Huang’s husband.

There have been reports that Kang Wei met Jensen Huang in the 2010s, when his investment firm was heavily involved in Chinese gaming companies. It’s not clear if this introduction predated Kang’s relationship and marriage to Alice, but sources close to Ms. Huang said that she was able to get close to Jensen by the 2020s. Despite being a couple, the WSJ reported that Kang seemingly accepted Alice’s relationship with Jensen, with people close to the couple saying that he would often joke that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire.

Recent findings suggest that kang Wei is not just an average business executive, though. He made a name for himself in the finance world as a strategist for Shenyin Wanguo before taking over the Zhonghai Fund in 2007. This made him one of the youngest mutual fund chiefs in China at that time, before finally setting out on his own and founding Shanghai Hexi in 2010.

In a recent development, it was also around this time that Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, entered the financial industry, first working at HSBC’s private banking arm in Hong Kong, before moving to CITIC Securities, where she attained a vice president position. It was during her time at CITIC that Alice crossed paths with Kang. Shanghai Hexi signed a deal with the securities firm in 2014 and 2015, and by 2016, corporate registry records show that Ms. Huang had joined the investment firm.

Recent findings suggest that the Economic Times reports Alice Huang’s move into Shanghai Hexi resulted in her getting a 25% stake in the manufacturer, all of which came from Kang. The remaining shares were shared between Kang Wei, with 48.75%, and his business partner, Zhu Xiaoming, with 26.25%, with Alice Huang’s 25% ownership stake being held through Shanghai Yuxi Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd. Meanwhile, Kang also started introducing Alice Huang as his wife to his business associates and investors.

One year later, Zhu and Kang had a falling out when one of their investments under a Hexi fund resulted in a major windfall, with the two partners disagreeing on how the profits were to be shared. Nevertheless, the massive profit generated by the deal allowed Shanghai Hexi to purchase Hangzhou Shengfeng, a video game organization, for around 500 million yuan from Chinese conglomerate Century Huatong.

In a recent development, two years after the transaction, in 2019, Hangzhou Shengfeng’s ownership was transferred to an offshore entity, which was eventually consolidated under Osmanthus Vale Holdings — a holding organization incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and listed Huang Le, Alice Huang’s Chinese name, as its sole owner. It was then purchased by 7Road Holdings less than two months after it was founded. While Ms. Huang was the signatory in this deal, it’s believed that she served as a “white glove,” a person who operates on behalf of another to conceal their identity — but it remains unclear if this was for Shanghai Hexi and Kang Wei or some other third party.

Sources indicate that there is not much information on Alice Huang’s activities between 2019 and 2021. However, Shanghai Hexi invested in Shanghai Longjing Information Technology, a data center-focused subsidiary of Century Huatong in 2020, where Ms. Huang served as a director between 2021 and 2022, according to a report by The Wire China. At about the same time, 7Road Holdings expanded into cloud computing, just before ChatGPT brought AI LLMs to the forefront. The U.S. government’s ban on the export of Nvidia chips to China put this investment in jeopardy, though, forcing it to spin off the business as 7Road International in Singapore.

We don’t know when 7Road Holdings sold its Singapore subsidiary, but corporate records show that by the time the manufacturer was renamed Megaspeed in March 2023, it was already under the ownership of Huang Le Limited and led by Ms. Huang. It was sold again in November 2023 to Swiftdata, a company owned by Singaporean Tan Yong Pong. Axios said that she left the firm as a managing director soon after this acquisition, but sources said that she kept working with the company afterward, with Kang Wei helping her get it off the ground.

In a recent development, in the same year, Shanghai Century Litong was founded to build AI data centers in Shanghai and Shenzhen, with Jiangsu Lettall Electronic Co., an electronic components manufacturer, holding a 90% stake, while the remaining 10% is owned by Century Longteng, as reported by BigGo Finance. It should be noted that Century Longteng was renamed from Shanghai Yuxi Investment Management, with the firm pivoting its business from finance to cloud computing, and that even though Alice Huang has already exited the organization by this time, it’s under the control of Huang Yu, who some sources say is Ms. Huang’s sister.

It has been revealed that A year after these data center acquisitions, Alice Huang began to be spotted in public with the former Nvidia CEO. A LinkedIn post showed her having drinks with a leather-clad Jensen Huang alongside other tech executives from NetThunder and Gigabyte at a post-Computex 2024 event. She was once again seen having dinner with him in a Taipei restaurant as reporters tried to interview him while one kid demanded his attention off camera.

Sources indicate that but more than these public sightings, Alice herself boasted about her “closeness” to the then CEO. People close to her noted that she regularly posted photos with Jensen on her WeChat account, and even shared others with potential customers to help establish her credibility. She even reportedly claimed that Mr. Huang would celebrate her birthdays with restaurant dinners and gifts, with one Nvidia China sales employee also saying that she was a familiar face at the company’s annual event for China partners.

An investigation revealed that from 2023 to 2025, Megaspeed imported $4.6 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips, while another $2 billion was routed through Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s subsidiary with offices in Johor, Malaysia. Shanghai Century Litong also reportedly bought AI GPUs from other sources, with estimates putting the total number of banned chips moved through Alice Huang’s assistance at around 240,000, putting the shipments’ worth at around $7.5 billion.

But even as Ms. Huang was making her international moves, Kang Wei was facing trouble at home. Chinese regulators fined him 2.5 million yuan, or approximately $380,000, in 2025, for violating sections of China’s Securities Law. This also led to a warning letter against him, issued in August 2026 by the China Securities Regulatory Commission. Despite running into trouble with the authorities, this massive paper trail showed how Kang Wei actively made moves that put Alice Huang close to Jensen Huang.

Some questions remain, though, about the U.S. intelligence community’s claims that she worked with the Ministry of State Security (MSS), China’s primary intelligence and counterintelligence agency. If it’s true that Alice Huang worked with the MSS and passed on information to the agency, did she specifically target Jensen Huang, or did the spy agency simply discover their indiscretion and use that to force her to cooperate? Was all this planned by the MSS, or were they just shrewd business moves that allowed Kang to make more money while going under the radar of regulators? These are questions that only Kang Wei and Alice Huang (or the Chinese spy agency) can answer. But no matter the case, the fact remains that China acquired advanced AI chips that were supposed to be out of its reach because of this couple’s connections.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that leading semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis believes that Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia may have been driven not only by revelations about his personal extramarital relationships, but also by widespread illicit exports of advanced AI accelerators to China.
  • Over 1.5 GW of Nvidia hardware subject to U.S.
  • Industry observers note that the scale of the alleged diversions is particularly notable because modern AI accelerators require substantial power and infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that leading semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis believes that Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia may have been driven not only by revelations about his personal extramarital relationships, but also by widespread illicit exports of advanced AI accelerators to China. In its latest newsletter, analysts estimate that more than 1.5 gigawatts (GW) worth of restricted Nvidia hardware, which could be equivalent to up to 1.5 million GPUs, has reached the country despite U.S. export controls.

Over 1.5 GW of Nvidia hardware subject to U.S. export restrictions ultimately ended up in China in recent years, according to SemiAnalysis' Accelerator Model, which tracks AI accelerator production and destinations. The estimate excludes processors that Nvidia specifically developed to comply with U.S. export rules, such as the H20 or H800. The firm also claims that the U.S. Department of Commerce has reached a similar conclusion about the scale of unauthorized shipments. Yet, SemiAnalysis does not disclose the exact number of accelerators shipped to China illegally, or their split between Nvidia's product generations.

Industry observers note that the scale of the alleged diversions is particularly notable because modern AI accelerators require substantial power and infrastructure. While the report does not explain how it converts accelerator quantities into power figures, it is likely that the company uses package-level nameplate/rated power multiplied by the number of GPUs. Assuming that all of these AI GPUs were Nvidia H200 SXM rated for up to 700W, then China got around 2.142 million of such accelerators, while if all of these processors were B200 SXM rated for up to 1,000W, then we are talking about 1.5 million units. For a mixed deployment, the total would fall between these figures, depending on the proportion of H200 and B200 accelerators. To put these numbers into context, xAI's Colossus One had 220-230,000 Hopper H100 and H200 GPUs, whereas the Colossus 2 has a target of 1.2 million Blackwell B200 and B300 GPUs. That said, 1.5 GW of restricted Nvidia hardware in China represents an enormous amount of computing infrastructure, which is comparable, or even exceeds, the scale of xAI's entire existing Colossus operation.

While SemiAnalysis did not reveal all the cases in which restricted AI accelerators reached the People's Republic of China, it supports its assessment with two well-known cases of alleged GPU smuggling. The first involves Supermicro co-founder Wally Liaw, Taiwan sales executive Steven Chang, and contractor Willy Sun, who were charged in March 2026. According to the indictment, approximately $2.5 billion worth of servers were sold to a organization in Southeast Asia, with $510 million worth of equipment subsequently diverted to China and obtained by Alibaba. Prosecutors allege that the defendants used substitute servers and transferred identification labels to conceal the actual destinations of the hardware during audits.

The second case involves nine individuals associated with Nvidia, Albatron, Chief Telecom, Flying Tiger, and Supermicro in Taiwan. The authorities accuse the group of arranging unauthorized exports of 130 Nvidia B300-based servers, 74 of which eventually reached China. The suspects used shell companies, forged documents, and declared Japan as the destination for servers that were actually bound for China, according to prosecutors. Taiwanese authorities discovered the operation during a drug smuggling investigation. Both cases are still before the courts.

Amidst the ongoing fallout and reports into Jensen's Huang's extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was an executive at Megaspeed, one report claims that Ms. Huang was personally responsible for facilitating the smuggling of $7.5 billion of Nvidia AI hardware into China, around 240,000 GPUs, mostly H100 and H200 models.

SemiAnalysis suggests that the scale of these violations may explain why Huang's personal conduct became a major matter at this very point in time. The company's analysts speculate that some members of the U.S. intelligence community sought to remove Jensen Huang because he opposed more aggressive restrictions on China's access to American AI hardware. However, the report provides no direct evidence that intelligence agencies influenced Nvidia's board or that Huang participated in unauthorized exports.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The timing also coincides with congressional efforts to advance the Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which passed the House of Representatives on January 12. The legislation is meant to extend U.S. export-control authority to remote access to advanced AI hardware hosted outside China, including data centers in Europe and the Middle East. SemiAnalysis reports that Nvidia and Oracle have actively opposed the proposal.

The analysts believe that Huang's departure essentially removes an influential opponent of stricter restrictions and accelerates efforts to block Chinese companies from accessing American AI hardware in the cloud. However, SemiAnalysis warns that truly all-inclusive restrictions could encourage Chinese developers to adopt domestic accelerators (something that Jensen Huang has consistently warned about), undermine international AI software collaboration, and ultimately weaken American high-tech companies.

Sources indicate that continued Chinese access to American AI accelerators offers several advantages to the U.S. technology industry, according to SemiAnalysis. Firstly, it generates revenue for American companies such as AMD, Nvidia, and cloud service providers. Secondly, when Chinese companies rent GPU capacity from data centers outside China, U.S. authorities retain the ability to monitor their activities and potentially terminate access if necessary due to national security concerns. Thirdly, prolonged reliance on American hardware reduces incentives for Chinese developers to adopt domestic AI accelerators, which could eventually compete with AMD and Nvidia in international markets.

Industry observers note that another important aspect is the contribution of Chinese developers to the global software ecosystem. On the one hand, Chinese laboratories have developed open-source technologies such as DeepEP, DeepGEMM, and MSA, which improve the efficiency of AI workloads on Nvidia hardware and benefit developers worldwide. In addition, American companies also depend on Chinese engineers, component suppliers, and manufacturers. Therefore, legal curbs that completely restrict Chinese developers' access to American AI accelerators could undermine international cooperation, reduce availability of open-source optimizations, and encourage Chinese companies to develop software specifically for domestic hardware.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, access to advanced AI accelerators from AMD or Nvidia enables Chinese laboratories to develop increasingly sophisticated AI models, which will rival leading-edge models developed in America and perhaps create national security risks. To that end, SemiAnalysis acknowledges the need to limit China's access to advanced AI accelerators from U.S.-based companies, as they could, among other things, be used to develop weapons of mass destruction or undermine American national security in different ways. Yet, SA analysts argue that restrictions should focus on the amount and capabilities of hardware available to Chinese entities rather than completely prohibit any access.

Recent findings suggest that semiAnalysis seems to favor a system in which Chinese developers can rent computing capacity from trusted providers outside China under U.S. oversight. Such an approach could preserve American technological influence and commercial benefits and limit China's ability to acquire advanced AI infrastructure independently.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence companies are increasingly turning toward nuclear energy as electricity demand rises alongside expanding computing infrastructure.

X-energy has secured federal permission to construct modular reactors at a chemical manufacturing complex in Texas.

The approval allows the nuclear startup to bring its technology closer to commercial deployment, although operational reactors remain years away.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has authorized construction of four Xe-100 reactors at a Dow industrial facility in Texas.

Each unit is designed to generate 80 megawatts (MW) of electricity alongside another 200 MW of thermal energy - so together, the proposed installation would provide 320 MW of electrical generation, giving the chemical manufacturer an additional source of industrial power.

X-energy describes the regulatory decision as the first construction authorization for an advanced nuclear installation at an American industrial location.

However, receiving permission to begin construction does not mean the reactors are ready to supply electricity for data centers.

The company expects Dow's installation to enter service sometime during the early 2030s, leaving several years before commercial operation begins.

The proposed technology uses uranium-bearing fuel pellets, with helium gas circulating through the reactor to carry away generated heat.

X-energy argues this arrangement offers safety advantages over conventional nuclear power systems, although independent experts have questioned those assurances.

The Union of Concerned Scientists also criticized the regulatory process, particularly the handling of outstanding safety considerations before construction approval.

“The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date,” said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.

He argued that regulators should have resolved those outstanding concerns before authorizing construction at the industrial location.

Demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure operators has given emerging nuclear developers another potential source of commercial interest.

Large technology companies need substantial electricity supplies for computing facilities, particularly as increasingly powerful AI systems require additional processing capacity.

Conventional electricity providers face growing pressure to accommodate those requirements, creating opportunities for alternative generation technologies.

Amazon has become one of X-energy's major financial supporters through its Climate Pledge Fund investment.

The technology company led a $500 million Series C-1 financing round in October 2024 and separately committed to purchasing 5 gigawatts of nuclear generating capacity, an agreement which gives X-energy a significant potential customer as it works toward developing commercial reactors.

The startup also attracted substantial investor interest through its initial public offering earlier this year, which generated $1 billion in proceeds.

However, enthusiasm among investors has moderated since the April listing, suggesting that commercial expectations remain sensitive to development timelines.

The tech giant still faces the challenge of turning regulatory permission and financial commitments into functioning electricity-generating infrastructure.

Small modular reactors have attracted attention because their developers expect factory-oriented production and smaller installations to simplify construction.

Those proposed advantages include shorter development schedules and lower costs, although neither benefit has been conclusively established.

No small modular reactor currently operates commercially in the United States, leaving X-energy's proposed installation dependent on successful construction and regulatory oversight.

  • Industry observers note that why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • It has been revealed that sennheiser is one of my go-to audio brands for quality consumer and reference audio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a lot to talk about with the Momentum True Wireless 5, because they're an upgrade compared to the Momentum TW 4 in almost every way that matters. From sound quality to ANC and quality-of-life improvements, if you prioritize sound over ANC, Sennheiser’s latest is worth serious consideration.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

It has been revealed that sennheiser is one of my go-to audio brands for quality consumer and reference audio. And for good reason: they often produce products that have crystal clarity, are well-balanced with great detail retrieval, while still being fun to listen to rather than clinical.

When it comes to their Bluetooth devices, they prioritize audio quality over active noise canceling, but with the introduction of their new Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5, they’re closer than ever to ANC market leaders Sony and Bose.

Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5.

Bluetooth 6.0, Multipoint support.

7 mm TrueResponse dynamic drivers.

SBC, AAC, aptX Adaptive, aptX Lossless (Snapdragon Sound).

Up to 6 hours (ANC on), 20-25 total with charging case; User-replaceable batteries.

USB-C, 2 hrs for full charge; 8 min charging for up to 1 hr playtime.

8-band EQ (app), Personalized sound.

6 mics combined with 2 bone-conduction voice accelerometers.

Copper, Cream, Graphite, Denim, Lavender.

While I love Sennheiser’s sound quality, their boxy Bluetooth earbuds have not been the stuff of aesthetic excellence.

I’ve never called previous models “ugly,” but their looks have been rather dull. The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 (Momentum TW5 from here on) look like an artisan took the TW4 and carved away the boxy shape, smoothing those angular edges into a sleek, aerodynamic aesthetic (see the photo comparison in the gallery above).

This year, I have the Copper colorway, which is a combination of beautiful copper earbuds and case trim with textured brown case exteriors and the signature Sennheiser logo in copper on the ‘buds and silver on the case top. The case fits much better in my pants’ coin pocket this year than last year. Gone is the small, boxy case. Instead, you get a slim, pocketable case with wired and wireless charging, plus other features I’ll touch on shortly.

The earbuds from the previous generation fit my ears well, thanks to their shape and the silicone wings around the edges. The wings are gone now, but with the newly introduced shape and ergonomics, they fit my ears just as well as they did before, and that’s despite actually being heavier than the Momentum TW4, which also feels bulkier in my ears compared to the new Momentum TW5.

Though the aesthetic upgrade is definitely welcome, the most key upgrades for many people will likely be the audio improvements in both sound reproduction and active noise canceling.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Let’s talk ANC, first. During my day one testing, I realized I’d need to pull out my previously tested Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds because my first listen had me wondering whether Sennheiser had upped their ANC game to those levels; it was that good!

When it comes to noise-canceling earbuds, you can focus on either sound quality or aggressive noise canceling. Prioritizing one often comes at the expense of the other, so while Sennheiser’s ANC on previous models was good, it wasn’t market-leading. This time, Sennheiser’s engineers have greatly improved ANC across the frequency spectrum.

According to recent reports, though I wouldn’t run out to upgrade my earbuds just for improved ANC, this year’s model is definitely more aggressive at canceling noise than the Momentum TW4. You’ll hear more complete cancellation across the frequency spectrum. That means that you’ll hear less high-pitched urban traffic noise or subway sounds. Keyboard keystrokes should be a bit quieter. Cars whizzing by you; their engine noises will have decreased compared to the previous generation.

According to recent reports, and while that's true when you compare the Momentum TW5 to the TW4, Sony’s WF-1000XM6 still hushes more of those same frequencies than the TW5. The difference in 2026 is that Sennheiser has closed the distance between the ANC it offers and what you’ll get from Sony.

While the durability hasn’t changed, the Momentum TW5 carries the same IP54 rating as the previous generation; Sennheiser has upgraded the longevity of this year’s model with user-replaceable batteries in both the earbuds and the charging case.

On the charging case, that upgrade is pretty clear if you look at the single Philips head screw on the bottom right side of the case, across from the oddly placed USB-C charging port on the left. I’m guessing that port placement is the result of making the battery removable.

It has been revealed that the Momentum TW5 comes with a prying tool to remove the battery, but you’ll need to provide the Philips PH000 screwdriver. This is a Phillips head (the “star”) screwdriver with a 7mm blade. Sennheiser lists the battery part number as BA 501, but it isn’t listed for sale on their site yet.

According to recent reports, I thoroughly enjoy Sennheiser’s sound signature. I use their IE900 IEMs as reference in-ear headphones, and their HD660S as one of my over-ear reference audio headphones, along with pairs from Dali and Fosi. The Momentum TW5 expands sound quality across the frequency range, with its signature focus on the mid-range to deliver great instrument separation and strong vocal presentation without sacrificing low-end energy.

Listening to Charles Mingus’ “Moanin’,” the TW5 does a much better job than the Sony WF-1000XM6 at maintaining a strong sense of instrumentation during the song's most frenetic parts. Where Sony turns those sections into a pot of mashed potatoes, Sennheiser allows you to continue to hear where the sound of different instruments comes from in the stereo image.

Industry observers note that listening to various folk songs, including Paul Simon’s “Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes,” where his voice can get sibilant with audio products that have harsher, or overly energetic high-frequency reproduction, the TW5 were smooth. No sibilance from Simon, and no eardrum-fatiguing high notes from Joni Mitchell’s “River (With French Horns) [Blue Sessions].”.

Around the minute mark on Mitchell’s song, she hits some sustained high notes that drive me batty on clinical headphones or those with poor high-frequency reproduction, but again, the TW5 are more on the smooth end of the spectrum.

If you listen and disagree with my assessment, the good news is that this year the Sennheiser Smart Control+ app has expanded its five-band EQ to eight bands, so you’ll have more control over shaping the sound to your preferences, and the pair of buds take well to EQ adjustments.

My only real concern with the TW5 was the microphones when making phone calls. They sound excellent indoors, but outdoors, they'll block noise superbly, but at the cost of audio stability. At times, when the AI is working hard to block background noise, I've found that audio quality can take a hit. Overall, you'll sound great, and so will the folks calling you, but be aware that, depending on ambient noise, you may experience some finicky behavior.

It has been revealed that in terms of battery life, I've found that I can get a day's use out of them with ANC off. For me, that's around 10 hours, including a trip to my local climbing gym. ANC on has given less, though a little better than some competitors, getting a little over six hours in my testing. More bass-heavy tracks in your rotation will affect that, though.

In a recent development, in the final analysis, you have Bluetooth earbuds that folks love for various reasons. Some lock you into an ecosystem and are superior in part because of how they work inside that walled garden, while others are more open and fully stand on their own.

The Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are the latter, and while they aren’t market leaders in ANC or calling, they’re solid performers in those areas and offer a delightfully entertaining, engaging sound signature that you’ll get extra years out of, thanks to their user-serviceable batteries.

Sennheiser gives consumers a worthy upgrade over the Momentum True Wireless 5. They've improved the sound and noise-cancelling quality, made the batteries removable in both the buds and the case, and refined the exterior. A worthy upgrade!

Google has also made voice feedback more conversational, enabling users to add details or revise their messages before sending them. Connected displays and speakers should also start playing broadcasts more quickly.

Sources indicate that the Google Home app upgrade fixes a number of camera problems, especially for older Nest hardware that has been moved to the newer app. Google has fixed some live-streaming connection challenges with the first-generation Nest Cam Indoor, Nest Cam Outdoor, wired Nest Doorbell (Nest Hello), and both Nest Cam IQ models.

The fixes target particular network setups like PPPoE connections, fiber internet, and mobile hotspots. Nest Cam IQ owners should also get back event thumbnails, and improved clock accuracy should provide more reliable timestamps on recorded footage. Google also updated security certificates and fixed stability issues that could lead to unexpected camera restarts.

Android owners also get a handful of smaller, but welcome, fixes, like more reliable camera history controls, fewer unwanted Nest account-linking prompts, and clearer instructions on how to re-link third-party cameras. The ability to remove an offline, unmigrated 1st-generation Nest Doorbell is also returning.

According to recent reports, google Home MCP is also getting an expansion. AI agents can now set up and manage home automations and get extra controls for devices like appliances, robot vacuums, EV chargers, thermostats, and more.

Over the coming days, make sure your devices enhancement to the latest firmware—or pull the update manually via the Google Home app—to see these camera fixes and Gemini features go live.

According to recent reports, japanese workers dealing with the impacts of Microsoft's ongoing 365 outage have reportedly taken to analog measures, including using fax machines to deal with the ongoing blackout, the Japan Times reports. An outage that has now lasted nearly 24 hours was still going on Friday when employees turned up to work.

The downtime has meant businesses reliant on Microsoft 365 are unable to use Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, with workplaces hit with error messages and blank screens, forced to reschedule meetings or delay work. For some, the outage has proven a respite from Japan's notoriously workaholic culture. "I couldn’t open Outlook and panicked … I got in touch with my boss and was told to stay home," one person reported on X, while another remarked that the only task they could carry out at work was to clean the coffee machine in the production room.

But while some employees and companies are throwing in the towel and calling it an early weekend, others are taking a novel, more analog approach. "Microsoft’s server glitch has made it impossible to get any work done since this morning. I guess phones and fax machines really are unbeatable. … We’re going full analog!" one user claimed. The report cites another employee who confirmed that their company was switching to fax machines to send the regular updates the company normally sends out as PDFs. "Analog is strong," they rejoiced.

Recent findings suggest that some 78% of Japanese companies rely on Microsoft for their digital infrastructure. The outage began on Thursday, with mass disruption to Outlook, Teams, Copilot, OneDrive, and Microsoft 365 as a whole. It's a saga impacting entire sectors, including UK health care, businesses, travel, and transport.

Microsoft's latest update said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe, while the situation in America was improving, but warned some customers may still experience intermittent concerns. The company has also denied rumblings that the outage was caused by a cybersecurity breach. The outage has even caused some companies, such as Switzerland's luxury Richemont (Cartier) outfit, to delay giving their latest earnings report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app.

Officially, Google notes “Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence.” Examples include “complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery.”.

In the model picker, 4 Argon is for “Code & analysis” and 4 Carbon is for “Most complex work.” Notably, the Gemini app has removed 3.1 Pro with this launch.

Sources indicate that to showcase performance on larger, more complex projects, Google Antigravity is previewing /swarm. This turns a “single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time.”.

Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

For legal, finance, and enterprise work, Carbon is stated to bring “higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis.” This includes how the model will follow “strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.”.

In a recent development, existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agents (MKA) benchmark. Carbon ranks #1 while using 3X fewer tokens than the next best model across 200 tasks that test a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows.

Other domain highlights include:.

It has been revealed that the introductory pricing for Carbon is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

#312. Lenovo Googlebook 15 review: Google botched it, yet again

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2032 w)
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Androidcentral

Lenovo Googlebook 15 review: Google botched it, yet again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a classic case of a product that shouldn't exist.
  • Lightweight carbon-fiber chassis with a silk-touch finish.
  • Solid port selection with Thunderbolt 4, HDMI & more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a classic case of a product that shouldn't exist. Not because of the hardware, which is as premium as its $1,099 price tag would indicate, but because of the software. Lenovo paired a 15.3-inch 120Hz OLED display with an array of ports and an understated silk-touch finish, and put it inside a 2.84-pound featherweight body. Google then proved it doesn’t know Android that well by thinking it would suit a desktop OS. The result is a product no one should buy. Not just this one, but all Googlebooks. They’re that useless. Lenovo gets top marks for the hardware, but Google gets none for the software.

Lightweight carbon-fiber chassis with a silk-touch finish.

Gorgeous 15.3-inch 2.8K 120Hz OLED touchscreen.

Solid port selection with Thunderbolt 4, HDMI & more.

Handy Gemini tools like Rambler and Magic Pointer.

Googlebook OS is useless as a desktop OS with stretched phone/tablet apps.

$1,099+ price puts it up against full MacBooks and Windows ultrabooks.

Underwhelming battery life (~5.5 to 7.5 hours depending on workload).

Very little future potential for improvement given Google's track record.

ARM-on-x86 app stutters and broken desktop trackpad/right-click habits.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I don’t know why the Lenovo Googlebook 15 exists. More importantly, I don’t think Google can defend why it does, either. Not just this one… but all Googlebooks.

Make no mistake: this isn't on Lenovo. On paper and in the hand, the hardware here is phenomenal. The 15.3-inch 2,8K 120Hz OLED display is vibrant with solid touch response, and Lenovo also packed quad Dolby Atmos speakers, an array of ports, and a Glowbar RGB alert bar into a 2.84-pound featherweight body. This would not be out of place on any true premium laptop.

In a recent development, which makes what Google did to it even harder to forgive. We’ve been down this road before. We’ve been down this road before. Google created Chromebooks as simple, $200 to $300 browser-first machines, and through sheer determination and low pricing, carved out a real niche. Those early laptops had clear limits, but they were forgivable because they were affordable. Then came Chromebook Plus in 2023, pushing prices from $399 up toward $749 on the theory that better specs and AI perks justified a bigger spend.

From that trajectory, it’s no surprise Google tried to move even further upmarket with the Googlebook. Given how half-baked many of Google’s hardware and software pivots are, it’s also no surprise that Googlebook OS is the most half-baked of them all. Why? Because running Android apps sounds great in theory until you remember that most of them still lack proper desktop features on foldables and tablets, let alone when you try to use them as your primary computer.

According to recent reports, the crazier part is Google’s hubris. The manufacturer had enough confidence in this half-finished platform to talk five prominent PC makers (Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo) into launching Googlebooks. The problem is that Google paired their hardware with an operating system that makes Windows Vista look like Windows 11. Seriously: do not buy any Googlebook.

According to recent reports, google wants you to pay a flagship premium for a platform it hasn’t bothered to finish. It’s almost certainly destined for the Killed by Google scrapyard, and that’s where it belongs. Google has yet again proved it doesn’t understand desktop computing, and all five PC makers should rightly think twice before trusting Google with a new category again. It’s time for Google to leave desktop computing to the adults in the room.

Pricing is where the Lenovo Googlebook 15 and all Googlebooks immediately trip over themselves. The cheapest Googlebook from each of the five PC makers ranges from $899 to $1,299, with the base Lenovo Googlebook 15 variant starting at $1,099.99. That gets you an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 processor, 16GB of LPDDR5X RAM, and 256GB of storage. Stepping up to the 512GB configuration pushes the price to $1,149.99 (though Lenovo throws its "AI Mouse" into the box), while European buyers face an eye-watering €1,379 sticker price.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

At $500 or $600, you can forgive rough software edges as the cost of admission. At $1,100, forgiveness evaporates. That price puts the Googlebook 15 directly in the crosshairs of Apple's MacBook Air, Apple's cheaper MacBook Neo, and dozens of capable Windows 11 ultrabooks. All of those machines run mature desktop operating systems with decades of pro-grade software behind them. Crucially, Microsoft and Apple actually know how to build desktop platforms, and Google’s naivety shines right through in Googlebook OS.

Google is asking customers to pay full flagship laptop prices for the privilege of beta-testing a first-generation platform. It’s barely ready for a free beta release, let alone a four-figure price tag. That creates an obvious chicken-and-egg trap: mainstream buyers will not spend over a thousand dollars on a machine that relies on mobile apps, and without a massive install base, major developers have zero incentive to build proper desktop-class apps for Googlebook OS.

Simply put, there’s no reason anyone should root for the Googlebook, from computer makers and developers to retailers and customers.

It has been revealed that strip away Google’s half-baked OS, and Lenovo’s engineering prowess shines. Picking up the Lenovo Googlebook 15 for the first time is a pleasant surprise because a 15.3-inch laptop has no business feeling this light yet premium. Weighing 2.84 pounds and measuring 0.63 inches thick, the magnesium-aluminum and carbon-fiber chassis is lighter than my 14-inch MacBook Pro and feels much better in the hand. This is one of the few Lenovo laptops to feature a textured coating, reminiscent of Asus’ Ceraluminum, and the soft, unglazed-porcelain feel on the off-white Cloud Gray chassis is beautifully designed and made.

The 15.3-inch 2.8K (2880 x 1800) OLED touchscreen is the star of the show. Text looks razor-sharp, blacks are properly inky, and the 120Hz refresh rate keeps scrolling fluid. It is an ideal canvas for running two browser windows side by side or kicking back with HDR movies on a flight. Lenovo also nailed the port layout by placing a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 port on both sides of the chassis alongside a full-size HDMI 2.0 port, a 10Gbps USB-A port, and a headphone jack. Being able to charge from either side without carrying a dongle is how every modern laptop should be built.

Industry observers note that then there’s biometrics: some people prefer face unlock, others prefer a fingerprint sensor. The Lenovo Googlebook 15 gives you both choices, like any good Android phone, and while it might seem superfluous to some, it’s a pattern I’d like to see on all laptops.

Then there is the Glowbar, an exterior LED strip mounted along the lid near the hinge in a deliberate throwback to the original Chromebook Pixel. When the laptop is closed, it acts as a handy battery fuel gauge and pulses with a Gemini gradient during voice sessions. Across a table, it is a neat visual cue. Once you open the lid to actually use the computer, however, it’s as pointless as much of the OS, since you can’t see a single pixel of it.

The only real problem with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a terminal one: Googlebook OS.

According to recent reports, built on a hybrid of Android 17 and ChromeOS windowing, it feels like the big-organization equivalent of prompting AI to build this and forgetting the details. It looks pretty, then falls apart in seconds.

Sources indicate that this is not fresh to Android. The chief complaint with Android foldables and tablets is that Android apps are poorly optimized for larger, more varied form factors. It's no surprise, then, that they are incredibly poorly optimized for desktop. The core problem is that Google still thinks scaled-up Android apps are an acceptable substitute for desktop software.

Yes, you can resize Play Store apps into floating windows, and Google touts optimized versions of apps like Adobe Photoshop, Lightroom, and Spotify. In practice, most of them still behave like stretched tablet apps. Basic desktop muscle memory breaks constantly: right-click menus are inconsistent, click-and-drag gestures don't always register where you expect, and UI elements feel oversized and awkward when you navigate with a trackpad rather than a fingertip.

It has been revealed that more often than not, running the browser-based web app version of a service works better than installing its native Android counterpart. That begs an uncomfortable question: if web apps are still doing the heavy lifting, what exactly is the $1,100 upgrade over a $450 Chromebook Plus?

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, running ARM-compiled Android apps on an x86 Intel Core Ultra 5 325 chip causes occasional stutters and compatibility hiccups. Even Google seems painfully aware of how rushed this launch build was. Earlier this month, Google pushed an emergency November software upgrade specifically to patch NPU memory leaks and browser tab bloat, freeing up between 3GB and 6GB of RAM on 16GB systems. Needing a day-ten rescue patch just to stop a 16GB laptop from choking on its own AI overhead tells you everything you need to know about how ready Googlebook OS was.

Recent findings suggest that to be fair, Google did get a few ecosystem touches right. If you carry an Android flagship, initial setup links your phone seamlessly. Features like Continue On app handoff and instant access to your phone's local files feel effortless, showing that Google could one day build desktop-mobile integrations as slick as Apple's Continuity suite. Gemini integration is also thoughtfully executed in spots: Rambler does an impressive job turning rambling voice dictation into clean, structured checklists, and Magic Pointer lets you hover over on-screen text for instant contextual actions.

Sources indicate that sounds great, right? Don’t get too excited: these few redeeming software features cannot rescue an OS that lacks real desktop depth, nor can they fix mediocre endurance. Despite a sizable 70Wh battery, real-world stamina hovers around six to eight hours of mixed work with noticeable overnight standby drain, trailing both Apple silicon and modern Windows ultrabooks by a wide margin. Lenovo already knows how to build laptops with excellent battery life, so I’m putting this firmly on how unoptimized Googlebook OS actually is.

It has been revealed that no, not at $1,099. In fact, there’s little reason to buy any Googlebook; the OS is that bad.

If you love the idea of a featherweight 15-inch OLED laptop, buy an ultrabook from Lenovo’s Yoga or Slim lineups, or look at the MacBook Air. Either option will cost you roughly the same money (or less), give you vastly better battery life, and run genuine desktop software without forcing you to compromise your workflow. Conversely, if you live entirely inside Google Workspace and Chrome, buy a Chromebook Plus for half the price and keep $600 in your pocket.

The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a painful reminder of what happens when hardware and software teams operate on completely different wavelengths. Lenovo highlighted up ready to build a flagship laptop; Google showed up with a half-baked mobile OS and expected consumers to pay a premium. Until Google figures out what a desktop operating system actually needs to be, skip this entirely.

At this point, I doubt it ever will. So don't buy the Lenovo Googlebook 15. Do not buy any Googlebook. Unless something drastic changes with Google’s approach, I probably wouldn't buy any Google desktop computer, ever.

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that 2026 has been huge for the Nintendo Switch 2.
  • It has been revealed that yes, the Switch 2’s library already feels surprisingly fleshed-out for a console that’s not even two years old yet, and it’s certainly become my main gaming device in 2026, squeezing more than 800 hours of playtime out of me.
  • Specifically, I want to look at exclusives here and run through the very best titles that have released since the dawn of the newly introduced year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that 2026 has been huge for the Nintendo Switch 2. This year, it really feels like the console has come into its own, with a number of critically acclaimed first-party exclusives, as well as some heavy-hitting third-party titles that were beautifully optimized for the system (such as Resident Evil Requiem).

It has been revealed that yes, the Switch 2’s library already feels surprisingly fleshed-out for a console that’s not even two years old yet, and it’s certainly become my main gaming device in 2026, squeezing more than 800 hours of playtime out of me. And looking back on the year as a whole got me thinking. What have been the best Nintendo Switch 2 games of 2026?

Specifically, I want to look at exclusives here and run through the very best titles that have released since the dawn of the newly introduced year. I’ll be ranking my top six picks here, but if you have a different list, make sure to drop it in the comments!

Before Yoshi and the Mysterious Book reared its whimsical head, I felt that our green dino was in something of a rut, with releases like Yoshi’s Wooly World and Crafted World failing to evoke the sense of wonder and thrill that the series conjured up in its youth.

But all of that changed with Mysterious Book, which focused a lot more heavily on exploration, seeing Yoshi venture through the pages of the living Encyclopedia, Mr. E., in order to learn about the mysterious creatures that live within his pages.

Thanks to this game’s stellar art direction, the pages come to life, both literally and figuratively speaking. The brilliant blend of beautiful 3D environments and hand-drawn watercolor-style characters results in a massively charming and immersive experience, with stop-motion animation giving each critter distinct, memorable personalities and traits.

It’s not all about the visual style, though. Yoshi and the Mysterious Book is a blast from the moment you start playing until the credits roll, with no end of oddities to discover. While the game’s core puzzles are relatively straightforward, tracking down some of the collectibles is a genuine challenge — you’ll have to get creative with creature abilities and regularly stray from the beaten path in order to find secret areas and Smiley Flowers.

Industry observers note that while I would’ve liked to have seen some tougher boss battles and a bit more narrative depth from Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, it’s easily my favorite game that the series has produced in over a decade. I’ve still got so many secrets to uncover, and I’m looking forward to diving back in over the holidays.

It has been revealed that nintendo Switch Sports Resort is to the original Nintendo Switch Sports exactly what Wii Sports Resort was to Wii Sports. It brought more sports, more depth, and more replayability to the table, all while maintaining the simplicity that makes this series so beloved to gamers of all ages.

Industry observers note that yes, I felt that the original Nintendo Switch Sports was seriously lacking in single-player content, had an underwhelming selection of events, and had a flawed points system, but all three of those woes were remedied in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. It truly feels like Nintendo took the time to listen to its audience, with a newly introduced Island Crown mode adding a competitive single-player edge, a grand total of 12 sports packed in, and the points system applied to both offline and online play, rather than just the latter.

Industry observers note that the core experience is great too. Every single sport feels fantastic to play, and I continue to be astonished by just how responsive and accurate motion controls are here.

Some of my highlights include: Table Tennis, which added more strategy and depth with enhanced spin and curve mechanics; Skateboarding, which uses the Switch 2’s mouse controls to great effect for fast-paced racing and explorative segments; and Thumb Wrestling, which somehow made something seemingly mundane feel highly satisfying and exciting to play.

I have a few gripes, mainly the removal of Football (or Soccer) and Chambara at launch, but I’m hoping they’ll be added down the line through some sort of patch or DLC. If you want a simple yet exhilarating game to play with family and friends during the upcoming holiday season, this is easily my top recommendation.

I have to say that I was a bit skeptical about Splatoon Raiders when it was first shown off.

I’ve been playing Splatoon since the original dropped on Wii U (yes, I was one of the five people who bought one), and the idea of pivoting away from the iconic Turf War into a more single-player-oriented experience felt like a bold move.

But boy, did it pay off. In our glowing five-star Splatoon Raiders review, we called it “a wonderful solo reinvention of the popular multiplayer series filled with smartly designed missions and endlessly engaging progression systems”.

This third-person looter shooter is jam-packed with content; there’s a vast array of missions to run through with various difficulty levels, more than a hundred weapons to choose from, and even an online co-op mode including gear, weapon parts, and more. Pair that with a stellar progression system, stunning visuals, and intelligent level design, and you’re looking at an exceptional Switch 2 experience.

I think it’s fair to say that Pokémon Pokopia is the biggest surprise hit of 2026. Of course, the Pokémon name itself is always going to entice a number of players, but not many could’ve foreseen the universal acclaim and social media attention that this spinoff would receive. In fact, Pokopia proved to be such a phenomenon that there were global shortages of the physical edition of the game that even affected me personally.

But when I did get my mitts on Pokémon Pokopia, it gripped me in a way that no ‘cosy’ game has managed to do since my time with Animal Crossing: Upcoming Leaf back in 2013. And, in my view, Pokopia takes the Animal Crossing formula and dials it up to 11.

It has been revealed that you’ve still got that core duty to assist your fellow villagers by building homes, upgrading infrastructure, and sprucing up your locality, but the individual Pokémon feel so much more distinct and charismatic than Animal Crossing’s residents, and the sheer scale of the world is something to behold. The main story also has a surprisingly dark tone to it, as you take control of Ditto to investigate humanity's disappearance.

You can spend hundreds of hours in Pokopia building fancy custom houses, filling out the Pokédex, or just interacting with your favorite pocket monsters — it’s the perfect game to relax and unwind with, and now there are even latest DLC areas to explore, which we’ve loved so far.

Pokémon Pokopia is the highest-rated Pokémon title in history according to Metacritic, and while I’d personally put a couple of mainline entries ahead of it, I really couldn’t recommend the game enough.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is my most-played game of 2026. I racked up more than 200 hours for my review, and to say it had me hooked would be an understatement. For me, this is the best game the series has produced thus far, with staggering scale, excellent tactical combat, a mesmerizing cast, and a stellar soundtrack to match.

In Fortune’s Weave, you take control of four heroes, known as the Flame Lords, in their mission to win the Heroic Games, and have a wish granted by Divine Sovereign Solel. However, an impending threat is on the horizon, with the land of Dagda thrust into turmoil after the demonic god Balor sews disorder.

Being able to play as all of the Flame Lords and experience their interwoven stories one by one was an absolute joy. Seeing each unique yet interconnected story unfold, recruiting allies, and building the ultimate units has never felt so satisfying, and it all builds to an epic conclusion which makes the time investment feel genuinely rewarding.

Dungeon sections add some welcome variation and keep the experience feeling well-paced; fresh mechanics like Blaze Arts add even more combat depth, and the map designs are brilliant right across the board (though they reach a real peak towards the back end of the game). The visual upgrade over Fire Emblem: Three Houses is also considerable, and performance is stable even in the busiest moments.

If you played Three Houses and loved that, or if you’re just an RPG fan at all, I think Fortune’s Weave is a true must-play — it's easily among the best Switch 2 games you can play today, and I firmly stand by the perfect five-star score I bestowed upon it.

In a recent development, you saw this coming, right? The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is an all-time great of gaming, and the Switch 2 remake is pretty much flawless.

According to recent reports, ocarina of Time is a true masterclass in design. A combination of expertly composed music, distinctly crafted domains, and legendary characters helps to imprint a memory of each area you explore in the mind for eternity. Dungeons are exceptionally varied, filled with fun puzzles and grandiose boss battles. And the narrative, though simple, is executed fantastically as the Hero of Time ventures through the world of Hyrule both as a child and as a young adult.

It has been revealed that the remake, while staying very faithful to the source material, adds some excellent quality-of-life changes that make the game far more palatable for modern audiences. Manual jumping, button-mapped items, free camera control, and roll-to-sprint make the adventure feel a whole lot smoother. Combat feels far snappier and more impactful too, with steadier movement helping you feel in control during skirmishes.

Recent findings suggest that and the visual reimagining is sensational too — the lighting, the character models, the small details… they all add up to something magical. And you also get a near frame-perfect 60fps gameplay experience here as well — I barely noticed a single drop during my entire playthrough.

Industry observers note that as relentless as the flow of time may be, our love for Ocarina of Time is unchanged. As our reviewer, Josephine Watson, stated: “Whether you’re an adult or a child, when you boot up the remake, it’s not a game you’ll forget in a hurry”.
