📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly called himself “a piece of sh**" as he left the company he built over 33 years. Bloomberg reports that the co-founder, known for his legendary energy and outgoing demeanor, surrendered and looked “broken and shattered” during the board meeting where he resigned from the AI hardware firm after admitting to at least one extra-marital affair, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. But despite his resignation and the controversies surrounding him, it seems that Nvidia employees are still rallying behind him, with thousands of comments on the company’s internal “suggestion box” showing support for the disgraced leader, according to Wired.

Recent findings suggest that “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one commenter said, while another one wrote, “We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance.” An Nvidia staffer told Wired privately, “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” even as another employee sent a manufacturer-wide email demanding transparency into his resignation. “I stand by Jensen. Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” They also added, “If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”.

According to the report, internal calls for Huang's reinstatement have drawn more than 1,600 comments on Nvidia's internal forums, "the majority in full support of reinstalling him." The company has more than 42,000 employees worldwide.

Rumors about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, being close to Jensen Huang first circulated in late October, with Nvidia vehemently denying there was any impropriety. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. However, things took a turn for the worse for the Nvidia CEO when reports came out that he actually had an affair with Ms. Huang.

Sources indicate that nvidia General Counsel and Secretary of the Board Tim Teter confronted Jensen at his house when this came out, after which he confessed. The founder soon released a statement admitting to and apologizing for his actions, while the firm’s board formed an independent committee to investigate. However, another scandal broke out revealing that the former Nvidia chief had another affair — this time with a subordinate. This was apparently the last straw for the board, and the Nvidia co-founder was forced to resign soon after.

According to recent reports, reports say that Jensen Huang was a hands-on leader, with over 60 executives at the tech giant reporting directly to him, and that he was known to respond to emails quickly, whether it was day or night. But, more importantly, he was the face of the company who was particularly loved by many people, giving rise to the term “Jensanity” in his home country of Taiwan. Regardless of his status as a billionaire, people still find him trying out street food, eating at fast food chains, and even honoring his humble beginnings as a busboy at Denny’s.

According to recent reports, aside from these latest scandals, many gamers castigate Huang for abandoning the core market that supported Nvidia before it became an AI giant, with consumer graphics cards now drastically more expensive than ever before. He was also often criticized for his all-out push on artificial intelligence and stance on selling chips to China. Still, those complications did not detract from his aura, with his trademark leather jacket raising nearly $1 million at a charity auction. It remains to be seen what will happen to Jensen after his monumental fall from grace, with SpaceX and Tesla mogul Elon Musk noting it would be an honor to hire Huang.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honor has officially lifted the curtain on its next batch of mid-range phones in China, where buyers can now place a deposit for the upcoming Honor 700S, Honor 700, and Honor 700 Pro.
  • If the manufacturer’s previous releases are any indication, the budget-oriented 700S is unlikely to see the light of day in the West, but the more premium 700 and 700 Pro could hit shelves in the coming months.
  • And, honestly, I’m hoping that they do, because both models are set to bring some impressively high-end features to a market segment otherwise dominated by boring-looking slabs like the Oppo Reno 16, Xiaomi 17T, or Google Pixel 10.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honor has officially lifted the curtain on its next batch of mid-range phones in China, where buyers can now place a deposit for the upcoming Honor 700S, Honor 700, and Honor 700 Pro.

If the manufacturer’s previous releases are any indication, the budget-oriented 700S is unlikely to see the light of day in the West, but the more premium 700 and 700 Pro could hit shelves in the coming months.

And, honestly, I’m hoping that they do, because both models are set to bring some impressively high-end features to a market segment otherwise dominated by boring-looking slabs like the Oppo Reno 16, Xiaomi 17T, or Google Pixel 10.

With that in mind, here are the three reasons the Honor 700 is worth looking forward to — and one reservation that could put a damper on the global launch...

You might think cool rear displays are exclusive to high-end flagships like the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, but Honor is set to bring them to a cheaper price point with the Honor 700 series. All three models come with a small color display on the rear, and the brand has already been showing off what you can do with them in a flurry of posts on the Chinese social media site Weibo.

This includes the ability to play some cute little time-killing mini-games or unwind by tapping it to rotate a virtual wooden meditation bracelet. It also has some more practical applications, like reading your notifications at a glance without having to pick up the phone when it’s face down on your desk, or seeing a live preview of the rear camera when you’re shooting photos for easier posing. These aren’t exactly brand-newly introduced features in the world of phones with rear screens, but the idea of them being available at a more affordable rate is certainly appealing.

For its part, Honor does seem to have some innovation up its sleeve too. One video reveals how easy it is to change its appearance with your own pictures, emojis, or GIFs. A newly introduced option appears when you hold your finger down to activate the Honor Magic Portal feature. Drag an image to it, and it’ll appear on the rear screen, which seems like a very Gen-Z approach to customization.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

I can already imagine promptly tweaking it to reflect my mood, or show off the latest TV show I’m watching or game that I’m playing.

According to recent reports, there’s another surprising feature buried here as well, revealed in a recent image post. It appears as though the phone will be able to read your heart rate and blood oxygen level, conveying it with a little graphic on the rear display.

It’s not exactly clear how it will do this, but there’s most likely some kind of sensor hidden somewhere on the exterior of the device that you’ll have to hold for a few seconds in order to get a reading.

Smartwatch owners might shrug, but as an analog watch wearer who relies on their phone for step tracking and logging exercise routines, I think it's a pretty cool addition that gives you access to some more health data without the need for a standalone accessory.

Honor hasn't officially revealed the specs of any of the 700 series phones just yet, but the folks over at GSMarena have put together a 700 Pro spec sheet based on the latest leaks from internet tipsters — and it's certainly promising.

It looks like a very well-considered follow-up to the already excellent Honor 600 Pro, maintaining the same glass back and aluminum frame build that made that phone feel impressively premium despite its less-than-flagship price.

The main screen will seemingly be a very similar AMOLED panel, with the same smooth 120Hz refresh rate and incredible 8,000 nits peak brightness to ensure legibility in even the harshest of lighting conditions.

Industry observers note that the camera setup appears to be identical too, with a 200MP main shooter, 50MP telephoto lens, and a 12MP ultrawide on the rear, and the same 50MP selfie shooter on the front. I used the Honor 600 Pro as my daily driver for multiple weeks and couldn’t fault its camera performance given its market position. It offered poppy, bright pictures that were perfect for a social media feed, so I can understand Honor not wanting to shake things up this time around.

That mentioned, I am disappointed that the phone will still apparently ship with a USB 2.0 connector, meaning that it will suffer from very slow file transfer speeds if you hook it up to a PC to export all of your pics.

The biggest improvements will likely be to the SoC, with the more recent Qualcomm SM8845 Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 replacing the Qualcomm SM8750-AB Snapdragon 8 Elite for a solid performance boost.

The battery is also getting an upgrade, coming in at 9,000 mAh rather than the 7,000 mAh (or 6,400 mAh in Europe) of the last model for even longer-lasting performance — very promising given I was able to squeeze multiple days of use out of the 600 Pro in my testing. Of course, whether markets outside of China get lower capacities is yet to be seen.

The real elephant in the room here is price, as it could make or break the Honor 700 series as a package.

I’m hoping that Honor will be able to maintain the price point of the 600 line (which would help explain the overall rather similar specs), though this might be tricky given the huge hike in costs of key components like RAM and flash storage.

The Honor 600 Pro retailed for £899.99 in its 12GB of RAM and 512GB storage configuration, though it is almost perpetually discounted to around £599.99, where it represents pretty incredible value. The base Honor 600, meanwhile, retails for £549.99, though, again, it is frequently on sale for £449.99.

Sources indicate that if the 700 series is available for the same rates, I could see it being a seriously tempting proposition when put up against major flagships. I'll be following the China launch closely.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whoop has released Whoop Humans, an opt-in social network inside its app that lets members follow friends and family and share sleep, recovery, and workout data. It comes with every membership tier at no extra cost and sits alongside the existing Teams feature rather than replacing it.

Sometimes when trying to lose weight or stay in shape, having someone hold you accountable or share your journey with is a good way to stay on your strategy. So, if you’re a Whoop user, the tech giant has recently launched the “Humans” social network.

Sources indicate that whoop just launched Whoop Humans, a social network that lives inside the app. It is available for members on November 12. Through the social network, you can follow friends and family. You can also share the fitness and health data you pick. Sleep, recovery, and workouts are all included. However, for those worried about privacy, nothing goes out unless you choose it.

In a recent development, members also get to decide which workout types and achievements appear. They can also remove followers whenever they want. A new feature called Moments lets people post photos from workouts and personal milestones. Followers can reportedly react and comment too. Reports say members can also flag inappropriate comments or photos for review.

According to CEO Will Ahmed, every account belongs to a real person with a “verified heartbeat.” That’s Whoop’s answer to bots and AI-generated posts. Whoop Humans also reportedly comes with every membership tier at no extra cost.

It has been revealed that now, Humans isn’t Whoop’s first time at trying to make its platform more social. Remember when comparing stats on Whoop meant joining a Team? If you’re wondering how that differs, that setup works for groups and leaderboards. However, it’s not as elegant when you only want to follow one friend. The launch of Humans doesn’t mean that Teams is going away. Both features will continue to live side-by-side.

The launch of Humans is interesting. For a while, Whoop was the leader in the screen-less fitness tracker space. However, we’ve seen several other companies hop on that bandwagon. This includes Luna, Google, and if the rumors are true, Apple is reportedly considering something similar as well.

So, having a social networking space could give Whoop users a reason to keep using its platform.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

In a recent development, legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Industry observers note that ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

Recent findings suggest that 9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

#301. Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1042 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google

Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance, but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware.
  • Google Pixel Tag is now available for purchase at the Google Store and Amazon.
  • In a recent development, there are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance, but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware. Over two years later, that’s finally arriving in the Google Pixel Tag which, even just a few days in, is the obvious gold standard in the race to build an AirTag for Android devices.

Google Pixel Tag is now available for purchase at the Google Store and Amazon.

In a recent development, there are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market. Pebblebee and Chipolo have been long-standing examples of how to build good dual-network trackers that work on both Android and iOS, while Motorola’s Moto Tag series has delivered two Android-only trackers that deliver better performance and more focused features. But even with the Moto Tag, there’s a clear compromise. Features like the ability to ring your phone are tied to a separate app and, in turn, have some inherent clunkiness.

Pixel Tag is the device that finally brings it all together, and it’s brilliant so far.

I’ve only had the Pixel Tag for a week and, frankly, it’s impossible to properly review a tracker in that time. There are only so many ways to artificially test out how a tracker works, as most cases where you’ll find value in this sort of product can only occur in real life.

So, with that noted, let’s focus on the fundamentals.

In a recent development, google Pixel Tag pairs to your Android phone just like any other Find Hub tracker – though much faster compared to some others I’ve tested – but the differences are obvious towards the end of that process. The final screen reveals options for setting ringer volume and an option to set up “Ring this phone.”.

It has been revealed that those fresh features are what make the Pixel Tag so good, and so appealing compared to all of the competition. A quick double-tap on the Tag’s button rings whichever phone you connected it to, assuming it’s in range, and it works pretty reliably. You can also set up “left behind” alerts (now available on other Find Hub trackers too) for when the phone leaves the tracker behind – you can set up exclusion zones such as your home or work address.

Industry observers note that one of my favorite examples of the added polish from Google is the ability to adjust the ringer volume on the page where you actually want to ring the tracker. In a crowded but quiet space where you know the tracker is close by, being able to quickly set the volume to low is a great addition. In my book, it’s the reason to buy Pixel Tag over any other Android tracker.

According to recent reports, UWB, of course, only makes up-close finding all the better. I found this decently reliable on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, but it is a little bit frustrating that the directional cues vanish within about 10-12 feet. Fine for a backpack or something like that, potentially a problem if your Tag is attached to a set of keys.

Sources indicate that on that note, my biggest hardware complaint is that Google took the Apple route of having no built-in mounting mechanism. The super thin and light hardware of Pixel Tag is wonderful, don’t get me wrong, but being forced to buy a separate accessory just to attach it to my bag is frustrating! One of Google’s partners, Bellroy, built one of these accessories and it’s simple enough – a silicone case with a rope. I wish I didn’t need it, but it works, and at least you get two of them in a pack for $25.

The hardware itself is pretty good across the board, really, with the battery door also being slightly easier to open compared to the Moto Tag. Inside is a standard CR2032 battery that Google says will last “over one year.” I’d personally still prefer a rechargeable battery with USB-C or wireless charging, but this is a good enough solution given the amount of time the battery lasts – hopefully Google’s claim lives up.

Industry observers note that rounding out some of the key aspects here, it’s worth saying that the built-in speaker is more than loud enough at its highest setting, but the value for me so far has really come in that the low setting is actually low enough to not be a nuisance. I do find it a little strange that there’s no visual indication of where the Tag’s button is, but the packaging and app both do a good enough job of letting you know.

I really just wish it would have a rechargeable battery, preferably via USB-C. It would have been the only tracker on the market to support UWB and be rechargeable.

It has been revealed that overall performance in Find Hub seems fine, but as mentioned at the outset, this is a really hard thing to test artificially, all the more so in the span of just a few days. Google’s Find Hub network has gotten a lot better in the past two years, but it’s still hit or miss in my experience. It’s very clear that Google is making an effort to reverse the privacy-inspired decision to effectively disable the Find Hub network outside of crowded areas, but the damage has been done. I’m not sure the network will ever fully recover from that misstep, regardless of what tracker you’re using it with.

It has been revealed that I’m looking forward to seeing how Pixel Tag performs as the travel season spins back up, so stay tuned for a later long-term review of Google’s tracker in the coming months. Initial impressions, though, are solid. Sound off in the comments below if you have any questions around Pixel Tag, I’ll answer everything I can!

Google Pixel Tag is now available at the Google Store and Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that picture this: you upgrade your phone, and it feels like a fresh start. You can finally make the most of advanced features and upcoming tech, but some of them are paywalled behind a silly subscription — well, that’s what the future Samsung experience could look like.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this week, it was leaked that Samsung might experiment with charging for Galaxy AI, meaning that tools such as Bixby Action, Daily Briefing, and Gen Video will be shunned into a subscription strategy. It got me thinking: if you spend good money on a device, would these additional services make the experience any better?

According to recent reports, this is something that Apple is particularly notorious for, and once you’ve scored a new device, there’s a whole manner of add-ons out there. Of course there are its flagship streaming services, Apple Music and Apple TV+, but Apple One is a handy way to cut the cord on services by bundling them into one subscription plan.

The difference with Apple is that these add-ons are designed as almost entirely separate services even though they still exist within the Apple ecosystem. For example, Apple Music is an Apple brand, but it operates as its own entity like Spotify or any other major music streaming platform. It’s also available to non-Apple users.

As smartphones develop alongside the evolution of AI tools, more phone manufacturers are starting to embed them into the core mobile experience. Just look at Gemini and Pixel Phones.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, is it fair to charge for tools that are already built into the device when you take it out of the box? According to Samsung Galaxy users, it’s not.

While some existing features (Now Brief, Browsing Assist, and Samsung Keyboard tools) are expected to remain free for now, not everyone is thrilled about the possibility of having to pay extra for the complete Galaxy AI experience, as one user on Reddit bluntly puts it (see below).

It has been revealed that the other problem is the value that’s being brought to the table. Because the market is becoming increasingly saturated, there are a plethora of AI services that can assist you with all manner of things, but for existing Galaxy users, the quality just isn’t there with Galaxy AI.

With Google’s own Gemini services taking the reins of the tech giant’s smartphones and home tech devices, the competition is fierce. In response to the Redditor above, another user added, ‘Most of which can be done better directly with Google services anyway. If I want AI I'll just use actual AI services, though I appreciate there's a local option (which dumbs most of these features down). There are a few useful things, but the vast majority of it is a solution in search of a problem.'.

Equally, ChatGPT gives Galaxy AI a run for its money, but even though its premium features are also paywalled, the value factor is unmatched, making it even more difficult for Samsung to compete with the substantial dogs.

‘The only thing of 'value' is the device automation, which requires device integration. Otherwise, people are better off using external frontier models,’ a Redditor concludes.

It has been revealed that the Made by Google 2026 lineup is finally complete with tomorrow’s retail launch of the Pixel Tag. You can find our review here, while there are some additional details about the device since the August announcement.

The Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker with NFC. Google did not mention this connectivity specification in August, with Near Field Communication letting you tap the tracker to the back of your phone to immediately open device settings. The NFC area on the Pixel Tag is below the circular battery door, which you hold down and twist counterclockwise to open.

According to recent reports, on Android 17 QPR2, tapping immediately opens the details page. On QPR1, you first get a system notification that you need to click. NFC joins Bluetooth 6.0 with Channel Sounding and Ultra Wideband (UWB).

The Pixel Tag has a physical button on the rear side below the battery cover. Clicking twice plays a loud sound on your phone if both devices are nearby. Once found, you can tap the button once to silence, or turn it off from your phone. This feature can be disabled from the Pixel Tag’s device details page on a tracker-by-tracker basis.

Google does not have a first-party case for the Pixel Tag. Instead, it’s working with Made for Google partner Bellroy.

There are two models available from the Google Store, with the first made of silicone. The Bellroy Lite Case Duo costs $24.99 and comes in a pack of two: Mist and Shadow colorways. It wraps everything but the face of the Pixel Tag (and its speaker cutout), while giving you a hole in the corner and color-matching cord.

There’s also the Bellroy Leather Tag Case in Artichoke, Azalea, Black, Pewter, and Red Ochre for $29.99.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, malaysia and Singapore have intensified scrutiny of AI hardware shipments amid concerns about the potential circumvention of U.S.
  • In a recent development, malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is examining whether Speedmatrix, the Malaysian subsidiary of Singapore-based Megaspeed, re-exported any of the AI processors and servers it had imported for use in local data centers.
  • The Malaysian ministry remarked it was cooperating with customs authorities as well as officials in Singapore and the U.S., and could introduce additional restrictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, malaysia and Singapore have intensified scrutiny of AI hardware shipments amid concerns about the potential circumvention of U.S. export restrictions on China. Malaysia has introduced an investigation into whether AI hardware imported by a subsidiary of the ill-fated Megaspeed was subsequently exported to other countries, reports Reuters. Meanwhile, Singapore has charged another executive over questionable purchases of 917 servers that may contain Nvidia accelerators, according to The Straits Times. The news follows the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over claims he had multiple extra-marital affairs, including with a possible Chinese intelligence asset who facilitated GPU smuggling into China. Analysts speculate that systematic chip smuggling may be the reason behind his departure.

In a recent development, malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is examining whether Speedmatrix, the Malaysian subsidiary of Singapore-based Megaspeed, re-exported any of the AI processors and servers it had imported for use in local data centers. Apparently, after months of investigating, authorities have yet to find out whether any such shipments occurred and, if they did, whether they complied with Malaysian laws. Malaysia introduced restrictions on the export, transit, and trans-shipment of advanced U.S.-developed AI accelerators in July 2025, so it now requires companies to obtain appropriate permits.

The Malaysian ministry remarked it was cooperating with customs authorities as well as officials in Singapore and the U.S., and could introduce additional restrictions. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there was no evidence that Megaspeed-related AI hardware had left Malaysia, but he promised to cooperate with international investigations.

Sources indicate that speaking of Megaspeed, the manufacturer remarked on November 12 that it had hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a comprehensive inventory of its AI GPUs and independently assess its compliance with U.S. export-control regulations, reports DigiTimes. The company also confirmed that it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and was prepared to cooperate with other U.S. government agencies if necessary.

In a recent development, james Tan Yong Pong, chief executive of Megaspeed, stressed that compliance with U.S. export rules as well as transparent operations were always a priority for the tech giant. However, Megaspeed did not disclose how many GPUs it owns and which GPU models it has, what BIS examined during its inspections, or whether the authorities had identified any violations.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Singaporean authorities have brought 41 criminal charges against Shi Bingzhe, a 34-year-old Chinese citizen who served as director of Superphi and chief operating officer of NJ Global Financial. The two companies purchased 917 servers containing restricted Nvidia hardware from Aperia International in 41 transactions between May 2024 and February 2025, according to prosecutors. Authorities allege that the companies had reason to believe the servers were linked to criminal activity by Aperia International. Superphi now faces six charges, while NJ Global Financial faces 35.

The latest charges expand a case that now involves five individuals and six companies. Four firms — Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech, Aperia Cloud Services (II), and Luxuriate Your Life — were charged in July over allegedly making false claims when purchasing servers. Meanwhile, the exact nature of those claims was not disclosed in the report. Authorities have frozen the disposal of a property worth approximately S$55 million and confiscated around S$1 million from bank accounts. Shi faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of S$500,000 per charge if convicted. His next court appearance is scheduled for January 4, 2027.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that the two cases largely highlight the significance of Malaysia and Singapore in the supply chain of restricted AI hardware to places where it should not be, such as China. Singapore's investigation focuses on alleged fraud and transactions involving proceeds of criminal activity, whereas Malaysia seeks to find out whether imported AI equipment was subsequently shipped abroad in violation of local regulations.

Neither investigation has found that the hardware ultimately reached China, but both illustrate difficulties that authorities face as they attempt to enforce restrictions on advanced AI hardware across international supply chains.

Industry observers note that the Google Fi app gains a “Your super network” card in the Home tab that shows whether you’re connected to the Primary or Secondary network. “See activity” lets you view switching history and when it last occurred. Google will also note if you’re in range of W+ networks.

Sources indicate that google today is also expanding its Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ network beyond Pixel phones to select Samsung Galaxy (S23, Fold/Flip 5, and newer) and modern Motorola phones. According to recent reports, the final patch today sees the companion app gain “Ask Fi.” This AI-powered chat is meant to quickly provide answers and guided troubleshooting for common issues. You can request human support with seamless handoff that keeps the chat context.

#290. Samsung’s Smart Ring Stylus Patent Is Clever, but It’s Holding One Catch Back

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (539 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidheadlines

Samsung’s Smart Ring Stylus Patent Is Clever, but It’s Holding One Catch Back

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidheadlines

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A Samsung patent application describes using two smart rings to add stylus-like control to finger drawing.
  • Sources indicate that samsung might have found a way to make finger drawing on your phone feel more like using a stylus, and it involves wearing two smart rings.
  • Sources indicate that patentlyze dug into the filing, published November 12 as US 2026/0358914 A1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Samsung patent application describes using two smart rings to add stylus-like control to finger drawing. One ring senses finger bend for pressure and the other senses tilt, which the phone turns into line thickness, transparency, and shading. It doesn’t need a pen-sensing screen, but you’d need a ring on each hand.

Sources indicate that samsung might have found a way to make finger drawing on your phone feel more like using a stylus, and it involves wearing two smart rings. A new patent application describes how a pair of rings could add pressure and tilt control to drawing with a bare finger on Android phones without built-in stylus support.

Sources indicate that patentlyze dug into the filing, published November 12 as US 2026/0358914 A1. Samsung filed it in July, and it continues an earlier international application from 2024.

Sources indicate that the problem it’s trying to solve is pretty simple. When you draw on a phone with your finger, every line comes out the same width and shade, no matter how hard you press. A stylus fixes that, but most phones don’t support one, and it’s easy to leave at home.

Samsung’s idea splits the work between two rings. One goes on a finger of your free hand and measures how much you bend it, which the phone treats like pressing harder. The other goes on your drawing finger and tracks how you tilt it.

Sources indicate that the phone turns those readings into brush settings. Pressure controls how thick or transparent a line is, and tilt controls gradation, or how one shade blends into the next. In one example from the filing, a stroke drawn with no tilt has a single tone, while a stroke at 60 degrees has four tones and a thicker line.

Industry observers note that there’s more to it. The phone can subtract its own angle to figure out your finger’s tilt against the screen, and it can factor in how much of your finger is touching the glass. Sliders let you adjust how much each ring affects the brush. The filing also describes a preview that pops up when a ring gets close to the screen, an eraser that uses the same pressure and tilt controls, and an ink bleed effect.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage is that the screen doesn’t need a special pen layer. The rings do all the sensing.

The obvious catch is that you’d need two smart rings, one on each hand. Most people don’t own one, let alone two. And curling a finger on your other hand to press harder would take some getting used to.

It has been revealed that samsung already sells the Galaxy Ring, but it only works as a health and fitness tracker today. This is also one of several recent ring-related patents from Samsung, including one for a foldable phone that can charge a smart ring. Like any patent, there’s no guarantee this will ever become a real feature.

For now, if you want real pressure-sensitive drawing on a Samsung phone, you need the S Pen, which is still limited to Samsung’s Ultra models like the Galaxy S27 Ultra expected next year.

Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Sources indicate that available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. Rather, this is a smart lock designed for your standard single-bore latch, meaning it’s available for doors that other smart locks aren’t compatible with. You can still have a deadbolt, but you’ll need enough space for both (per Wyze’s guidelines below).

In a recent development, the Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze says recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second. It uses local storage for biometric data and works to improve that data with each successful unlock.

According to recent reports, the PIN has a clever feature (though it’s presented in somewhat poor taste) that lets you input random digits before or after your actual code to prevent onlookers from being able to see your code. There’s also a physical key backup as well as a USB-C input on the outside in the case that the battery dies – Wyze notes it lasts about 12 months on a charge using eight AA batteries.

The Wyze Lever Lock is available today for $99.98 and shipping immediately.

Industry observers note that enhancement 11/13/26 at 12:10pm ET: Intel has confirmed the 260K Plus as a "limited-availability" SKU and indicates it's not right now available as a boxed retail chip. Specs should go live on Intel's website within the next few days.

Recent findings suggest that A new Intel Arrow Lake SKU is listed for sale in multiple prebuilt PCs on Newegg, despite no official acknowledgement of the model from Intel. The Core Ultra 7 260K is a downclocked version of the Core Ultra 7 265K from Intel's main Arrow Lake stack, not the Arrow Lake Refresh stack that's infiltrated our list of the best CPUs for gaming. Outside of a few areas on Newegg's website, you'll find no mention of the CPU elsewhere online (including Intel's official Core Ultra Series 2 specs page).

According to recent reports, although retailer-exclusive and late-generation variants are common from AMD and Intel — we recently reviewed the Ryzen 5 5500F, for instance — they almost never fly completely under the radar, as is the case with the Core Ultra 7 260K. The chip itself is identical to the Core Ultra 7 265K based on the specs we know, fitted with 20 cores, eight of which are P-cores. The 260K tops out at 5.4 GHz, however, while the 265K reaches 5.5 GHz.

In a recent development, otherwise, the specs are all the same. It comes with the same 125W TDP, same 30 MB of L3 cache, and same support for up to 256 GB of memory running at DDR5-6400. We only know of these specs from an image shown on the two ABS prebuilt listings available with the 260K. It's available in the ABS Kaze II paired with an RTX 5060, as well as the Flux II Aqua with an RTX 5070.

Sources indicate that the image is below, captured hastily, as you can see, from a Microsoft Teams call. Again, we weren't able to find any information from Intel about the chip outside of this slide.

Recent findings suggest that one critical detail this slide confirms is that the Core Ultra 7 260K belongs to the Arrow Lake family, not the range of Arrow Lake Refresh processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus. It tops out at DDR5-6400, while Arrow Lake Refresh climbs up to DDR5-7200. That means the chip doesn't have access to the hardware-level enhancements available in Arrow Lake Refresh, nor the software-based Intel Binary Optimization Tool that boosts performance in select games.

Although that's enough to categorize the 260K, there are some details that are unclear. In the two PCs it's available in, the chip is referred to as the 260K across the full product page except in Newegg's option selector (pictured below), where it's referred to as the U7-260KF. Intel's KF models are unlocked for overclocking but lack integrated graphics.

Additionally, the slide from Intel referenced above shows the chip boosting up to 5.4 GHz, but the product page lists the chip at 5.2 GHz for maximum boost clock.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, newegg has told us that the chip is exclusive to the retailer and will only be sold through its in-house ABS prebuilts. ABS machines are normally sold with components Newegg already sells piecemeal, offering a convenient way to get a full rig with parts you can identify. The ABS Flux II Aqua, which is available with the chip, is on sale at Newegg now for $300 off.

The ABS Flux II Aqua gaming PC comes with an Intel CPU, an Nvidia GeForce GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, a 1TB NVMe SSD with Gen 4 speeds, and 32GB of DDR5-6000 RAM. This is a 1440p gaming powerhouse with the potential for 4K.

We've reached out to Intel to get more details about the Core Ultra 7 260K, and we'll update this story when we hear back (see update log above). Although the specs suggest the 260K should perform almost identically to the 265K, we haven't had a chance to test the CPU ourselves. And, as you can see from the rankings in our CPU benchmark hierarchy, we recommend most Intel shoppers move toward an Arrow Lake Refresh SKU.

It follows a mercenary called Vander, who rescues a young woman from a sinister ritual and assembles a squad of warriors called Primals to take on a sinister force that threatens the world.

Each Primal is descended from an ancient god and brings their own distinct abilities and roles to combat. There are currently more than two dozen to unlock, with more on the way, including Conan the Barbarian thanks to an official crossover collaboration.

Character progression is an notable part of the game, with unique character quests and the ability to develop platonic (and even romantic) relationships with your team.

Otero claims that "console games on mobile" has been an aspiration for years, and this release finally "delivers on that promise." He adds that UnGoldy offers "the same depth, fidelity, and experience you'd expect on PC or console.".

The game is presently available on the Google Play Store, with an enhanced experience and more precise controls for those playing on PC via Google Play Games for PC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung may be working on something more exciting than another Galaxy Z Fold or Z Flip refresh. The company is reportedly developing a smartphone with a sliding display that can change shape depending on how you want to use it.

The latest information comes from well-known leaker Ice Universe, who shared concept renders on X that demonstrated the device may switch between 16:9 and 21:9 aspect ratios. The images reveal a slightly squat handset that tapers off into a more traditional smartphone shape.

As per the leak, this device could expand vertically instead of folding in half, so you get a small phone when you want it but a taller screen when you want more screen.

Samsung is developing a phone with a display that can extend from 16:9 to 21:9. Some people prefer a wider screen, while others like a taller form factor. This design could accommodate both, letting owners adjust the proportions to suit what they’re doing. If Samsung can make it work, it could be a very appealing solution. Battery capacity is the massive challenge, though. The sliding mechanism would take up a considerable amount of internal space, leaving less room for the battery. How much capacity could Samsung fit inside? And would it deliver enough battery life with the screen fully extended? Those are questions it needs to answer before this becomes a practical everyday device.November 11, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that it's not an entirely latest idea. Samsung Display has been working on rollable panels for quite some time, and Samsung even demoed a similar concept at MWC 2026. But that prototype required manual shifting and not a fully automated mechanism.

According to recent reports, samsung’s patent filings give us a better idea of what might be going on behind the scenes. One application consists of two sections of housing, which move relative to each other, connected by a flexible display.

Instead of users having to pull the screen out, it could roll around an internal mechanism and extend when needed, maybe by a motor.

Of course, fitting a motorized screen into a smartphone has some compromises. The sliding assembly occupies space inside the chassis, and this space is no longer available for the battery. A bigger screen could also mean higher power consumption when extended, making battery life a particularly important question.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

In a recent development, samsung’s patent work reveals reinforced sliding rails and supporting slats behind the flexible panel to protect it in motion. The tech giant might also look at silicon-carbon battery technology to get more capacity into the tight space, just like it did to the Galaxy Z8 series. But these are still possible solutions, not confirmed specs for a finished phone.

According to recent reports, samsung has not confirmed whether the device will be available in stores. Earlier reports have suggested a 2028 commercial launch could be possible, but that's a long way from being a firm commitment.

For now it suggests Samsung is looking beyond traditional foldables, exploring ways to make a phone’s screen adapt to its owner rather than the other way around.

#279. Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (842 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview.
  • Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.
  • Industry observers note that microsoft has released a public preview of a local command-line interface for Azure Logic Apps Standard, shipped as the logicapp extension for the Azure CLI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview.

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.

Industry observers note that microsoft has released a public preview of a local command-line interface for Azure Logic Apps Standard, shipped as the logicapp extension for the Azure CLI. It adds project creation, workflow authoring, a local runtime, connector and connection management, run inspection, and test scaffolding to a tool that until now only managed deployed apps, so that a Standard workflow can be created, run, and tested without Visual Studio Code.

The extension installs automatically the first time an az logicapp developer command runs on Azure CLI 2.67.0 or later, and adds 19 command groups with 64 commands beside the thirteen existing cloud-management commands, which it leaves untouched. On the authoring side, project create creates or adopts a local project; workflow create, set, export, and validate work on individual workflow.json files with offline validation by default, and runtime start, stop, and show manage a local host on port 7071, launching the Azurite storage emulator when the project is configured for development storage.

Recent findings suggest that the remaining groups reach into running and deployed apps. connector and connection inspect built-in and managed connectors and wire connections into a project or a deployed app, run and trigger history start, wait on, cancel and resubmit executions and download an action’s recorded inputs and outputs, and deployment package produces what the documentation calls a deterministic deployment package. Named context shortcuts hold a target so later commands do not repeat it.

(Source: Microsoft Community Hub).

The doctor and test commands say the most about who the tool expects to be typing. runtime doctor only reads: project files, tool versions, cached bundle evidence, loopback ports. It "never installs, downloads, starts, stops, repairs, decrypts settings, changes context, or contacts cloud storage," and it exits 1 for a required failure and 2 when a required check comes back unknown. Testing is split into three steps for the same reason. test create scaffolds a native SDK test project and stops before restoring a package or running anything, test plan writes a preflight report without executing a test, and test run is the only command that builds and runs them, under a deadline. The announcement lists limitations on that last step. In the pull request that added the extension, author Riley Evans goes further: native SDK test code is trusted rather than sandboxed, and the agent bootstrap command does not exist yet.

Sagar Sharma, a Microsoft MVP, wrote on LinkedIn that this is deliberate. The CLI is "literally pitched as adding determinism to local AI-assisted coding": an agent validates, runs, inspects and tests, then repeats until the run is green, and secrets reach it through stdin rather than on the command line. Sharma had already called the CLI the sleeper hit of Microsoft's recent Logic Apps announcements in an earlier write-up, on the grounds that an agent without a deterministic way to validate and run a workflow is guessing. Named contexts, capability discovery and the handling of secrets were his evidence that someone had designed for that case.

Sonny Gillissen, also a Microsoft MVP, put the same point in terms of a team's week. A latest hire clones a repository and has a local runtime up "in minutes, instead of hours." A coding assistant drafting a workflow from a business requirement works "with an authoritative shell instead of assumptions." Integration flows get tested from the CI/CD pipeline instead of by hand. He called the CLI a bridge from today's development process to a fully automated one and, in passing, said an agent could test a workflow locally "without ever touching Azure at all.".

That passing remark is the one Christos Panagiotidis, a Microsoft MVP and certified trainer, would test first. His pilot initiative is explicitly a proposal rather than a report of a run, and its two main cautions come straight from Microsoft's own walkthrough. That walkthrough uses live Azure and Microsoft 365 resources, and some of its commands change deployed connections, so a local run has remote effects, whatever the terminal suggests.

Microsoft itself notes that validation "does not establish authorization or business correctness." Panagiotidis adds a housekeeping point: CLI extensions do not patch with the CLI, so anyone comparing results across runs needs the CLI, extension, runtime and project versions recorded next to each result.

Microsoft has said a broader command surface will follow soon. Until then, the designer stays in VS Code. The CLI edits workflow.json directly; it cannot change the state of a running local app, and the pull request's own limits section concedes that Linux CI results prove neither native SDK execution nor execution against live Azure.

#276. Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.
  • The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.
  • AMD also announced that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.

The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.

AMD also announced that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.

Recent findings suggest that google's April 2026 launch split its eighth generation hardware into the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference. Google bills this as the first time it has introduced four TPU systems in one year, but as ServeTheHome points out, the two newcomers are system configurations built on existing chips rather than fresh designs.

As per Taiwanese outlet INSIDE, the 8tx inherits the 8t's 12.6 petaflops of FP4 compute and 216GB of HBM, but swaps in the lower-latency Boardfly network used by the 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty, and pitches the system at regulated enterprises and governments that want to fine-tune, distill, and train agents on private data without moving it between clusters.

Sources indicate that AMD indicates Epyc handles orchestration, data preparation, and the high-throughput link to the accelerators. Its Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) works with the TPU to extend the protected environment out to the accelerators, checking each one's identity and security configuration before granting direct access to protected memory.

Sources indicate that prompts, model weights, and intermediate data stay encrypted in host memory and in transit, according to AMD, with hardware isolation while the TPU runs. Google, for its part, described the result as "keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use.".

Recent findings suggest that google hasn't directly said why it passed over Axion, the Neoverse V2-based chip it unveiled in 2024 as its first data center processor. Its own documentation offers a strong hint, however: Google's list of supported Confidential VM configurations runs entirely on AMD SEV and Intel TDX machines, with no Axion-based C4A or N4A instances, and states that TPUs can't right now be attached to Confidential VMs at all.

AMD's release adds that Google security experts have performed deep reviews of AMD's security processor firmware, and that SEV already underpins Google's Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, and confidential Spark and Dataflow services.

It could be argued here that confidential computing is only as credible as the years spent attacking it, and Google's audited chain of trust runs through x86. Building an equivalent on Axion would mean qualifying new hardware before shipping a product whose entire selling point is the "trust" it comes with, making it a moot point.

The move however is not a win for AMD's latest silicon; ServeTheHome reported that Google chose Turin to match the TPU 8t's PCIe Gen5 x16 interface, noting that a Gen6 host such as Venice would add no accelerator bandwidth, and tying the decision to Google's 2027 qualification schedule. Venice is AMD's 2nm flagship; the 8tx runs on a chip based on a family of CPUs that launched in October 2024.

Recent findings suggest that mark Lohmeyer, who runs AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, told reporters that select customers will be able to deploy the 8tx in their own data centers, Data Center Knowledge reported, noting that Oracle recently noted it will offer TPUs on its cloud. INSIDE quoted Lohmeyer arguing that the technology lowers the risk of physical operators reaching sensitive data, even in third-party facilities.

According to recent reports, as TPUs spread beyond Google's own campuses, hardware attestation becomes the mechanism that lets a model owner place weights on hardware someone else runs. That interestingly puts AMD as a crucial part at the root of Google's off-campus trust offerings, a bigger role than the 8tx's niche positioning would initially suggest.

According to recent reports, it also revives August's rumor: A SemiAnalysis client note reported by Tom's Hardware, noted "Market chatter suggests [Google] is working with AMD on a TPU project in the v10 generation," possibly with CPU cores on the same package. The 8tx confirms neither claim as its Epyc chips sit in separate sockets, and nothing confirmed on November 9 involves AMD in accelerator design, but it does lend credence to potential future collaborations between the chip designer and the AI juggernaut.

The news saw AMD closing at $508.58 on November 9, up 13.26%, after trading as high as $515.18 on more than twice its recent average volume and while not all of it can be attributed to this particular development even as Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer upgraded AMD to Outperform with a $600 target, calling its server and data center success "undeniable", one could argue that it was a sizeable, if not the overwhelming catalyst in play that day.

The TPU 8tx arguably won't turn AMD's Epyc into a formidable TPU business overnight, and Google has left enough unpublished that its confidential computing claims deserve scrutiny once customers can test them.

However, one does need to account for the fact that when Google needed a host CPU to stake its first confidential TPU on, it picked AMD over its own chip, and that endorsement will outlast one day's share price increase as the latter aims to broaden its AI business even as its CEO recently branded the organization as "Data center-first" entity even as PC sales continue to plummet.

  • It has been revealed that mechanical keyboards don't usually come cheap, but there are several budget-friendly boards that any keyboard lover would be thrilled to receive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Keyboards are one of the most key, if not the most important, PC peripherals. You use your keyboard constantly — it's the primary input source for just about everyone (there are a few exceptions). And everyone deserves a keyboard that's a little nicer than the $5 board that was tossed in for free with your last PC purchase. Or — god forbid — whatever's built into your laptop.

Sources indicate that if you've got a gamer, a writer, or, well, anyone who uses a computer for any reason in your life, they could probably use a keyboard upgrade. Even keyboard enthusiasts with multiple mechanical boards will appreciate a upcoming one, especially if it fills a niche — say, a low-profile board that's portable and perfect for traveling, or a nostalgia-inducing retro-inspired board that's reminiscent of their favorite old-school game console.

It has been revealed that mechanical keyboards don't usually come cheap, but there are several budget-friendly boards that any keyboard lover would be thrilled to receive. And if they've already got the board of their dreams, pick up a fun accessory — a cool-looking cable, some pretty keycaps, or a wrist rest — to really elevate their typing experience.

Sources indicate that there aren't a ton of budget-friendly mechanical keyboards built for keyboard enthusiasts, but there are a few. These are all pre-built, so your recipient won't need to know how to assemble anything, but you can also often pick up bare-bones keyboard kits for cheaper than their fully built counterparts.

This full-size wired mechanical keyboard comes with red (linear) or brown (tactile) switches and has a hot-swappable PCB, PBT keycaps, and up to a 1,000 Hz polling rate — so it's great for both work and play.

Industry observers note that this compact 75% keyboard comes with Leobog Reaper switches, PBT keycaps, and a programmable knob. The shell is mostly plastic, but the layers of sound-dampening material make for a nice "thock.".

In a recent development, this 75% wireless mechanical keyboard features a gasket mount design, PBT keycaps, bright RGB backlighting, and a customizable TFT screen, as well as a programmable knob. And a hot-swappable PCB so you can bring your own switches.

Sources indicate that this low-profile wireless 75% mechanical keyboard comes with a wrist rest that doubles as a keyboard stand to adjust the angle. The board comes with low-profile linear switches and features a full aluminum body, so it looks and feels premium — but still costs under $100.

This 87-key Bluetooth/2.4GHz/USB keyboard has all the retro vibes of a classic IBM-style keyboard, but without the huge price tag! Kailh Box Switch V2 White mechanical key switches, dye-sub PBT keycaps, and multiple connection options make this a great keyboard for retro computing and getting work done.

An OG-Xbox-inspired 87-key keyboard with RGB backlight! You get 87 keys with Kailh Jellyfish X switches, double-layered ABS keycaps, and a lovely translucent green plastic shell! The colored cursor keys are beautiful.

If you're shopping for a keyboard enthusiast — or anyone who already has a keyboard they love, getting them a keyboard as a gift probably won't go over quite as well. But that doesn't mean you can't still pick up an accessory or two to complement their favorite board.

Sources indicate that cables are a part of life, but that doesn't mean they have to be ugly. This coiled USB-C cable from Keychron comes in four colors and is specifically designed to fit Keychron's K, K Pro, K Max, and K HE series boards, but will work with most USB-C boards. It comes with a 14cm coiled section and a 94cm straight cable that connect via a detachable aviator port, plus a USB-C to USB-A converter.

It has been revealed that not all keyboards have hot-swappable switches, but almost all of them have swappable keycaps. Glorious' cherry-profile keycaps are made of double-shot PBT and come in a variety of pretty, ombre colors.

In a recent development, just about every keyboard user could use a wrist rest, and this cooling gel-filled memory foam wrist rest from HyperX is one of our long-time favorites. It's durable and comfortable, and comes in multiple sizes to fit everything from compact to full-size keyboards.

Gel/foam wrist rests are comfortable, but wooden wrist rests are aesthetic (and comfortable, not everyone needs cushion under their wrists). This wooden wrist rest is designed to put your wrists in a neutral position and features non-slip feet to keep it from moving around. It comes in four sizes to fit everything from 60% to full-size keyboards.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that samsung and Google are finally launching their Android XR smart glasses, as previously reported.
  • The Korean tech giant announced today that preorders have now opened, but you’ll have to check if your phone is on the compatibility list to get a pair.
  • The idea with this collection is that it looks like regular eyewear, not another piece of conspicuous tech strapped to your face.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that samsung and Google are finally launching their Android XR smart glasses, as previously reported. The first collection pairs Samsung’s hardware prowess with designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker and will include 30 frame variations.

The Korean tech giant announced today that preorders have now opened, but you’ll have to check if your phone is on the compatibility list to get a pair.

The idea with this collection is that it looks like regular eyewear, not another piece of conspicuous tech strapped to your face. Gentle Monster has six different frame styles, each with a different lens treatment, whereas Warby Parker has three styles: Alden, Reid, and Wren.

Both collections come in various colors and prescription lens options. The glasses weigh around 41 grams, which is relatively lightweight for all-day wear, Samsung notes.

Industry observers note that the real attraction is more than just taking pictures without reaching for your phone. With Gemini in particular, you can identify landmarks, interpret unfamiliar objects, translate restaurant menus, and provide turn-by-turn directions through Google Maps. It can summarize meeting whiteboards and save the results to Samsung Notes.

Sources indicate that you interact with Gemini through voice commands or by tapping the frames. The glasses can also make phone calls, read out notifications, and help with day-to-day tasks. You get a 12MP HDR camera for photos and video, two open-ear speakers, and four mics.

Recent findings suggest that qualcomm’s Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 platform is the engine behind the experience, with up to nine hours of battery life. The included charging case provides up to seven additional charges.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

According to recent reports, warby Parker’s collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster’s more premium frames start at $449 and go up to $489. That’s an affordable starting price compared to some rival smart glasses, but expect the final cost to be impacted by prescription options and individual frame choices.

Of course, when you start putting cameras and microphones on people’s faces, it raises some questions. Samsung claims there’s an external LED that should indicate when the camera is recording, with safeguards in place to prevent it from recording if someone covers the indicator or disables it. Gemini also automatically blurs faces of bystanders in visual requests. Google says it doesn't use visuals captured for AI training or ad targeting.

According to recent reports, there’s another catch, however: it’s not universally compatible. Supported devices are newer Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 based on Android 17, Google Pixel 7 and later, and iPhone 13 Pro or later.

Preorders are now available through Google, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker ahead of its December 10 launch in the US and South Korea (Gentle Monster models only).

I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get.
  • There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track.
  • But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience.

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

It has been revealed that unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

Sources indicate that it’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without matter. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

Recent findings suggest that it does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

It has been revealed that because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

According to recent reports, the Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

Sources indicate that I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

It has been revealed that I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

According to recent reports, on the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It has been revealed that it uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only problem I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

Industry observers note that the homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

It has been revealed that the buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

It’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

It has been revealed that as far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

Industry observers note that I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector.

Hannes Hapke shares how Dataiku’s open-source Kiji Inspector applies Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) directly to decision tokens to expose why agents pick specific tools. Moving past superficial chain-of-thought narratives, he discusses causal ablation, layer activation extraction via patched vLLM engines, and production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders.

Hannes Hapke leads 575 Lab, Dataiku's Open Source Office, focusing on responsible AI, privacy, and ML explainability. He is the co-author of four ML books, including Generative AI Design Patterns and ML Production Systems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that the search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the company undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week.
  • Rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the manufacturer before leaving in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter. Haas is among several candidates under consideration, although it remains unclear whether he will get a formal offer and/or agree to take the position.

Recent findings suggest that the search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the company undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week. For now, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress serves as interim CEO. The company's board is currently searching for a permanent replacement and is reportedly evaluating both internal and external candidates. Neither Arm nor Nvidia commented on the matter to FT.

Rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the manufacturer before leaving in 2013. During his tenure as vice president at Nvidia, he was responsible for multiple projects, including notebook GPUs, Windows-on-Arm, and Tegra system-on-chips. Given that he held senior management positions, he certainly gained experience with Nvidia's operations, corporate culture, and relationships with customers and partners.

Furthermore, Haas has experience with the development of consumer and data center CPUs as well as GPUs and GPU IP, a combination that is hard to find in the industry. Haas reportedly maintains close ties with Jensen Huang and several members of Nvidia's board, which could make him a particularly attractive candidate for a organization whose strategy and management structure have orbited around its founder for more than three decades.

While at Arm, Haas has demonstrated a willingness to make substantial strategic changes at the firm. Since Haas took the reins in 2022, Arm has introduced its Compute Subsystems (CSS) initiative, providing customers with complete and validated processor platform design, making it easier for newcomers to enter the market. Arm also introduced its first own-brand AGI CPU, putting the company in direct competition with some of its traditional customers. Both initiatives represent significant departures from Arm's traditional business model; however, they demonstrate Haas' readiness to pursue latest revenue opportunities despite risks and the possibility of damaging relationships with long-term partners.

Sources indicate that another advantage is Haas' extensive experience with the semiconductor industry in general. Arm's CPU and GPU technologies are used in system-on-chips developed by hundreds of companies that have very distinctive requirements, including Nvidia itself, Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek, just to name a few.

It has been revealed that in addition, Haas led Arm through its initial public offering in 2023 and therefore has experience with investors and regulators. Also, Haas happens to be the CEO of SoftBank, the parent of Arm.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, nevertheless, Haas' potential appointment would not be without challenges, primarily because he has never managed a company the scale of Nvidia. Arm has around 10,000 employees worldwide; it develops and licenses various semiconductor IP, primarily CPU and GPU technologies, to a wide range of customers with distinct needs. By contrast, Nvidia designs CPUs, GPUs, networking equipment, complete AI systems, and software platforms and has a headcount of about 42,000. As a result, if Haas becomes the boss of Nvidia, he will have to manage a considerably bigger organization with a dramatically more complicated product portfolio and supply chain. Furthermore, replacing Huang, who has led Nvidia since its establishment in 1993 and personally shaped its technology strategy and business tactics, would be a formidable task for virtually any executive.

Ironically, Haas' appointment (if it happens) would create an unusual situation in which Nvidia will be led by the chief executive of a firm it attempted to acquire in 2020 and abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid regulatory opposition.
