#263. Nearly 20 years after launch, ancient AMD Radeon HD 2000 and 3000 GPUs finally get a Linux fix for corrupted video playback

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (760 w)
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Nearly 20 years after launch, ancient AMD Radeon HD 2000 and 3000 GPUs finally get a Linux fix for corrupted video playback

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves.
  • Sources indicate that I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8).
  • According to recent reports, interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves. As spotted by Phoronix, the fix targets the Unified Video Decoder (UVD) engine across the RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635, and RV670 silicon families, making up the Radeon HD 2000 and HD 3000 families released starting in 2007. Linux users running these cards experienced visual corruption during hardware-accelerated video playback whenever the GPU was simultaneously handling active 3D or desktop drawing workloads; those issues should now be resolved.

Sources indicate that I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8). When the decoder was reading compressed video from system memory while the GPU was drawing, it would corrupt video frames. Moving the input to VRAM allowed frames to decode correctly. Disabling graphics draws also stopped the corruption. Here is a proposal to keep UVD buffers in VRAM for this family of devices, as the driver already does for some other chips. The patch covers RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635 and RV670. These chips share the RV6xx decoder path and legacy R600 firmware, so I think they are likely to have the same hardware requirements. Someone with the other hardware would need to verify that. I tested this on Debian. I used Codex to help with the investigation, testing and patch.

According to recent reports, interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path. The culprit turned out to be a memory placement oversight: the driver wasn't consistently keeping UVD input buffers pinned inside dedicated VRAM. When graphics draw calls competed for resources, frames failed to decode properly. By forcing those buffers to stay in VRAM — a behavior the Radeon kernel driver apparently already enforced for several other chip families — video playback cleans right up.

According to recent reports, it is easy to forget just how pivotal the R600 generation was for PC graphics. Launching in 2007 as the first desktop GPU lineup built under the AMD banner following that firm's blockbuster acquisition of the Canadian ATI Technologies Inc., the Radeon HD 2000 series marked the fresh AMD graphics division's transition away from separate pixel and vertex pipelines on the desktop, after implementing the tech first for the Xbox 360. The move to a unified shader architecture arrived alongside DirectX 10 and Windows Vista, so it was a time of many transitions.

In a recent development, while the flagship Radeon HD 2900 XT famously struggled against Nvidia's dominant GeForce 8800 GTX in raw gaming rasterization and power draw, the R600 family brought serious multimedia chops to the table. The introduction of the first-generation Unified Video Decoder (UVD) on the mainstream RV610 and RV630 chips, and later the refined RV670 powering the beloved Radeon HD 3850 and 3870, allowed even budget PCs to offload heavy H.264 and VC-1 Blu-ray decoding from the CPU. In 2007, smooth 1080p playback without maxing out a dual-core processor was a major selling point for many owners, but none more so than home theater PC (HTPC) builders.

It has been revealed that of course, almost nobody is daily driving a TeraScale 1 graphics card in 2026, especially when modern integrated graphics run circles around them at a fraction of the wattage; the contributor who submitted the patches wants them for his ancient Core 2 Duo-based iMac. Yet, there is something quietly heartwarming about the longevity of open-source Linux drivers. Whereas proprietary Windows support for the HD 2000 and 3000 series was sunsetted over a decade ago, the mainline Linux kernel continues to carry the torch. Combined with recent AI-assisted cleanup efforts across the Mesa R600 user-space driver, vintage Radeon hardware is arguably in better software shape today than it was during its actual retail lifespan.

  • Over a hundred thousand frustrated users were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that upgrade (Nov 13, 6:57 am ET): Microsoft indicates recovery efforts are now in phases, with some affected infrastructure already back online and traffic slowly returning to normal. Initially, the firm blamed high infrastructure loads across many regions, but the investigation eventually revealed a more specific problem with automated server health checks. The tech giant has revealed that automated server health checks misfired, kicking healthy infrastructure offline and triggering cascading connection failures across Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot. There are automated health checks that can detect failing hardware and take it out of rotation before your inbox breaks. Instead, a particular server component that does those checks started failing its own tests. Multiple regions lost their healthy servers, and the rest of the infrastructure buckled under heavier-than-usual loads, preventing users around the world from loading their mailboxes or sending messages. Now, Microsoft’s recovery playbook relies on working around its referee. Engineers made a targeted change to work around the faulty health-check component on some servers to see if they would stay online, while rolling out safeguards to stop other machines from dropping out. Automated recovery systems have been activated to minimize the disruption, and teams are also working in parallel to rebuild the affected servers with previous configurations.

Over a hundred thousand frustrated users were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

Outlook users in the Americas began reporting they could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes, and the complaints were rolling in fast, with Downdetector reporting more than 125,000 complaints as of this writing.

If you attempted to refresh your inbox only to be greeted by infinite loading screens, you were not the only one. Users are reporting being completely locked out of their accounts across desktop apps, web browsers, and mobile clients. Microsoft’s official 365 Status account confirmed the hiccup on X, blaming Exchange Online, the cloud backbone that powers your Outlook email, calendar, and contacts.

We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.November 12, 2026.

The tech giant initially said the connection failures were limited to the Americas, but the company later confirmed that the connectivity bug could be hitting users in just about any region.

The problem is due to the way Outlook clients authenticate and connect to Exchange Online mailboxes using different connection methods.

Microsoft engineers are currently scrambling to resolve problems on the server end and mitigate the impact, but the tech giant has not yet provided a concrete timeline for a full fix.

Apps in Microsoft 365 that rely on the same service connectivity may also be slow or throw error codes until the dust settles, though Exchange Online takes the biggest hit. For now, the best course of action is to keep an eye on the official Microsoft 365 status feed, enjoy a rare, guilt-free excuse to ignore your boss’s emails, and wait for the servers to wake back up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have explained how they tried to modernize the Bond franchise while retaining its classic roots.

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, Henson and Smith discussed their inspirations for the game's soundtrack and revealed that their primary goal was to push the franchise into a more contemporary direction while keeping the familiar elements fans love.

According to recent reports, "Luckily there is a huge catalogue of music, film and novels to dive into, and we took inspiration from all of them, as well as other sources not in the Bond world," Henson noted. "Our mission we set ourselves was to give the franchise a gentle nudge into the modern day, without completely reinventing it. It was always going to sound like James Bond.".

Smith added that he loves the original Ian Fleming novels and used First Light "as an excuse to re-read them on the train into work each day.".

Sources indicate that "But like we mentioned before, one of the great things about this franchise is its ability to stay current and adapt," he said. "So, the possibility of going some different places with the music was always there.".

While the pair's catalogue of inspiration was "huge" and offered plenty of references, Henson confessed that they tried not to look too much at the previous Bond games, but "we took the time to watch the film series to study the scores in a different light, now that we knew we’d be working on our own.".

"So many great composers have added their voice to the franchise, from John Barry to Eric Serra, Michael Kamen to Hans Zimmer, and it is fascinating to hear how each one approaches the material," the composer said.

According to recent reports, smith added, "That made it easier, actually. The fact that the music has gone in so many different directions already made us more confident to pursue our own.".

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

#258. Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing.
  • Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.
  • Sources indicate that technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing.

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.

Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:.

If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.

Industry observers note that debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our upcoming learning.

Sources indicate that debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.

It has been revealed that yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:.

Recent findings suggest that every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.

The challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao remarked. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.

According to recent reports, technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we enhancement our understanding, Yao explained:.

The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.

AI introduces a new challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.

Agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.

InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?

Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.

Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.

InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?

Industry observers note that yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.

Industry observers note that A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

#256. Samsung’s Smart Glasses Won’t Let You Live Stream to Social Media

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (505 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidheadlines

Samsung’s Smart Glasses Won’t Let You Live Stream to Social Media

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidheadlines

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s latest privacy rules block apps on Samsung Intelligent Eyewear from social live streaming, something Ray-Ban Meta glasses can do.
  • Recent findings suggest that samsung’s smart glasses won’t let you go live on social media, and that’s by design.
  • Shahram Izadi, Google’s VP and GM of XR, detailed the protections in a blog post on November 12, as SamMobile points out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s latest privacy rules block apps on Samsung Intelligent Eyewear from social live streaming, something Ray-Ban Meta glasses can do. The glasses also detect a covered recording light, blur bystanders’ faces before sending images to Gemini, and keep camera data out of AI training. They’re up for pre-order now and ship in mid-December.

Recent findings suggest that samsung’s smart glasses won’t let you go live on social media, and that’s by design. Google indicates its Play Store rules block apps from using the camera on Intelligent Eyewear for social live streaming, which sets these glasses apart from Meta’s. It’s one of several privacy rules Google laid out just as the glasses opened for pre-order this week, and they’re meant to pair with the Android phones you already have.

Shahram Izadi, Google’s VP and GM of XR, detailed the protections in a blog post on November 12, as SamMobile points out. He said privacy on glasses has to protect both the person wearing them and the people in front of them.

Google Play’s policies now bar apps from social live streaming, real-time facial recognition, and changing how the outward recording light works. That’s a substantial difference from Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which can stream straight to Instagram and Facebook.

Every pair has an outward-facing light that turns on when you take a photo or record video. If you cover it or tamper with it, sensors are designed to notice and block the camera. Google indicates this light was the feature bystanders found most helpful in its testing.

The glasses are also designed to blur the faces of people around you before an image gets sent to Gemini. The microphones focus on your voice by default, not the conversations around you. There’s also a physical switch to turn the glasses off completely.

Google states what the camera sees isn’t used to train its AI models or to target ads, and it isn’t saved in your Gemini history. Data on the glasses is encrypted, and so is anything sent to your phone or the cloud. Third-party apps have to ask permission before they can use the camera, and you can revoke that access at any time.

The rules extend to the people wearing them. To use the glasses, you have to agree not to record people without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the light. Breaking those rules can get your glasses disabled. Setup also requires a Google account for someone 18 or older.

Google’s timing makes sense. Meta has been under pressure for months over how its glasses get used, including a letter from Senators Ron Wyden and Ed Markey asking about LED tampering and footage of people recorded without their consent. Google is clearly trying to get ahead of those questions before its glasses ship.

Samsung Intelligent Eyewear runs Android XR and opened for pre-order on November 12 through Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, with deliveries expected in mid-December. It releases first in the US and South Korea.

#255. Industry News: Mechatronics student builds 3D printer made from 92% LEGO for less than $180

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (532 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Industry News: Mechatronics student builds 3D printer made from 92% LEGO for less than $180

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO.
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers.
  • It has been revealed that turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.

It has been revealed that turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.

Turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.

In a recent development, there are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.
